quiz.question: The three pair-only club regions contain 7, 3 and 2 students; another 3 join all three. How many join exactly two clubs?
quiz.hint: Add the three pair-only regions.
quiz.explanation: 7 + 3 + 2 = 12. The all-three group is excluded.

quiz.question: The three pair-only club regions contain 7, 3 and 2 students; another 3 join all three. How many join at least two clubs?
quiz.hint: Include exactly two and all three.
quiz.explanation: 12 join exactly two and 3 join all three: 15 altogether.

lessons.takeaway: Exactly two excludes the centre; at least two includes it.
lessons.mistake: Adding the three club totals to count distinct people.

reference.name: Union
reference.note: In A or B or both.

reference.name: Intersection
reference.note: In both sets.

reference.name: Difference
reference.note: In A but not B. Irish exam papers write set difference with a backslash: A \ B.

reference.name: Complement
reference.note: Inside the universal set, outside A.

reference.name: Two-set counting
reference.formula: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
reference.note: The overlap was counted twice.

reference.name: Three-set counting
reference.note: The pair intersections include the triple overlap.

reference.name: Number families
reference.note: In Irish exams ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}: 0 is an integer but not a natural number.

toolkit.strategy: Translate every statement into a region or a whole set. Distinguish people from memberships. Fill fixed overlaps first, then use totals, ratios or equations; every region must be non-negative.

methods.title: Read membership, cardinality and subset symbols
methods.when: The question asks about members, sizes or relationships between sets.
methods.rule: a∈A is membership; B⊂A means every member of B is in A; n(A), written #A on exam papers, counts distinct elements.
steps: Identify whether the item is an element or a set.
Ignore order and repetition when counting a set.
Use the stated universal set for complements.
methods.check: List all members of a proposed subset and check each lies in A.
methods.trap: {0} has one element; ∅ has none.

methods.title: Locate number families
methods.when: A set contains natural, integer, rational or real numbers.
methods.rule: ℕ⊂ℤ⊂ℚ⊂ℝ; the irrationals ℝ\ℚ are in ℝ but not ℚ.
steps: Remember ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}: 0 is not a natural number.
Express rational numbers as integer fractions with non-zero denominators.
Use a counterexample to reject a reversed inclusion.
methods.example: −6∈ℤ and −6=−6/1∈ℚ, while √3∉ℚ.
methods.check: 1/2 is rational but not an integer, so ℚ is not a subset of ℤ.
methods.trap: Every integer is rational, but not every rational is an integer.

methods.title: Apply union, intersection, complement and their properties
methods.when: A statement uses “either”, “both”, “outside”, or regrouped set operations.
methods.rule: A∪B=B∪A; A∩B=B∩A; (A∪B)∪C=A∪(B∪C); (A∩B)∩C=A∩(B∩C). A′=U\A; n(A′)=n(U)−n(A).
steps: Translate union as either or both, and intersection as all named sets.
Work inside brackets first.
Use membership to verify that swapping or regrouping ∪ or ∩ preserves the result.
methods.check: Test each possible element against the two membership descriptions.
methods.trap: A union includes its overlap.

methods.title: Respect the direction of set difference
methods.when: The task asks for A but not B.
methods.rule: A\B=A∩B′; difference is neither generally commutative nor associative.
steps: Start with the first set.
Remove members that also lie in the second.
For nested differences, resolve brackets exactly as written.
methods.check: Element 3 distinguishes the two groupings.
methods.trap: Do not swap or regroup difference as if it were union.

methods.title: Fill three-set regions and inclusive intersections
methods.when: Three overlapping sets are described.
methods.rule: AB-only=n(A∩B)−n(A∩B∩C). n(A∪B∪C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)−n(A∩B)−n(A∩C)−n(B∩C)+n(A∩B∩C).
steps: Place the triple region.
Subtract it from each inclusive pair total.
Subtract all overlaps inside each circle from its whole-set total.
Add the seven regions for the union, then subtract from U for outside.
methods.example: If AB=11, triple=3, then AB-only=8; if A=25, AC-only=4, then A-only=25−8−4−3=10.
methods.check: Add the four regions in each set to recover its original total.
methods.trap: Writing the inclusive pair count in the pair-only region counts the centre again.

methods.title: Find an unknown region or total
methods.when: Regions contain x, or a whole-set/union count is missing.
methods.rule: Disjoint regions add without overlap; union = universal total − outside.
steps: Label each disjoint region once.
Choose a given total containing the unknown.
Form and solve the equation.
Check every region is a permissible count.
methods.example: Regions x, x+3 and 9 fill a universe of 30: 2 x+12=30 → x=9.
methods.check: The regions 9,12,9 add to 30.
methods.trap: Negative or non-integer people indicate an invalid interpretation or solution.

methods.title: Find feasible two-set bounds
methods.when: A set size, overlap or outside count is not fixed.
methods.rule: max(0,a+b−N)≤n(A∩B)≤min(a,b); n(A∪B)=a+b−overlap.
steps: Write the union identity.
Require each region, including outside, to be non-negative.
Translate these conditions into lower and upper bounds.
Show an arrangement attaining each claimed extreme.
methods.example: In U of 50 with n(A)=32 and n(B)=27, overlap lies from 9 to 27; outside lies from 0 to 18.
methods.check: At overlap 9 the union is 50; at overlap 27 the union is 32.
methods.trap: The maximum overlap cannot exceed the smaller set.

methods.title: Combine percentages, ratios and memberships
methods.when: A Venn problem gives a percentage, a region ratio or total memberships.
methods.rule: Membership total = E₁+2 E₂+3 E₃; union = E₁+E₂+E₃.
steps: Convert percentages using the stated base total.
Subtract known overlaps before dividing exclusive counts in a ratio.
Keep “exactly two” separate from “at least two”.
For memberships, count a person once per set joined.
methods.example: If 80 join at least one, 20 join both, and A-only:B-only=2:3, then the 60 single-only people split into 24 and 36.
methods.check: Set totals are 44 and 56; their sum 100 equals union 80 plus overlap 20.
methods.trap: A ratio of exclusive regions is not automatically a ratio of whole-set totals.

checks: Each person appears in exactly one disjoint Venn region.
Inclusive pair intersections include the triple intersection.
All region counts are non-negative and fit the universal total.
A total of memberships can exceed the number of distinct people.

challenges.title: Solve a three-club region equation
challenges.question: A survey contains 50 students. For clubs A, B and C, the disjoint regions are: A-only=x, B-only=x+2, C-only=5, AB-only=4, AC-only=3, BC-only=2, all three=1, none=7. (a) Find x. (b) Find n(A), n(B), n(C) and n(A∩B). (c) Find the number joining at least one club and the total number of club memberships. Explain why those two totals differ.
hints: All eight disjoint regions must total 50.
A whole-circle total includes its single region, two pair-only regions and the centre.

solution.title: Use the universal total
solution.reason: Disjoint regions may be added directly.

solution.title: Find the unknown
solution.reason: The A-only and B-only regions are 13 and 15.

solution.title: Recover whole-set totals
solution.reason: Each membership total includes every region inside that circle.

solution.title: Read the inclusive pair and union
solution.reason: The pair intersection includes the centre.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: The 9 people in exactly two clubs each add one extra membership, and the triple member adds two.

challenges.answer: x=13; n(A)=21, n(B)=22, n(C)=11; n(A∩B)=5; union 43 people, membership total 54.
challenges.check: Exactly one=33, exactly two=9, exactly three=1: 33+9+1=43 people, but 33+18+3=54 memberships.

challenges.title: Find the smallest and largest possible set
challenges.question: In a group of 80 students, 46 belong to A and 18 belong to neither A nor B. Write b=n(B). (a) Express n(A∩B) in terms of b. (b) Find the smallest and largest possible b, explaining how each can occur. (c) If 12 students belong to both, find all four disjoint region counts.
hints: The union is fixed even though B is not.
Use 0≤overlap≤46 after writing 46+b−overlap=62.

solution.title: Fix the union
solution.reason: Everyone except those in neither lies in the union.

solution.title: Express the overlap
solution.reason: The overlap is subtracted because it was counted twice.

solution.title: Apply feasibility
solution.reason: An overlap is non-negative and cannot exceed A.

solution.title: Show the extremes can occur
solution.math: b=16: B disjoint from A. b=62: B contains all of A and 16 further students.
solution.reason: A bound is sharp only if a valid arrangement attains it.

solution.title: Use the specified overlap
solution.math: t=12 → b=28; A-only=34, B-only=16, both=12, neither=18
solution.reason: Subtract the overlap from each whole-set total.

challenges.answer: Overlap=b−16; minimum b=16, maximum b=62. With overlap 12: A-only 34, B-only 16, both 12, neither 18.

challenges.title: Percentages and ratios in two clubs
challenges.question: Of 120 students, 25% join neither rugby nor music. Exactly 18 join both. The numbers in rugby-only and music-only are in the ratio 3:5. (a) Find all four regions. (b) Find each whole club total. (c) What percentage joins exactly one club? (d) Find the total memberships and explain how to check it.
hints: Remove neither, then remove the overlap before applying 3:5.
The exclusive total is split into eight equal ratio parts.

solution.title: Convert the percentage
solution.reason: The base for 25% is the entire surveyed group.

solution.title: Find the exclusive total
solution.reason: The overlap is not part of either single-only region.

solution.title: Apply the ratio
solution.reason: The ratio has 3+5 parts.

solution.title: Recover club totals and percentage
solution.reason: Whole-set totals include the 18 shared members.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: Each member in both is counted twice in the membership total.

challenges.answer: Rugby-only 27, music-only 45, both 18, neither 30; club totals 45 and 63; exactly one 60%; memberships 108.
challenges.check: 27+45+18+30=120 and 27:45=3:5; the membership identity gives 90+18=108.

challenges.title: Recover how many joined two or three
challenges.question: There are 100 students and three clubs. Ten students join none, 46 join exactly one, and the sum of the three whole-club totals is 142 memberships. (a) Find how many join exactly two clubs and all three clubs. (b) Decide whether the three individual club totals are uniquely determined. Support your answer by constructing two different valid arrangements.
hints: Let E₂ and E₃ be the exactly-two and triple counts. Count people once, then memberships by 1,2,3.
Use E₂+E₃=44 and 46+2 E₂+3 E₃=142.

solution.title: Count distinct people
solution.reason: Everyone in the union joins one, two or three clubs.

solution.title: Count memberships
solution.reason: Exactly-two people contribute two memberships each.

solution.title: Eliminate the double count
solution.math: 2 E₂+2 E₃=88; subtract to get E₃=8, then E₂=36
solution.reason: The two counting equations use the same underlying regions.

solution.title: Construct one valid arrangement
solution.math: Single-only (A,B,C)=(20,16,10); pair-only (AB,AC,BC)=(12,14,10); triple=8; none=10. Club totals=(54,46,42).
solution.reason: These exclusive counts satisfy all supplied totals.

solution.title: Construct a different arrangement
solution.math: Change single-only to (21,15,10), keeping all other regions. Club totals become (55,45,42).
solution.reason: The same aggregate information can support different individual club totals.

challenges.answer: Exactly two=36; all three=8. Individual club totals are not unique, as the two displayed arrangements demonstrate.
challenges.check: Both arrangements have 46+36+8+10=100 people and 46+2×36+3×8=142 memberships.

title: Applied Arithmetic
intro: Follow the money: identify the base amount, apply the stated rate, and check the units.

lessons.title: Use and reverse percentage multipliers
lessons.goal: Calculate a percentage change and recover an original amount.

steps.title: Name the base amount
steps.text: A classroom example uses an €80 price before VAT and an example VAT rate of 23%. The base is the pre-tax price.
steps.why: The percentage applies to the original amount.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Example rate: 23%</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = €98.40</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Example rate: 23%</text></svg>

steps.title: Combine the whole and the percentage into one multiplier
steps.text: The original is 100%, so the inclusive price is 123% of €80. Multiply once by 1.23.
steps.why: A multiplier combines the original and its increase.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>100% + 23% = 123%</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><rect id="block1" x="586.5853658536585" y="100" width="120.41463414634144" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="648.2926829268292" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">18.4</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="648.2926829268292" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">VAT</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = €98.40</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">100% + 23% = 123%</text></svg>

steps.title: Reverse with division
steps.text: To recover the original from €98.40, divide by 1.23. Do not remove 23% of the inclusive price.
steps.why: 23% of €98.40 is more than 23% of €80, so subtracting it from the inclusive price overshoots; dividing by 1.23 undoes the multiplication exactly.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Reverse: divide the whole €98.40 by 1.23</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="533.5853658536585" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="318.29268292682923" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="318.29268292682923" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">original</text><rect id="block1" x="586.5853658536585" y="100" width="120.41463414634144" height="130" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value1" x="648.2926829268292" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">18.4</text><text id="blocklabel1" x="648.2926829268292" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">VAT</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = €98.40</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Reverse: divide the whole €98.40 by 1.23</text></svg>

steps.title: Transfer the method to a discount
steps.text: For a 15% discount, retain 85%. A €60 item therefore costs €51.
steps.why: Decrease multipliers are one minus the decimal rate.

quiz.question: Using an example VAT rate of 20%, what is the inclusive price of an €80 item?
quiz.hint: 100% + 20% = 120%: write that as a decimal multiplier.

quiz.question: A price after a 10% discount is €72. What was the original?
quiz.hint: The sale price is 90% of the original.

lessons.takeaway: Write the multiplier before using the calculator.
lessons.mistake: Reversing a percentage by applying it to the wrong base.

lessons.title: Distinguish markup from profit margin
lessons.goal: Use the correct denominator for a profit percentage.

steps.title: Find the profit amount
steps.text: An item costs a shop €80 and sells for €100. Its profit before other expenses is €20.
steps.why: Profit is selling price minus cost price.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Selling price: €100</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="block0" x="50" y="100" width="525.0" height="130" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text id="value0" x="314.0" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">80</text><text id="blocklabel0" x="314.0" y="265" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">cost</text><line id="whole" x1="50" y1="83" x2="710" y2="83" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="total" x="380" y="60" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">Whole = 100</text><text id="label0" x="50" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Selling price: €100</text></svg>

steps.title: Measure markup against cost
steps.text: Markup asks how large the profit is compared with the €80 cost. Divide by 80.
steps.why: Cost is the denominator for markup.

steps.text: Profit margin asks how much of the €100 selling price is profit. Divide by 100.
steps.why: Selling price is the denominator for margin.

steps.title: Check which percentage the question names
steps.text: The same €20 profit gives different percentages because the bases differ. For loss percentage, compare the loss with cost.
steps.why: A percentage is a ratio; the denominator gives it meaning.

quiz.question: An item costs €60 and sells for €75. What is the markup?
quiz.hint: Use profit divided by cost.

quiz.question: An item costs €60 and sells for €75. What is the profit margin?
quiz.hint: Use profit divided by selling price.

lessons.takeaway: Markup uses cost; margin uses selling price.
lessons.mistake: Using the same denominator for both percentages.

quiz.question: A bill has a €12 fixed charge and 50 units at €0.30 each. Find the pre-tax subtotal.
quiz.hint: Calculate usage, then add the fixed charge.

quiz.question: A rate is 18 cents per unit. What is its euro value?
quiz.hint: There are 100 cents in one euro.

lessons.takeaway: Fixed charge + measured usage × unit rate; then apply the stated tax.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying the standing charge by usage.

lessons.title: Calculate net pay from supplied bands
lessons.goal: Apply each rate only to its band, then subtract the specified credits and deductions.

steps.title: Use the question’s classroom rates
steps.text: Assume annual pay of €40,000. In this invented example, the first €30,000 (the standard rate cut-off point) is taxed at 20% and the remaining €10,000 at 40%.
steps.why: Band rates apply to separate slices, not the whole income.

steps.title: Apply tax credits
steps.text: The example tax credit is €2,000. Subtract it from the gross income tax, giving €8,000 net income tax (the tax payable).
steps.why: Credits reduce tax due; they are not subtracted from income before calculating the bands.

steps.text: For this exercise only, USC is 1% of the first €10,000 plus 3% of the remainder, giving €1,000. PRSI is an example flat 4%, giving €1,600.
steps.why: Calculate each deduction using its own stated rules; these are not current statutory rates.

steps.text: Subtract all deductions from gross pay. Keep every figure annual until the annual result is finished.
steps.why: Mixing weekly deductions with annual income gives an invalid result.

quiz.question: In an invented tax system, the first €20,000 is taxed at 10% and the next €5,000 at 20%. What is gross tax on €25,000?
quiz.hint: Apply each rate only to its slice.

quiz.question: Gross income tax is €3,000 and the supplied credit is €800. What is net income tax?
quiz.hint: A credit reduces tax due.

lessons.takeaway: Slice income into bands; subtract credits from tax; deduct each other charge separately.
lessons.mistake: Using example classroom rates as current tax rules, or taxing all income at the highest rate.

lessons.title: Choose the direction of currency conversion
lessons.goal: Use units to decide whether to multiply or divide by an exchange rate.

steps.title: Read the rate as a statement
steps.text: Suppose the example rate is €1 = £0.85. One euro buys 0.85 pounds.
steps.why: An exchange rate has a direction and units.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the rate as a statement</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">€1 → £0.85</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Read the rate as a statement</text></svg>

steps.title: Convert euro to pounds
steps.text: Multiply the number of euro by the number of pounds per euro. €240 becomes £204.
steps.why: The euro unit cancels, leaving pounds.

steps.title: Reverse the conversion
steps.text: To convert £170 to euro, divide by 0.85. This gives €200.
steps.why: You are asking how many groups of £0.85 make £170.

quiz.question: At the example rate €1 = $1.10, how many dollars are €50?
quiz.hint: Multiply euro by dollars per euro.

quiz.question: At €1 = £0.80, how many euro are £64?
quiz.hint: Use the reverse operation.

lessons.takeaway: Write the currency units beside the rate to reveal the operation.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by the same rate in both directions.

quiz.question: €500 grows by 10% per year for two years. What is the final balance?
quiz.hint: Apply 1.10 twice.

quiz.question: Why is the second year’s interest larger at a fixed positive compound rate?
options: Interest is earned on the updated balance
quiz.hint: What is the base for the next percentage?
quiz.explanation: The next period earns interest on the principal plus earlier interest.

lessons.takeaway: Compound means multiply the updated amount again.
lessons.mistake: Using simple-interest addition when the question specifies compound growth.

lessons.title: Reverse growth and model depreciation
lessons.goal: Recover a starting value or rate and use a decreasing multiplier.

steps.title: Recover the original principal
steps.text: If a balance reaches €1,323 after two years at 5%, divide by the complete growth factor.
steps.why: Undo every period of multiplication, not just one.

steps.title: Recover a repeated rate
steps.text: A value grows from €1,200 to €1,323 over two equal-rate periods. Divide final by initial, then take the square root: the multiplier 1.05 means the rate is 5%.
steps.why: The square root undoes two repeated equal multiplications.

steps.title: Use a reduction multiplier
steps.text: An €800 device loses 10% of its current value each year. It retains 90%, so multiply by 0.90 each year.
steps.why: A percentage loss is applied to the reducing value.

steps.text: After three years the model gives €583.20. The total loss is €216.80, not three identical €80 losses.

quiz.question: An item is worth €810 after two years of 10% annual depreciation. What was its initial value?
quiz.hint: Two years of keeping 90% give one combined multiplier; undo that multiplier.

quiz.question: A value increases from €100 to €121 in two years at a fixed annual compound rate. Find the rate.
quiz.hint: Take the square root of 121/100.
quiz.explanation: The yearly multiplier is √1.21 = 1.1, giving 10%.

lessons.takeaway: Reverse the entire multiplier; depreciation retains a fraction of the current value.
lessons.mistake: Subtracting a fixed annual loss for a percentage depreciation model.

reference.name: Percentage
reference.note: Identify the base amount before applying a rate.

reference.name: Increase or decrease
reference.note: Use plus for increase and minus for decrease.

reference.name: Reverse a percentage
reference.note: Do not subtract the percentage of the final amount.

reference.name: Markup and margin
reference.note: The denominator changes.

reference.name: Compound growth
reference.note: Fixed rate r per period, n matching periods. The Formulae and Tables booklet writes this as F = P(1 + i)ᵗ with i = r/100.

reference.name: Depreciation
reference.note: A fixed percentage of the reducing value (the reducing-balance method).

reference.name: Income-tax calculation
reference.formula: Net income tax = max(0, gross income tax − credits)
reference.note: Use the rates, bands, credits and deductions given in the question.

toolkit.strategy: Draw the order of events first. Identify the base for every percentage, the currency and time period, then use one multiplier for each stage. All rates in these worked examples are invented classroom figures, not current financial rules.

methods.title: Percentages, VAT and reverse prices
methods.when: A price changes by a stated percentage.
methods.rule: New=old(1±r/100); old=new/(1±r/100), with a non-zero multiplier.
steps: Name the original base.
Convert the rate to a decimal multiplier.
Multiply forwards or divide backwards.
Round the final money result, not every intermediate expression.
methods.example: An invented 12% tax turns €75 into €84; reversing gives 84/1.12=€75.
methods.trap: Subtracting 12% of €84 would use the wrong base.

methods.title: Profit, loss, markup and margin
methods.when: A question compares buying and selling prices.
methods.rule: Profit=S−C; markup%=profit/C×100; margin%=profit/S×100; loss%=loss/C×100.
steps: Find the euro profit or loss first.
Choose the denominator named by the question.
For a reverse problem, write S=C(1+markup rate) or C=S(1−margin rate).
methods.example: Cost €120 and sales €150 give profit €30, markup 25% and margin 20%.
methods.trap: Markup and margin are not interchangeable.

methods.title: Tiered bills and fixed charges
methods.when: Usage is charged at different rates across bands.
methods.rule: Subtotal=fixed charge+Σ(units in each band × band rate).
steps: Split the usage at every threshold.
Charge each slice once.
Add fixed charges.
Apply any stated tax to its stated subtotal, then check the units.
methods.example: Invented bill: fixed €12; first 100 units at €0.20, next units at €0.30. For 160 units: 12+20+18=€50 before tax.
methods.check: The band quantities 100+60 recover all 160 units.
methods.trap: The higher rate applies only to units above the threshold, unless the question says otherwise.

methods.title: Gross pay, overtime and tiered commission
methods.when: Pay contains basic earnings plus differently priced hours or sales.
methods.rule: Gross pay=basic+overtime+commission; each band uses only its own quantity.
steps: Separate guaranteed pay from variable pay.
Apply overtime or commission rates to the correct bands.
Add the pay components before deductions.
For an unknown sales amount, first identify the relevant band.
methods.example: Invented weekly pay €400 plus 3% of first €2,000 sales and 5% above: sales €2,600 give 400+60+30=€490.
methods.check: The €90 commission is 3% of €2,000 plus 5% of €600.
methods.trap: Do not apply the highest commission rate to all sales.

methods.title: Income bands, credits, USC and PRSI structure
methods.when: The question supplies taxes, credits and other deductions.
methods.rule: Gross tax=Σ(band income×rate); net income tax=max(0,gross tax−credits); net pay=gross pay−all deductions.
steps: Keep all amounts in the same period.
Calculate income tax band by band.
Subtract tax credits from tax, not from income.
Calculate each other deduction under its own supplied rule and subtract it.
methods.example: Invented €30,000 annual pay: first €20,000 at 10%, rest at 20% gives gross tax €4,000; credit €700 gives net income tax €3,300 before any separately stated deductions.
methods.check: 20,000+10,000=30,000; gross tax − net tax equals the credit used.
methods.trap: USC and PRSI are separate calculations; do not assume they share income-tax bands or credits.

methods.title: Recover gross pay or a tax credit
methods.when: Net pay or tax paid is known, but gross income or a credit is missing.
methods.rule: Within one tax band, write net pay as an expression in gross pay G and solve. If some tax is actually paid, credit=gross tax−net income tax. If the tax bill is zero, the credit could be anything at least as large as the gross tax, so it cannot be found exactly.
steps: Express each deduction using the unknown.
Use the appropriate bands and any fixed deductions.
Solve the net-pay equation.
Check the solution lies in the band used. If payable income tax is zero, only a lower bound on an unknown credit may be recoverable.
methods.example: Invented flat tax 20%, credit €30 and other deduction €10: N=G−(0.2 G−30)−10=0.8 G+20. If N=500, G=600.
methods.trap: A reverse formula may cross a band or zero-tax floor. Credits exceeding gross tax cannot be uniquely recovered from a zero tax bill alone.

methods.title: Currency conversion and fees
methods.when: A rate is quoted in one currency per unit of another.
methods.rule: If €1=£r, pounds=euro×r and euro=pounds/r, r>0.
steps: Write the currency direction beside the rate.
Apply a fee in its stated currency and at its stated stage.
Multiply in the quoted direction; divide in reverse.
methods.example: With an invented €1=£0.80 and a €4 fee before exchange, €104 yields (104−4)×0.80=£80.
methods.check: £80/0.80=€100; adding the €4 fee restores €104.
methods.trap: The fee cannot be moved to the other currency without conversion.

methods.title: Compound growth or depreciation
methods.when: A fixed percentage applies repeatedly to the current amount.
methods.rule: A=P(1+r/100)ⁿ; depreciation A=P(1−r/100)ⁿ, using matching periods.
steps: Choose the retained multiplier.
Apply it once for each period.
Distinguish final balance from total interest or total loss.
methods.example: €900 losing an invented 20% a year for two years becomes 900×0.8²=€576; loss=€324.
methods.check: The successive values are 900,720,576.
methods.trap: Percentage depreciation is not a fixed euro deduction each year.

methods.title: Changing rates and intermediate transactions
methods.when: Rates differ by year or money is deposited or withdrawn between years.
methods.rule: A=(P m₁−W+D)m₂ for a withdrawal W and deposit D after period 1.
steps: Draw a timeline with the transaction between the correct periods.
Update the balance by the first multiplier.
Apply the cash transaction.
Apply the next multiplier to the new balance.
methods.example: €1,000 grows 4%, then €100 is withdrawn, then it grows 5%: (1000×1.04−100)×1.05=€987.
methods.check: Without the withdrawal the final amount is €1,092; the withdrawal reduces it by 100×1.05=€105.
methods.trap: Adding different annual rates loses the compounding effect.

methods.title: Reverse a principal or a repeated rate
methods.when: The final amount is given.
methods.rule: P=A/(m₁m₂…); for n equal periods, m=(A/P)^(1/n). Growth r%=100(m−1); depreciation r%=100(1−m).
steps: Undo later transactions and multipliers in reverse order.
If the same unknown rate repeats, divide final by initial and take the matching root.
Convert the multiplier into a percentage increase or decrease.
methods.example: An item worth €1,152 after two 20% falls began at 1152/0.8²=€1,800.
methods.trap: Subtracting the overall loss percentage from the final value does not recover the original.

methods.title: Tax deducted from interest
methods.when: A tax (called DIRT in Ireland) is charged on interest, rather than the whole balance.
methods.rule: Net interest=P×r×(1−t), when r and t are decimal interest and interest-tax rates.
steps: Calculate gross interest on the current principal.
Apply interest tax to that interest only.
Add the retained interest to the balance.
For an unknown rate, divide the net increase by P(1−t).
methods.example: Invented principal €2,000, gross rate 4%, tax on interest 25%: gross interest €80, tax €20, closing balance €2,060.
methods.trap: Do not deduct interest tax from the principal or subtract its rate directly from the interest rate.

checks: Each percentage uses its stated base amount.
Every fee, withdrawal and tax occurs in the stated order.
Rates and periods match, and all amounts use consistent units.
Exact intermediate values are retained until the final money rounding.
A reverse calculation has been checked by running the original sequence forwards.

challenges.title: A withdrawal between two different rates
challenges.question: Use these invented classroom rates and assume no tax or fees. €1,500 earns 4% in year 1. Immediately afterwards €200 is withdrawn. The remaining money earns 5% in year 2. (a) Find the balance after each event. (b) Find the total interest earned over the two years. (c) How much lower is the final balance than if no withdrawal had been made? Explain why the difference is not just €200.
hints: Write a four-point timeline: start, first growth, withdrawal, second growth.
Total interest equals final balance plus the withdrawal minus the initial deposit.

solution.title: Apply the first rate
solution.reason: The first year earns €60 interest.

solution.title: Make the transaction at the stated time
solution.reason: Only the remaining balance earns year-2 interest.

solution.title: Apply the second rate
solution.reason: The second year earns €68.

solution.title: Find total interest
solution.reason: The withdrawn money is still part of the total value received.

solution.title: Compare with no withdrawal
solution.reason: The €200 withdrawn also misses €10 of second-year interest.

challenges.answer: After year 1 €1,560; after withdrawal €1,360; final €1,428; interest €128; final-balance difference €210.
challenges.check: The separate interest amounts €60+€68 equal €128; the withdrawal effect is 200×1.05=€210.

challenges.title: Reverse two different depreciations
challenges.question: A device loses 20% of its value in year 1 and 15% of its then-current value in year 2. Its value afterwards is €1,360. Treat these as invented classroom rates. (a) Find the original value. (b) Find each year’s euro loss. (c) Find the overall percentage loss and explain why adding 20% and 15% is wrong.
hints: The retained fractions are 0.80 and 0.85.
Work backwards from €1,360, or divide by their product.

solution.title: Form the full retained multiplier
solution.reason: The second rate applies to the reduced value.

solution.title: Recover the original
solution.reason: Division reverses the two multiplicative stages.

solution.title: Calculate each loss
solution.reason: The bases are €2,000 and €1,600 respectively.

solution.title: Find the combined rate
solution.reason: The same result follows from 1−0.68.

solution.title: Explain the non-additivity
solution.reason: Adding rates incorrectly treats both losses as percentages of the original value.

challenges.answer: Original €2,000; losses €400 and €240; overall loss 32%.
challenges.check: Forward calculation gives 2000×0.80×0.85=1360 exactly.

challenges.title: Find an interest rate after interest tax
challenges.question: Use invented classroom figures. A €2,000 balance earns gross interest of 5% in year 1. Tax of 20% is deducted from the interest only. In year 2 the gross interest rate changes to r%, and the same 20% interest tax applies. With no deposits or withdrawals, the final balance is €2,184. (a) Find the year-1 closing balance. (b) Find the year-2 gross interest and r. (c) Find the total interest tax deducted over both years.
hints: Year-1 net interest is 80% of its gross interest.
In year 2, divide the observed net increase by 0.80 before finding the rate on the year-1 closing balance.

solution.title: Calculate year-1 interest and tax
solution.reason: Interest tax applies to the interest, not to €2,000.

solution.title: Find the next principal
solution.reason: The retained interest becomes part of the next base.

solution.title: Reverse the year-2 tax
solution.reason: €104 is 80% of the gross interest.

solution.title: Find the unknown rate
solution.reason: The year-2 base is €2,080.

solution.title: Add the tax amounts
solution.reason: Each year’s tax is based on that year’s gross interest.

challenges.answer: Year-1 closing balance €2,080; year-2 gross interest €130; r=6.25%; total tax €46.
challenges.check: 2080×(1+0.0625×0.80)=2184; total gross interest €230 minus tax €46 gives net growth €184.

challenges.title: Recover sales from net pay
challenges.question: Use this invented weekly pay system. Basic pay is €500. Commission is 3% of the first €4,000 sales and 5% of sales above €4,000. Income tax is 20% of gross pay minus a €40 credit; a separate fixed deduction is €20. Net pay is €540. (a) Find gross pay. (b) Find the commission. (c) Find the sales amount, checking which commission band applies. (d) Verify the net pay from the recovered sales.
hints: Let G be gross pay and write the deductions before solving.
Net=G−(0.20 G−40)−20. The first commission band can contribute at most €120.

solution.title: Write the net-pay equation
solution.reason: The credit reduces income tax, while the separate deduction remains.

solution.title: Recover gross pay
solution.reason: The stated equation is valid because the resulting tax is positive.

solution.title: Recover commission
solution.reason: Basic pay accounts for €500 of gross pay.

solution.title: Locate the correct commission band
solution.reason: €150 exceeds the first-band maximum, so sales exceed €4,000.

solution.title: Recover and verify sales
solution.reason: Both the band choice and original net-pay condition are satisfied.

challenges.answer: Gross €650; commission €150; sales €4,600; tax €90 and other deduction €20 give net €540.
challenges.check: Forward commission is 0.03×4000+0.05×600=150, and every later deduction reproduces €540.

title: Statistics 1 — Collecting data
intro: Ask a fair question, collect useful evidence and recognise what your sample cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Ask a question that data can answer
lessons.goal: Define the population, variable and data type before collecting.

steps.title: Expect different answers
steps.text: Ask how many minutes students in this year group spend travelling to school. Students will have different travel times.
steps.why: A statistical question anticipates variability.
steps.math: Population: all students in the year

steps.title: Define exactly what to measure
steps.text: Choose a typical school morning and specify travel time from leaving home to arriving at school. Record minutes.
steps.why: A clear definition makes answers comparable.
steps.math: Variable: morning journey time, in minutes

steps.text: Travel time is numerical continuous data. Number of siblings is numerical discrete; travel method is categorical.
steps.why: Measurements can take intermediate values, whereas counts use whole-number steps.
steps.math: Time: continuous; siblings: discrete; method: categorical

steps.text: Ask “How many minutes did your journey take?” rather than suggesting it was too long. Provide sensible response options when needed.
steps.why: Leading wording can change the answers you collect.

quiz.question: Which is a statistical question?
options: How many pets do students in this class have?
How many sides has a triangle?
quiz.hint: Expect variation across a group.
quiz.explanation: Students may have different numbers of pets, so data are needed to describe the group.

quiz.question: Which variable is numerical continuous?
quiz.hint: Think measurement rather than count.
quiz.explanation: Height can take intermediate measured values. Tries and players are discrete counts.

lessons.takeaway: Name the population, define the variable, specify units, avoid leading language.
lessons.mistake: Confusing a question with one fixed answer with a statistical investigation.

lessons.title: Collect and organise reliable data
lessons.goal: Distinguish sources and build a frequency table without losing observations.

steps.title: Identify the source
steps.text: Recording your own class survey gives primary data. Using a published survey gives secondary data.
steps.why: The distinction concerns who originally collected the observations.

steps.why: Reliability and relevance are different checks.

quiz.question: You use a report published by a sports organisation. What kind of data source is this for you?
quiz.hint: You did not collect the original observations.
quiz.explanation: It is a secondary source; its quality still needs to be assessed.

quiz.question: For 2,1,2,3,2,1, what is the frequency of 2?
quiz.hint: Count appearances of the value 2.
quiz.explanation: The value 2 appears three times.

lessons.takeaway: A frequency table must preserve the total number of observations.
lessons.mistake: Assuming a secondary source is either automatically trustworthy or automatically poor.

lessons.title: Choose a sample fairly
lessons.goal: Recognise selection bias and the limits of sample-based conclusions.

steps.title: Name the target population
steps.text: To study all students’ sports preferences, the population is all students in the school. A sample is the smaller group actually surveyed.
steps.why: Your conclusion should refer to the population you intended to study.

steps.why: Sampling error and selection bias are different problems.

quiz.question: Which sample best supports a claim about the whole school?
options: Students randomly selected across all year groups
quiz.hint: Who has a fair chance of being included?
quiz.explanation: Random selection across year groups is more representative than the other convenience samples.

quiz.question: Why might 5,000 votes on a fan-page poll still be misleading?
quiz.hint: A large number does not repair who was selected.
quiz.explanation: Fans and keen volunteers may differ from the intended population.

lessons.takeaway: Ask who was included, who was missed and how people were selected.
lessons.mistake: Claiming that a large sample must be unbiased.

reference.name: Statistical question
reference.note: Name the population and the quantity being measured.

reference.name: Data types
reference.note: Categories describe groups; discrete values count; continuous values measure.

reference.name: Frequency
reference.note: Frequencies should add to the number of observations.

reference.name: Sources
reference.formula: Primary: collect it yourself; secondary: already collected
reference.note: Judge both relevance and reliability.

reference.name: Sampling
reference.formula: Representative selection matters as well as sample size
reference.note: A larger biased sample can still be misleading.

toolkit.strategy: Before calculating, ask what population, variable and sampling method produced the data. A useful answer explains both the numbers and the limits of the conclusion.

methods.title: Define an investigation and data type
methods.when: You must write a question or classify its answers.
methods.rule: Population=target group; variable=recorded characteristic. Categorical data are labels; numerical discrete data are counts; numerical continuous data are measurements.
steps: Name the target population.
Specify one variable and any measurement unit.
Distinguish counts, measurements and categories.
Fix a time period or other ambiguous wording.
methods.example: “How many minutes did your journey to school take this morning?” measures continuous numerical data for the surveyed students.
methods.check: Two readers should know the same start, finish and units.
methods.trap: Rounding a measured time to minutes does not make time itself a count variable.

methods.title: Critique and repair questionnaire wording
methods.when: A questionnaire may steer answers or combine questions.
methods.rule: Use neutral wording, one idea at a time, and a precise reference period.
steps: Underline judgemental or leading words.
Separate double questions.
Replace vague words with a defined measure or category.
Write the improved question, not just a criticism.
methods.example: Replace “Don’t you agree that the bus is too slow?” with “How many minutes did your bus journey to school take this morning?”
methods.check: The rewritten question allows short and long journeys without favouring either.
methods.trap: A friendly tone does not automatically make a question unbiased.

methods.title: Make response options exhaustive and exclusive
methods.when: Answers are grouped into intervals or categories.
methods.rule: Each permitted response should fit exactly one option.
steps: Test boundary values against adjacent options.
Use consistent non-overlapping interval notation.
Include the largest possible values or an open-ended last group.
Include “other” or an appropriate non-applicable option when needed.
methods.example: For non-negative time t: 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20, 20≤t<30, t≥30.
methods.check: Exactly 10 minutes belongs only to the second group; 65 minutes still has a group.
methods.trap: “0–10, 10–20, 20–30” leaves boundary ownership unclear unless a note fixes it; exam papers often add “10–20 means 10 or more but less than 20”.

methods.title: Turn raw data into frequencies and percentages
methods.when: A list of observations must be summarised.
methods.rule: Relative frequency=f/N; percentage=100 f/N, with N the number of observations.
steps: List all values or valid categories.
Tally each observation once.
Add frequencies to verify N.
Calculate the requested percentage using the correct combined frequency.
methods.example: Data 0,1,1,2,2,2 have frequencies 1,2,3. At least one occurs 5 times, so its percentage is 500/6%=83⅓%.
methods.check: Frequencies sum to 6; exact category percentages sum to 100%.
methods.trap: The denominator is the observation count, not the number of distinct categories.

methods.title: Compare sources and samples
methods.when: You must decide whether results support a population claim.
methods.rule: Primary data are collected for your investigation; secondary data were already collected. Representativeness depends on selection, not simply sample size.
steps: Name who could enter each sample and who was missed.
Identify who was convenient to ask, who volunteered and who was left out.
Compare the method with the intended population.
Give a cautious conclusion; random selection reduces selection bias but does not remove uncertainty.
methods.example: A random sample across year groups better represents a whole school than a larger poll of the rugby team.
methods.check: Ask whether every relevant student had a fair route into the sample.
methods.trap: A large sample can precisely describe the wrong group.

methods.title: Allocate a proportional sample
methods.when: The population contains known groups of different sizes.
methods.rule: Group sample size = total sample size × group population / total population.
steps: Calculate each group’s share of the population.
Allocate the requested sample in those proportions.
Check the allocations add to the total sample.
Select randomly within each group rather than taking volunteers only.
methods.example: Groups of 60,90,150 in a population of 300 receive 6,9,15 places in a sample of 30.
methods.check: 6+9+15=30, and each group supplies 10% of its members.
methods.trap: Correct quotas do not cure biased selection within each group.

checks: The question is neutral, clear and about one variable.
Response options do not overlap and cover every permitted response.
Frequencies match the number of observations; percentages use that count.
The conclusion names the population and acknowledges sampling limitations.

challenges.title: Repair a journey-time questionnaire
challenges.question: A survey asks: “How many minutes do you waste on your journey to school?” Its choices are “0–20”, “20–40” and “40–60”. (a) Identify three distinct weaknesses. (b) Rewrite the question neutrally for this morning’s journey. (c) Give a complete set of non-overlapping numerical options for any non-negative journey time. (d) Classify the data type.
hints: Consider the tone, exactly 20 or 40 minutes, and journeys longer than an hour.
Use half-open intervals and an open-ended last interval.

solution.title: Identify the wording problem
solution.math: “Waste” suggests a negative judgement about travel time.
solution.reason: Leading language may influence how a respondent interprets or reports an answer.

solution.title: Check boundaries and coverage
solution.math: 20 and 40 have ambiguous groups; times over 60 have no group.
solution.reason: Options should be exclusive and collectively cover the allowed responses.

solution.title: Rewrite the question
solution.math: “How many minutes did your journey from home to school take this morning?”
solution.reason: This specifies a neutral measure, endpoints and time period.

solution.title: Rewrite the options
solution.math: 0≤t<20; 20≤t<40; 40≤t<60; t≥60. If needed, add “I did not make this journey today.”
solution.reason: Every non-negative measured time has exactly one numerical group; non-applicable responses remain separate.

solution.title: Classify the variable
solution.reason: Time is measured and can take intermediate values.

challenges.answer: Weaknesses: leading word, ambiguous boundaries, missing long journeys. The displayed neutral question and four half-open/open-ended intervals repair them; time is continuous numerical data.
challenges.check: Test 0,20,40,60 and 75 minutes: each falls into exactly one interval. A non-traveller is not forced to invent a time.

challenges.title: From pet counts to an honest conclusion
challenges.question: Twelve volunteers report these pet counts: 0,1,2,2,0,3,1,2,4,1,0,2. (a) Make a frequency table for 0 through 4 pets. (b) Give each category percentage, retaining exact fractions where helpful. (c) Find the percentage with at least two pets. (d) Explain why the result alone does not establish that same percentage for the entire school.
hints: Tally each entry once and verify a total of twelve.
For “at least two”, combine the frequencies of 2, 3 and 4 before dividing.

solution.title: Count each category
solution.reason: Each of the twelve observations enters one row.

solution.title: Convert to percentages
solution.reason: Divide each frequency by 12 and multiply by 100.

solution.title: Combine the requested categories
solution.reason: The event includes all counts of 2 or more.

solution.title: State the population limit
solution.math: 50% describes these twelve volunteers; a school-wide claim needs a suitable sampling method
solution.reason: Volunteers may differ from other students, and twelve observations still leave sampling uncertainty.

challenges.answer: Frequencies 3,3,4,1,1; percentages 25,25,33⅓,8⅓,8⅓; at least two pets 50%; a whole-school conclusion is unsupported by this sample alone.
challenges.check: The frequencies sum to 12 and exact percentages sum to 100%; six listed observations have at least two pets.

challenges.title: Build a better school sample
challenges.question: A school has year-group populations 120,200,180 and 300. A poll of 50 sports-team members finds 40 favour more sports time. A random sample of 80 students across the school finds 46 favour it. (a) Find both percentages. (b) Explain which sampling approach better supports a whole-school claim and why. (c) Allocate a new sample of 80 proportionally across the four year groups and describe how students should be chosen within each group. (d) Does this guarantee the exact school percentage?
hints: The school population is 800, so an 80-person proportional sample uses one tenth of each group.
Separate the source of bias from ordinary sample-to-sample variation.

solution.title: Calculate the observed percentages
solution.reason: Use each poll’s own number of respondents.

solution.title: Evaluate selection
solution.math: The school-wide random approach is better aligned to the target population
solution.reason: Sports-team membership is related to the preference being measured and excludes other students.

solution.title: Allocate proportionally
solution.reason: Each group supplies 10% of its population.

solution.title: Specify a fair procedure
solution.math: Use a random selection from each complete year-group list
solution.reason: Taking only willing friends within the quotas would reintroduce selection bias.

solution.title: Limit the claim
solution.math: The result remains an estimate, not a guarantee
solution.reason: A fair sample can still differ from the whole population by chance.

challenges.answer: 80% and 57.5%; the random school sample is better aligned. Proportional allocations:12,20,18,30, with random selection within groups. No exact percentage is guaranteed.
challenges.check: 12+20+18+30=80; each allocation divided by its population is 0.10. The claim concerns the whole school, not just sports-team members.

challenges.title: Compare a large voluntary poll with a small random sample
challenges.question: A school of 1,000 students posts an optional travel poll online. Of 300 respondents, 210 report travelling by bus. A separate random sample of 40 students reports bus 18, walking 10, cycling 6 and car 6. (a) Calculate the online bus percentage and the random sample’s four category percentages. (b) Find the difference between the two bus percentages in percentage points. (c) Assess the claim “Exactly 70% of the school travel by bus.” (d) Explain why the larger response count does not settle which estimate is better.
hints: Voluntary response affects who is represented; it is a different issue from sample size.
Use 40 as the denominator for the second set of category percentages.

solution.title: Summarise the online respondents
solution.reason: This percentage describes respondents to the optional online poll.

solution.title: Summarise the random sample
solution.reason: The counts total 40 and each is divided by 40.

solution.title: Compare the bus results
solution.reason: A difference between percentages is stated in percentage points.

solution.title: Assess the exact claim
solution.math: The claim about exactly 70% of all 1,000 students is not established
solution.reason: The optional poll counts only those who chose to answer, so it may be biased; neither sample is a count of every one of the 1,000 students.

solution.title: Compare the methods
solution.math: The random sample gives a better route to representation, although it is smaller and has sampling variability
solution.reason: More responses do not remove a systematic selection difference.

challenges.answer: Online bus 70%; random sample 45%,25%,15%,15%; difference 25 percentage points. The exact whole-school claim is unsupported.
challenges.check: The random-sample percentages sum to 100%. Distinguishing the 300 respondents from all 1,000 students prevents an unjustified change of population.

title: Perimeter — Area — Volume
intro: Choose the correct measurement: around a shape, inside a face, or filling a solid.

lessons.title: Separate perimeter from area
lessons.goal: Find missing lengths and distinguish boundary from interior.

steps.title: Choose what is being measured
steps.text: An 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle has perimeter 26 cm and area 40 square centimetres. These measure different things.
steps.why: Perimeter adds boundary lengths; area counts square units inside.

steps.title: Split a compound shape
steps.text: Remove a 3 cm by 2 cm corner rectangle. Subtract its area from the large rectangle.
steps.why: Non-overlapping areas can be added or subtracted.

steps.title: Trace the new boundary
steps.text: Cutting the notch from this corner removes 3 cm and 2 cm of outer edge but adds inner edges of 3 cm and 2 cm. The perimeter remains 26 cm.
steps.why: Removing area need not shorten the boundary: the notch adds as much edge as it takes away.

steps.text: One metre is 100 centimetres, so one square metre is a 100 cm by 100 cm square containing 100 × 100 = 10,000 square centimetres. Convert lengths before calculating when possible.
steps.why: Area has two dimensions, so its conversion factor is squared.

quiz.question: Find the area of a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
quiz.hint: Multiply length by width and use square units.

quiz.question: Convert 2 m² to cm².
quiz.hint: Square the length conversion factor 100.

lessons.takeaway: Around means perimeter; inside means area.
lessons.mistake: Using the same conversion factor for lengths and areas.

lessons.title: See why a parallelogram has area base times height
lessons.goal: Use perpendicular height, not the sloping side.

steps.title: Identify base and height
steps.text: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. The sloping side is not the height.
steps.why: Height measures the perpendicular distance between parallel bases.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,100 610,100 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="120,290 240,290 240,100" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="100" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="205" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="300" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Cut a corner triangle
steps.text: Imagine cutting the triangular piece from one side along a perpendicular line. The rest keeps its area.
steps.why: Cutting and rearranging without stretching preserves area.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,100 610,100 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="120,290 240,290 240,100" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="100" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="205" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="300" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Slide it to the other side
steps.text: Move that triangle into the gap on the other side. The pieces now form a rectangle with the same base and height.
steps.why: The rearranged pieces cover exactly the same area; nothing is stretched or lost.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,100 610,100 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="490,290 610,290 610,100" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="100" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="205" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="425" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text><line id="move" x1="290" y1="60" x2="560" y2="60" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="move-label" x="425" y="43" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">slide the cut piece</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate and transfer
steps.text: The area is 36 square centimetres. A triangle with the same base and height is half this area.
steps.why: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two equal-area triangles.
steps.math: A = bh = 36 cm²; triangle area = 18 cm²
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Cut and translate a triangle to turn the parallelogram into a rectangle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="remaining" points="240,100 610,100 490,290 240,290" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="cutpiece" points="490,290 610,290 610,100" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="height" x1="240" y1="100" x2="240" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><text id="height-label" x="205" y="200" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><text id="base-label" x="425" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text><text id="area" x="380" y="380" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">Same area: 9 × 4 = 36 cm²</text></svg>

quiz.question: A parallelogram has base 12 cm, perpendicular height 5 cm and sloping side 7 cm. Find its area.
quiz.hint: Use the perpendicular height.

quiz.question: A triangle has base 10 cm and perpendicular height 6 cm. Find its area.
quiz.hint: A triangle is half a matching parallelogram.

lessons.takeaway: Area uses perpendicular height.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by a sloping side because it looks like a height.

lessons.title: Circles, sectors and curved boundaries
lessons.goal: Choose radius or diameter correctly and take the required fraction of a circle.

steps.title: Identify radius and diameter
steps.text: A circle has radius 6 cm, so its diameter is 12 cm. Use the radius, not the diameter, in the area formula.
steps.why: Diameter passes through the centre and is twice the radius.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text></svg>

steps.title: Find a whole circle’s measures
steps.text: The circumference is 12π cm and the area is 36π square centimetres. Leave π exact unless a decimal is requested.
steps.why: One formula measures the boundary; the other measures the interior.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text></svg>

steps.title: Take the sector fraction
steps.text: A 90-degree sector is one quarter of a full turn. Its arc is 3π cm and its area is 9π square centimetres.
steps.why: Divide the angle by 360 degrees to find the fraction of the circle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text><path id="sector" d="M300 190 L415 190 A115 115 0 0 0 300 75 Z" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Add straight edges when finding perimeter
steps.text: The sector’s boundary contains the curved arc and two radii. Its perimeter is 3π + 12 cm.
steps.why: Arc length alone is not sector perimeter.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><circle id="circle" cx="300" cy="190" r="115" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="300" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="r" x="350" y="177" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">r</text><line id="diameter" x1="185" y1="190" x2="415" y2="190" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="diam" x="300" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">d = 2r</text><path id="sector" d="M300 190 L415 190 A115 115 0 0 0 300 75 Z" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="quarter" x="515" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">90° = ¼ turn</text></svg>

quiz.question: A circle has diameter 10 cm. What is its area?
quiz.hint: Halve the diameter before squaring.
quiz.explanation: r = 5, so area = π × 5² = 25π cm².

quiz.question: What fraction of a circle is a 120° sector?
quiz.hint: Divide the central angle by 360.

lessons.takeaway: Sector fraction = angle ÷ 360; perimeter includes any straight edges.
lessons.mistake: Using diameter as radius, or forgetting the radii in a sector perimeter.

lessons.goal: Distinguish surface area, volume and capacity.

steps.title: Count the six exterior faces
steps.text: There are two 6-by-4 faces, two 6-by-3 faces and two 4-by-3 faces. Their total area is 108 square centimetres.
steps.why: Surface area counts only the exterior faces, not the interior volume.

steps.title: Connect volume and capacity
steps.text: One cubic centimetre equals one millilitre, and 1,000 cubic centimetres equals one litre. A lidless box would omit its missing top face.
steps.why: Read whether the question asks for a closed solid or only exposed material.

quiz.question: Find the volume of a 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm cuboid.
quiz.hint: Multiply all three dimensions.

quiz.question: A cube has side 4 cm. What is its total surface area?
quiz.hint: There are six square faces.

lessons.takeaway: Volume fills the solid; surface area covers its exposed faces.
lessons.mistake: Reporting surface area in cubic units or counting a missing lid.

lessons.title: Use the constant cross-section of a prism
lessons.goal: Find the cross-sectional area before multiplying by prism length.

steps.title: Find the repeated face
steps.text: A triangular prism has a triangular cross-section with base 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Its length is 10 cm.
steps.why: A prism has the same cross-section all along its length.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Calculate the cross-sectional area
steps.text: The triangle’s area is half of 6 times 4, giving 12 square centimetres.
steps.why: Use the shape’s correct two-dimensional area formula first.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="cross" x="230" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">cross-section A</text></svg>

steps.title: Extend it through the prism
steps.text: Multiply 12 square centimetres by the 10 cm length. The volume is 120 cubic centimetres.
steps.why: Area times length measures the three-dimensional stack.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="cross" x="230" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">cross-section A</text><text id="length" x="500" y="300" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">length L</text></svg>

steps.title: Do not confuse the two heights
steps.text: The triangle’s perpendicular height was 4 cm; the prism’s length was 10 cm. Draw and label both before calculating.
steps.why: A length can play a different role in the cross-section and in the solid.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Identify the required measurement and its units.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="front" points="120,285 340,285 230,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><polygon id="top" points="340,285 600,210 490,30 230,105" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="hidden" x1="120" y1="285" x2="380" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/><line id="backbase" x1="380" y1="210" x2="600" y2="210" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="cross" x="230" y="250" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">cross-section A</text><text id="length" x="500" y="300" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">length L</text><text id="formula" x="380" y="365" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">Volume = A × L</text></svg>

quiz.question: A prism has cross-sectional area 18 cm² and length 7 cm. Find its volume.
quiz.hint: Multiply cross-sectional area by length.

quiz.question: A prism has volume 150 cm³ and cross-sectional area 25 cm². Find its length.
quiz.hint: Undo multiplying by the cross-sectional area.
quiz.explanation: Length = 150 ÷ 25 = 6 cm.

lessons.takeaway: Find the area of one repeated slice, then multiply by length.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying three displayed lengths without recognising the cross-sectional shape.

lessons.title: Read a scale drawing
lessons.goal: Convert between drawing and real lengths using consistent units.

steps.title: Read the scale as a ratio
steps.text: A scale of 1:200 means one unit on the drawing represents 200 of the same units in reality.
steps.why: A scale ratio compares like units.
steps.math: 1 cm on plan = 200 cm in reality

steps.text: A wall measuring 4.5 cm on the plan is 900 cm long in reality. Convert that to 9 m.
steps.why: Multiply a drawing length by the enlargement factor.

steps.title: Reverse for drawing a real object
steps.text: A real 12 m length is 1,200 cm. Divide by 200 to draw it as 6 cm.
steps.why: Convert units before reversing the scale factor.

steps.title: Scale areas and volumes differently
steps.text: Doubling every length multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8. A linear scale factor does not directly scale an area.
steps.why: Area has two dimensions; volume has three.
