quiz.question: At scale 1:100, how long is a real 7 m wall on the drawing?
quiz.hint: Put both lengths in the same unit before applying 1:100.

quiz.question: A shape is enlarged with length scale factor 3. What is its area scale factor?
quiz.hint: Area scales in two dimensions.

lessons.takeaway: Same units first; multiply to enlarge, divide to reduce.
lessons.mistake: Applying a length scale factor directly to area or volume.

reference.name: Rectangle
reference.note: Perimeter uses length units; area uses square units.

reference.name: Triangle and parallelogram
reference.formula: Triangle A = ½bh; parallelogram A = bh
reference.note: h is perpendicular to the base.

reference.name: Circle
reference.note: Radius is half the diameter.

reference.name: Sector
reference.note: Sector perimeter also includes two radii.

reference.name: Cuboid
reference.note: Count exposed faces carefully.

reference.name: Prism
reference.note: The cross-section stays constant.

reference.name: Scale factors
reference.formula: Length: k; area: k²; volume: k³
reference.note: Convert units before comparing lengths.

reference.name: Sector perimeter
reference.note: Add both exposed radii to the arc length. θ is measured in degrees; use this for a sector with two radial boundary edges.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether the question measures a boundary, a face, a filled solid or a scaled drawing. Label lengths and units before choosing a formula; remove hidden joined faces only from surface area, never from volume.

methods.title: Composite perimeter and area
methods.when: A field or region is assembled from familiar shapes.
methods.rule: Rectangle A=lw, P=2(l+w); trapezium A=(a+b)h/2 for parallel sides a,b and perpendicular h; rhombus/kite A=d₁d₂/2 for perpendicular diagonals. Add/subtract non-overlapping areas; trace the external boundary.
steps: Split the figure into standard shapes.
Find any missing lengths.
Add or subtract areas.
Trace the outer boundary separately, excluding internal joins.
methods.example: An 8 by 6 rectangle with a 3 by 2 corner removed has area 48−6=42 square units.
methods.check: Adding back the removed 6 restores the full 48; the area must lie between 0 and 48.
methods.trap: An area subtraction does not imply the same numerical perimeter subtraction.

methods.title: Parallelogram and triangle height
methods.when: A sloping shape has a stated base and perpendicular height.
methods.rule: Parallelogram A=bh; triangle A=½bh.
steps: Choose a base.
Identify the perpendicular distance to the opposite vertex or parallel side.
Apply the correct whole or half product.
methods.example: A triangle with base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm has area 63 cm².
methods.check: Two congruent copies form a parallelogram of area 126 cm².
methods.trap: A sloping side is not generally the perpendicular height.

methods.title: Circle, sector and semicircle measures
methods.when: A figure contains circular area or curved boundary.
methods.rule: C=2πr; A=πr²; arc=(θ/360)2πr; sector area=(θ/360)πr²; sector perimeter=2 r+arc for 0<θ<360°. Semicircle area=πr²/2; standalone perimeter=πr+2 r.
steps: Convert diameter to radius when needed.
Take the correct fraction of a full circle.
Add any straight radii or diameter needed for perimeter.
Exclude a shared diameter if it lies inside a composite region.
methods.example: A semicircle of radius 5 has area 25π/2 and a standalone perimeter 5π+10.
methods.check: Its curved boundary is half of 2π×5.
methods.trap: A semicircle’s perimeter includes the diameter only when that diameter is on the outside.

methods.title: Cuboid volume, nets and surface area
methods.when: A rectangular solid or its net is given.
methods.rule: V=lwh; closed SA=2(lw+lh+wh); 1 cm³=1 ml, 1000 cm³=1 litre.
steps: Identify the three perpendicular dimensions.
For volume, count base area times height.
For surface area, list every exposed face.
Remove a missing lid or opening if the object is not closed.
methods.example: A closed 7 by 4 by 3 cuboid has V=84 and SA=2(28+21+12)=122 in the corresponding cubic and square units.
methods.check: A net must have two faces of each area 28,21,12.
methods.trap: Do not use volume units for material needed to cover a box.

methods.title: Join solids and remove shared faces
methods.when: Two solids are glued face to face.
methods.rule: Exposed SA=SA₁+SA₂−2 A_shared, for one full shared face; volumes add if there is no overlap.
steps: Calculate each separate surface area.
Identify the actual contact area.
Subtract it twice because one face from each solid becomes hidden.
For minimum or maximum exposed area, compare permitted contact areas.
methods.example: Two identical cubes of side 2 joined on a full face have exposed SA=24+24−2×4=40; volume=8+8=16.
methods.check: The result is a 4 by 2 by 2 cuboid with SA=2(8+8+4)=40.
methods.trap: Subtracting the contact area only once leaves one hidden face counted.

methods.title: Prism volume and reverse dimensions
methods.when: A solid has a constant cross-section.
methods.rule: V=A_cross×L; L=V/A_cross, A_cross>0.
steps: Identify the repeated cross-sectional shape.
Find its area using the correct 2 D formula.
Multiply by prism length, or divide volume by the area to reverse.
Distinguish the cross-section’s height from prism length.
methods.example: A triangular section with base 8 and height 5 has area 20; volume 300 therefore needs length 15.
methods.trap: Multiplying all three displayed lengths without the triangle’s factor ½ doubles its volume.

methods.title: Surface area of a right prism
methods.when: A closed right prism has non-rectangular end faces.
methods.rule: SA=2 A_cross+P_cross×L, for a closed right prism.
steps: Calculate one end area.
Find the full perimeter of that end, using any required side calculation.
Multiply its perimeter by prism length for lateral faces.
Add both ends, or omit any explicitly open face.
methods.example: A prism whose cross-section is a right-angled triangle with perpendicular sides 3, 4 and hypotenuse 5, length 10, has SA=2×6+(3+4+5)×10=132.
methods.check: The rectangular side faces have areas 30,40,50; adding the two 6-unit ends gives 132.
methods.trap: The cross-section’s perimeter is not the same as its area.

methods.title: Map scales in both directions
methods.when: Drawing and real lengths are connected by a scale 1:n.
methods.rule: Real length=n×drawing length; drawing length=real length/n, using the same units.
steps: Convert all lengths to one unit system.
Multiply from drawing to reality, divide in reverse.
If changing map scale, pass through the real length.
methods.example: At 1:20,000, 3 cm represents 60,000 cm=600 m; at 1:10,000 the same length is 6 cm.
methods.check: 6 cm×10,000=60,000 cm, the same real length; the less reduced map shows the object larger.
methods.trap: A scale ratio compares like units, not centimetres directly with metres.

methods.title: Scale area, volume and a cost decision
methods.when: A scale drawing is used to find real area or a practical cost.
methods.rule: Length factor k gives area factor k² and volume factor k³; cost=quantity×unit price.
steps: Find real dimensions before calculating a physical area.
Use square or cube scale factors only for matching types of measurement.
Apply the cost rate to the correct quantity.
Compare the final cost with the budget, keeping exact intermediate values.
methods.example: A 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle at 1:100 represents 2 m by 3 m, area 6 m², not 0.06 m².
methods.check: The real lengths are 100 times larger, so area is 10,000 times larger in matching square units.
methods.trap: Applying a linear scale factor directly to an area gives the wrong dimensions.

checks: Perimeter uses length units, area square units, volume cubic units.
All lengths are in compatible units before substitution.
Shared interior faces are excluded from exposed surface area.
Curved formulas use radius, not diameter, and exact π is retained until the end.
The final result answers the requested cost, size or decision, not only an intermediate area.

challenges.title: Recover the length and cover a prism
challenges.question: A closed triangular prism has a right-angled triangular cross-section with perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. Its volume is 360 cm³. (a) Find its length. (b) Find the third side of the triangular cross-section. (c) Find the total surface area needed to cover all five faces.
hints: Find the triangular area before using the volume.
For surface area, use two triangular ends and one rectangular face for each side of the triangle.

solution.title: Find the cross-sectional area
solution.reason: The cross-section is a right-angled triangle.

solution.title: Reverse the volume
solution.reason: Volume is the repeated cross-sectional area times length.

solution.title: Find the missing edge
solution.reason: Pythagoras applies to the given right-angled triangle.

solution.title: Count every exterior face
solution.reason: There are two triangular ends and three rectangular lateral faces.

challenges.answer: Prism length 15 cm; third triangle side 10 cm; total surface area 408 cm².
challenges.check: The separate lateral areas 90,120,150 plus triangular areas 24 and 24 sum to 408; volume 24×15 returns 360.

challenges.title: A field purchase and fencing decision
challenges.question: A field consists of a 60 m by 40 m rectangle with a semicircle attached externally along one complete 40 m side. The shared diameter is inside the field. Land costs €2 per square metre and fencing costs €15 per metre around the outer boundary; these are invented classroom prices. (a) Find the exact area and outer perimeter. (b) Find the combined land-and-fencing cost. (c) Is a €9,400 budget sufficient? Keep π exact until the final money rounding.
hints: The semicircle’s radius is 20 m. Only three rectangle sides remain on the outside.
Area=2400+200π; perimeter=160+20π.

solution.title: Find the combined area
solution.reason: The two regions do not overlap.

solution.title: Trace the external boundary
solution.reason: The shared 40 m diameter is internal and is not fenced.

solution.title: Apply both prices
solution.reason: Area and length are charged at different unit prices.

solution.title: Round and decide
solution.reason: The budget covers the idealised specified costs, with about 89 cents remaining.

challenges.answer: Area 2400+200π m²; perimeter 160+20π m; total €7200+700π≈€9,399.11; the stated budget is sufficient by about €0.89.
challenges.check: Using A≈3028.3185307 and P≈222.8318531 gives 2 A+15 P≈9399.114858, independently matching the exact expression.

challenges.title: Choose the least or most exposed joined solid
challenges.question: Two identical closed cuboids each measure 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. They are joined flush along one complete matching face, with no overlap of volume and no gaps. (a) Find each separate surface area and volume. (b) Find the exposed surface area for each possible matching face size. (c) State which join gives the minimum and maximum exposed area, and give the resulting overall dimensions in each case. (d) Find the combined volume.
hints: The possible contact areas are 6×4, 6×3 and 4×3.
Subtract twice the contact area from the sum of the two separate surface areas.

solution.title: Measure one cuboid
solution.reason: Opposite faces form three equal pairs.

solution.title: Remove each possible shared pair
solution.reason: Both contacting faces become interior.

solution.title: Choose the minimum
solution.math: Largest contact 24 gives minimum 168 cm²; joined dimensions 6×4×6 cm
solution.reason: Maximising hidden area minimises exposed area.

solution.title: Choose the maximum
solution.math: Smallest contact 12 gives maximum 192 cm²; joined dimensions 12×4×3 cm
solution.reason: Minimising hidden area maximises exposed area among the permitted full-face joins.

solution.title: Add the volumes
solution.reason: The solids share a boundary face but no interior volume.

challenges.answer: One cuboid:108 cm²,72 cm³. Joined areas 168,180,192 cm². Minimum 168 for a 6×4 face; maximum 192 for a 4×3 face. Combined volume 144 cm³.
challenges.check: Direct cuboid formulas give SA(6,4,6)=168 and SA(12,4,3)=192, and both overall volumes are 144.

challenges.title: Redraw a field at a different map scale
challenges.question: On a 1:25,000 map, a rectangular field measures 3.2 cm by 2.0 cm. (a) Find its actual dimensions in metres, perimeter in metres and area in hectares, using 1 hectare=10,000 m². (b) Find the dimensions of the same field on a 1:10,000 map. (c) A separate 900 m route is drawn on the original map. Find its map length.
hints: Convert the real lengths from centimetres to metres after multiplying by 25,000.
For the new map, divide the real centimetre lengths by 10,000.

solution.title: Recover real dimensions
solution.reason: Scale ratios use the same units on both sides.

solution.title: Calculate the field measures
solution.reason: Perimeter and area use different formulas and units.

solution.title: Redraw at the new scale
solution.reason: The less reduced map displays larger lengths.

solution.title: Reverse the route scale
solution.reason: Divide the real length by the original scale denominator.

challenges.answer: Actual 800 m by 500 m; perimeter 2600 m; area 40 ha. New map 8 cm by 5 cm; route 3.6 cm on the original map.
challenges.check: The new drawing lengths are 2.5 times the old because 25000/10000=2.5; 3.6×25000 cm=900 m.

title: Statistics 2 — Averages and Variability
intro: Describe a data set with its centre and its spread, and choose summaries that answer the question.

lessons.title: Find mode and median
lessons.goal: Use frequency for mode and position for median.

steps.title: Order the data
steps.text: Use the values 2, 3, 3, 4 and 8. They are already in ascending order. Keep repeated values.
steps.why: Median depends on position in an ordered list.

quiz.question: Find the median of 9, 1, 4, 7, 3.
quiz.hint: Order the list first.
quiz.explanation: 1,3,4,7,9 has middle value 4.

quiz.hint: Find the most frequent value.
quiz.explanation: 4 appears three times, more than any other value.

lessons.takeaway: Mode counts appearances; median locates the ordered middle.
lessons.mistake: Taking the middle of an unordered list.

quiz.question: Find the mean of 4, 8, 9, 11.
quiz.hint: Add all values and divide by four.
quiz.explanation: The sum is 32; 32/4 = 8.

quiz.question: Four values have mean 7. Three values are 4, 6 and 8. Find the fourth.
quiz.hint: Find the required total first.
quiz.explanation: The total is 4 × 7 = 28. Known total is 18, leaving 10.

lessons.takeaway: Mean × number of observations = total.
lessons.mistake: Dividing by the number of distinct values instead of all observations.

lessons.title: Choose an average that fits the question
lessons.goal: Explain how outliers and categorical data affect the choice of average.

steps.title: Use mode for categories
steps.text: For shirt colours, the most common colour is meaningful, while adding and averaging colours is not. State why your chosen summary suits the data.
steps.why: Different data types support different calculations.

quiz.question: Which average is usually less affected by one extreme numerical value?
quiz.hint: Think position rather than all numerical distances.
quiz.explanation: The median is based on the ordered middle, so one extreme value usually affects it less.

quiz.question: Which summary describes the most popular shirt colour?
quiz.hint: Colours are categories, not numerical quantities.
quiz.explanation: The mode is the most frequent category.

lessons.takeaway: Choose the summary and justify it using the data type and shape.
lessons.mistake: Saying one average is always best for every question.

lessons.title: Use a frequency table for the mean
lessons.goal: Weight each value by how many times it occurs.

steps.title: Read values and frequencies separately
steps.text: Scores 1, 2 and 3 occur 2, 3 and 1 times respectively. There are six scores, not three.
steps.why: Frequency counts repeated observations.

reference.name: Mean
reference.formula: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values
reference.note: Use all observations, including repetitions.

reference.name: Frequency-table mean
reference.note: Multiply each value by its frequency first.

reference.name: Grouped-data mean
reference.note: Mid-interval values (midpoints) replace the unknown individual values, so this is an estimate.

reference.name: Median
reference.note: For an even count, average the two middle values.

reference.name: Mode
reference.note: There may be more than one mode or no useful unique mode.

reference.name: Range
reference.note: A simple spread measure that is sensitive to extreme values.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether you need frequency, position, total or spread. Recover totals before combining means, order the data before using a median, and check whether missing-value answers satisfy every stated condition.

methods.title: Mode and ordered median
methods.when: A question asks for the most common or middle observation.
methods.rule: Mode=most frequent; there may be several modes or no unique mode. Ordered odd N: median at position (N+1)/2. Even N: average positions N/2 and N/2+1.
steps: Keep all repeated observations.
Order the list.
Identify the middle position or pair.
For mode, compare frequencies rather than positions.
methods.example: For 2,4,4,7,9,12 the median is (4+7)/2=5.5 and the mode is 4.
methods.check: Three observations lie on either side of the middle gap.
methods.trap: The median need not be an observed value when N is even.

methods.title: Mean and a missing observation
methods.when: A total or mean is given with one unknown value.
methods.rule: Mean=total/N; required total=N×mean; missing value=required total−known total.
steps: Count the observations, including the missing one.
Recover the required total.
Subtract all known values.
Check the result is permitted in context.
methods.example: Five values have mean 12; four total 47. The missing value is 5×12−47=13.
methods.trap: Do not multiply by the number of known observations only.

methods.title: Combine means using group sizes
methods.when: Two or more groups have known means and counts.
methods.rule: Combined mean=(n₁m₁+n₂m₂+…)/(n₁+n₂+…).
steps: Recover each group total using count×mean.
Add those totals.
Divide by the combined count.
Use a direct average of means only when group sizes are equal.
methods.example: A group of 6 with mean 8 and a group of 4 with mean 13 have combined mean (48+52)/10=10.
methods.check: The result lies between 8 and 13 and nearer 8 because that group is larger.
methods.trap: (8+13)/2=10.5 ignores the unequal weights.

methods.title: Choose and justify a representative average
methods.when: The task asks for a typical value or compares summaries.
methods.rule: Mean uses all values; median resists a distant extreme; mode describes the most common value or category.
steps: Identify the data type and the question being answered.
Check for an outlier or uneven distribution.
Calculate the plausible summaries.
Choose one and give a reason connected to this data, not a universal slogan.
methods.example: For journey times 8,9,10,11,62, mean=20 but median=10. Median better describes the middle journey in this small sample.
methods.check: The chosen representative should be interpreted alongside the distribution.
methods.trap: “Median is always best” is not a valid general rule.

methods.title: Use a frequency-weighted mean
methods.when: Repeated values are organised into a frequency table.
methods.rule: Mean=Σfx/Σf.
steps: Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add products for the data total.
Add frequencies for the observation count.
Divide the two totals.
methods.example: Values 1,3,5 with frequencies 2,4,1 give mean (2+12+5)/7=19/7.
methods.check: Expanding the data list gives 1,1,3,3,3,3,5 with total 19.
methods.trap: Averaging 1,3,5 without weights loses repeated observations.

methods.title: Estimate a mean from grouped intervals
methods.when: Only interval frequencies are known.
methods.rule: Mid-interval value (midpoint)=(lower+upper)/2; estimated mean=Σ(f×midpoint)/Σf.
steps: Use consistent non-overlapping intervals.
Find each midpoint.
Multiply midpoint by frequency and add.
Divide by total frequency and label the result an estimate.
methods.example: Intervals 0≤t<10 and 10≤t<20 with frequencies 3 and 7 give estimated mean (3×5+7×15)/10=12.
methods.check: The estimate should lie inside the overall interval range.
methods.trap: The midpoint is a stand-in; the actual observations are not known.

methods.title: Range and missing extremes
methods.when: The smallest or largest value is unknown.
methods.rule: Range=max−min; max=min+range.
steps: Identify which entries really are the extremes.
Write the range equation.
Combine it with any mean-total equation.
Check the solved values keep the list ordered.
methods.example: Ordered a,5,8,10,b have range 14 and mean 9: b−a=14 and a+b=22, so a=4,b=18.
methods.check: The sum 45 gives mean 9, the extremes differ by 14, and 4≤5≤8≤10≤18.
methods.trap: A solution to the equations may fail the required order.

methods.title: Test whether statistics are possible together
methods.when: A problem claims a mean, median, range or integer condition.
methods.rule: All constraints must hold simultaneously; one contradiction makes a claim impossible.
steps: Translate each statistic into a total, position or difference condition.
Use the data type: whole-number observations require integer totals and entries.
Solve or construct an example.
For impossibility, state the exact contradiction.
methods.example: Three integer observations cannot have mean 2.5, because their required total would be 7.5.
methods.check: If a claim is said to be possible, exhibit a complete list satisfying every condition.
methods.trap: A plausible-looking average is not a proof that a data set exists.

checks: Mean uses all observations or their frequencies, not just distinct values.
Median is taken from the ordered list; an even count uses two middle values.
Grouped-data means are labelled estimates.
Missing values preserve the required ordering, range and data type.
The chosen average answers the contextual question, with outliers considered.

challenges.title: Combine two training groups correctly
challenges.question: Group A has 12 training scores with mean 14. Group B has 8 scores with mean 19. (a) Find the combined mean. (b) Explain why averaging 14 and 19 directly gives the wrong result. (c) One further score of 30 is added to the combined group. Find the new mean exactly and to two decimal places.
hints: Recover each group’s total before combining them.
The first combined count is 20; after the extra score it is 21.

solution.title: Recover the group totals
solution.reason: A mean multiplied by its count gives its total.

solution.title: Combine totals and counts
solution.reason: Each individual score receives the same weight.

solution.title: Explain the incorrect shortcut
solution.math: (14+19)/2=16.5 weights the two unequal groups equally
solution.reason: The group of 12 should influence the mean more than the group of 8.

solution.title: Add the extra observation
solution.reason: Both the total and the count change.

challenges.answer: Combined mean 16; a direct average of group means is inappropriate because counts differ; new mean 50/3≈16.67.
challenges.check: 12(14−16)+8(19−16)=−24+24=0, confirming the combined mean. The added score 30 is above 16, so the new mean must increase.

challenges.title: Estimate a grouped mean without inventing exact data
challenges.question: Eighteen journey times t minutes are grouped as follows: 0≤t<10 has frequency 4; 10≤t<20 has frequency 8; 20≤t<30 has frequency 6. (a) Estimate the mean using mid-interval values. (b) State the modal class. (c) Locate the median within a class and explain why its exact value cannot be recovered from this table. (d) Can the exact range be calculated?
hints: The midpoints are 5,15 and 25; weight them by their frequencies.
With 18 observations, the median uses positions 9 and 10 in the ordered list.

solution.title: Calculate midpoint contributions
solution.reason: Each midpoint represents the unknown observations inside its group.

solution.title: Find the estimate
solution.reason: The frequency total is 18.

solution.title: Identify the modal class
solution.reason: This interval has the greatest frequency, 8.

solution.title: Locate the median positions
solution.math: Cumulative frequencies are 4,12,18, so positions 9 and 10 are both in 10≤t<20
solution.reason: Their exact values are unknown, so the exact median is unknown; it lies in this interval.

solution.title: Explain the range limitation
solution.math: The exact minimum and maximum are not given, so the exact range is unknown
solution.reason: Interval endpoints are not necessarily observed values.

challenges.answer: Estimated mean 145/9≈16.11 min; modal class 10≤t<20; median lies in that class but is not exact; exact range cannot be recovered.
challenges.check: The midpoint-based total is 290 and 290/18≈16.11. Changing an observation within its interval leaves the table unchanged but can change the exact mean, median or range.

challenges.title: Find missing extremes and reject an impossible claim
challenges.question: Five whole-number journey times, in minutes, are ordered as a,4,7,9,b. Their mean is 8 and range is 12. (a) Find a and b. (b) Find the median and explain why the mean exceeds it. (c) Could a different pair of whole-number extremes in the same ordered pattern have mean 7 and range 12? Give a mathematical reason.
hints: The three middle values total 20; mean 8 fixes the complete total at 40.
For part (c), use a+b=15 and b−a=12, then check the whole-number condition.

solution.title: Translate mean and range
solution.reason: The mean gives a total, while range links the two extremes.

solution.title: Solve both conditions
solution.reason: Adding the equations eliminates a.

solution.title: Check order and median
solution.reason: The third of five observations is the middle one; the high 16 raises the mean above it.

solution.title: Test the alternate mean
solution.reason: The same algebra determines the only possible extreme pair.

solution.title: Use the data-type restriction
solution.math: That alternative is impossible for whole-number times
solution.reason: Both required extremes are non-integers, although they would be valid if fractional times were allowed.

challenges.answer: a=4,b=16; median 7, mean 8. Mean 7 with the same middle values and range 12 is impossible under the whole-number condition.
challenges.check: 4+4+7+9+16=40 and 16−4=12. In part (c), integer extremes with an even difference must have an even sum, contradicting the required sum 15.

challenges.title: Choose a useful summary when one time is extreme
challenges.question: Seven completion times in minutes are 5,6,7,7,8,9,70. (a) Find the mean, median, mode and range. (b) Choose a useful summary for a typical middle participant and justify it. (c) Replace 70 by 140 and recalculate the four summaries. (d) Explain why the mean may still be relevant if an organiser wants to estimate total participant-minutes.
hints: The first six times sum to 42.
An extreme replacement changes totals and endpoints, but not the ordered middle positions.

solution.title: Calculate the original summaries
solution.reason: Mean uses the total, median the fourth position, mode frequency and range the extremes.

solution.title: Choose a contextual centre
solution.math: Median 7 minutes is a useful middle-participant summary here
solution.reason: Six times cluster from 5 to 9 while 70 is far away; the median is not pulled by its distance.

solution.title: Replace the extreme value
solution.math: New total=182; mean=26; median=7; mode=7; range=135
solution.reason: The extreme replacement changes the total and maximum but not the centre position or repeated value.

solution.title: Explain the total-based purpose
solution.math: For a specified participant count, count×mean gives total participant-minutes
solution.reason: A useful average depends on the task; the mean preserves the total work represented by all observations.

challenges.answer: Original: mean 16, median 7, mode 7, range 65. After replacement: mean 26, median 7, mode 7, range 135. Median suits the middle participant; mean relates to total participant-minutes.
challenges.check: 7×16=112 and 7×26=182. Both ordered lists still have 7 in position 4 and 7 as the only repeated value.

title: Geometry 1 — Triangles, Quadrilaterals and Theorems
intro: Draw carefully, name the relationship, and give a reason for every angle or length. The theorem proofs examined at Higher Level (Theorems 4, 6, 9, 14 and 19) are in Chapter 16.

lessons.title: Recognise lines and angle relationships
lessons.goal: Use the relationship between lines before calculating an angle.

steps.title: Name the objects
steps.text: A line extends indefinitely both ways; a segment has two endpoints; a ray has one endpoint. Parallel lines in a plane never meet.
steps.why: Precise names tell you which geometric facts apply.
steps.math: Line AB; segment [AB]; ray from A through B

steps.title: Use a straight-line total
steps.text: Adjacent angles along a straight line add to 180 degrees. If one is 125 degrees, the other is 55 degrees.
steps.why: Together they form a straight angle.

steps.title: Identify parallel-line angles
steps.text: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. Corresponding angles and alternate angles are equal; same-side interior angles add to 180 degrees.
steps.why: These relationships depend on the lines being parallel.

steps.text: Mark the pair you are using, then write the relationship. A diagram that looks parallel is not enough without a given mark or a proof.
steps.why: A valid reason makes the calculation reliable.

quiz.question: An angle adjacent to 132° on a straight line is…
quiz.hint: Subtract from 180 degrees.

quiz.question: For parallel lines cut by a transversal, which pair is equal?
options: An acute and an obtuse angle
quiz.hint: Check their relative positions at the two crossings.
quiz.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel.

lessons.takeaway: Identify the relationship first, then calculate.
lessons.mistake: Assuming lines are parallel from appearance alone.

lessons.title: Use triangle and exterior angles
lessons.goal: Connect the 180-degree triangle total with an exterior angle.

steps.title: Start with the triangle total
steps.text: Two interior angles of a triangle are 55 and 65 degrees. Their total is 120 degrees.
steps.why: The three interior angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="130,285 510,285 300,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="185" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="290" y="139" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="423" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">?</text></svg>

steps.title: Find the missing interior angle
steps.text: Subtract 120 from 180. The third angle is 60 degrees.
steps.why: The missing angle completes the triangle’s total.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="130,285 510,285 300,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="185" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="290" y="139" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="423" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">60°</text></svg>

steps.title: Extend a side
steps.text: An exterior angle adjacent to the 60-degree angle is 120 degrees. They form a straight line.
steps.why: Adjacent interior and exterior angles are supplementary.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Interior angle plus its adjacent exterior angle makes a straight angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="130,285 510,285 300,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="angle0" x="185" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">55°</text><text id="angle1" x="290" y="139" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">65°</text><text id="angle2" x="423" y="262" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">60°</text><line id="extension" x1="510" y1="285" x2="700" y2="285" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="4"/><text id="exterior" x="556" y="249" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">120°</text><path id="exterior-arc" d="M565 285 A55 55 0 0 0 470 247" fill="none" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: See the exterior-angle rule
steps.text: The exterior angle also equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, the ones not adjacent to it. This gives the same 120 degrees.
steps.why: Subtracting the adjacent interior angle from the triangle total leaves the other two.

quiz.question: A triangle has angles 42° and 71°. Find the third.
quiz.hint: The total is 180 degrees.

quiz.question: An exterior angle is 110° and one interior opposite angle is 45°. Find the other interior opposite angle.
quiz.hint: The two interior opposite angles add to the exterior angle.
quiz.explanation: 110 − 45 = 65 degrees.

lessons.takeaway: Interior total 180°; exterior equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
lessons.mistake: Adding the adjacent interior angle instead of the two interior opposite angles.

lessons.title: Use quadrilateral properties
lessons.goal: Choose properties of the named shape without assuming extra symmetry.

steps.title: Split a quadrilateral
steps.text: A diagonal divides a simple quadrilateral (one whose sides do not cross) into two triangles. Their angle totals add together.
steps.why: Each triangle contributes 180 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Solve a missing angle
steps.text: If three angles are 80, 95 and 105 degrees, their sum is 280. The fourth is 80 degrees.
steps.why: The four interior angles must total 360 degrees.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="diagonal" x1="140" y1="285" x2="650" y2="105" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/></svg>

steps.title: Use a parallelogram’s extra structure
steps.text: A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal, opposite angles equal, and adjacent angles supplementary.
steps.why: Parallel-line relationships produce the angle properties.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,285 590,285 650,105 250,80" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="diagonal" x1="140" y1="285" x2="650" y2="105" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="4"/><text id="one" x="350" y="155" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="start">180°</text><text id="two" x="440" y="255" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">180°</text></svg>

steps.title: Separate special cases
steps.text: A rectangle has four right angles; a rhombus has four equal sides; a square has both. A general parallelogram need not have either property.
steps.why: Special shapes have extra conditions beyond the general definition.

quiz.question: A parallelogram has one angle 70°. What is an adjacent angle?
quiz.hint: Adjacent angles add to 180 degrees.

quiz.question: Which property is guaranteed for every rectangle?
options: Exactly one pair of parallel sides
quiz.hint: Use the definition of a rectangle.
quiz.explanation: Every rectangle has four right angles. Equal sides are guaranteed only for a square.

lessons.takeaway: Use only the properties guaranteed by the named shape.
lessons.mistake: Treating every parallelogram as a rectangle or every rhombus as a square.

lessons.title: Decide whether triangles are congruent
lessons.goal: Match corresponding information to a valid congruence test.

steps.title: Understand congruent
steps.text: Congruent triangles have the same shape and size. One can fit exactly over the other after moving, rotating or reflecting it.
steps.why: Orientation does not affect lengths or angles.
steps.math: Congruent → matching sides and angles equal

steps.title: Use SSS or SAS
steps.text: SSS matches all three sides. SAS matches two sides and the included angle between them.
steps.why: The angle must be the one between the two sides: two sides with a non-included angle do not fix the triangle.

font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">SAS: two sides and the angle between them</text></svg>

steps.title: Use ASA or RHS
steps.text: ASA matches two angles and their included side. RHS applies to right-angled triangles with equal hypotenuse and one corresponding other side.
steps.why: These data determine a unique triangle up to rigid movement or reflection.

steps.title: Reject tempting shortcuts
steps.text: Equal angles alone give similar triangles, which may differ in size. Two sides and a non-included angle are not a general congruence test.
steps.why: The information must rule out a differently sized or shaped triangle.
steps.math: AAA: similarity only; SSA: not a general test

quiz.question: Which information guarantees congruence?
options: Two equal corresponding sides and their included angle
quiz.hint: Look for a valid complete test.
quiz.explanation: Two sides and the included angle is SAS.

quiz.question: Two right-angled triangles have equal hypotenuses and one other equal corresponding side. Which test applies?
quiz.hint: The right angle is already known.
quiz.explanation: RHS uses a right angle, equal hypotenuse and equal corresponding side.

lessons.takeaway: Name the test and match its corresponding parts.
lessons.mistake: Using AAA to claim equal size.

lessons.title: Choose the correct side in Pythagoras
lessons.goal: Use the hypotenuse correctly and distinguish adding from subtracting squares.

steps.title: Identify the hypotenuse
steps.text: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
steps.why: Pythagoras applies only to a right-angled triangle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>The hypotenuse is opposite the marked right angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 540,300 150,90" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="vertex1" x="555" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex2" x="165" y="110" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><line id="right1" x1="150" y1="276" x2="174" y2="276" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="right2" x1="174" y1="276" x2="174" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="side0" x="115" y="190" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">6</text><text id="side1" x="345" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">8</text><text id="side2" x="370" y="185" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">c</text></svg>

steps.title: Add the two smaller squares
steps.text: Square each perpendicular side, then add. This gives 100, the square of the hypotenuse.
steps.why: The theorem relates squared lengths.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>The hypotenuse is opposite the marked right angle.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 540,300 150,90" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="vertex1" x="555" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex2" x="165" y="110" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><line id="right1" x1="150" y1="276" x2="174" y2="276" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="right2" x1="174" y1="276" x2="174" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="side0" x="115" y="190" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">6</text><text id="side1" x="345" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">8</text><text id="side2" x="370" y="185" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">c</text></svg>

steps.title: Return to a length
steps.text: Take the positive square root because a length is positive. The hypotenuse is 10 cm.
steps.why: 100 is an area-like square quantity, not the side length.

steps.title: Reverse for a missing shorter side
steps.text: If the hypotenuse is 13 cm and one shorter side is 5 cm, subtract squares and then take the root.
steps.why: Rearrange the same theorem; do not always add.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has perpendicular sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
quiz.hint: Add the squared perpendicular sides and then square-root.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 cm and one perpendicular side 6 cm. Find the other perpendicular side.
quiz.hint: Subtract the known perpendicular side’s square from the hypotenuse’s square.

lessons.takeaway: Hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the two other squares.
lessons.mistake: Adding squares when finding a shorter side, or forgetting the final square root.

lessons.title: Know what a proof is doing
lessons.goal: Distinguish a starting assumption from a conclusion and justify each link.

steps.title: Separate definitions and axioms
steps.text: A definition explains a term; an axiom is an accepted starting statement. Neither is a measurement from one drawing.
steps.why: A proof needs agreed meanings and starting facts.
steps.math: Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Separate definitions and axioms</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Separate definitions and axioms</text></svg>

steps.title: State the theorem precisely
steps.text: A theorem is a statement established by reasoning. Identify what is given and what must be shown.
steps.why: You cannot assume the conclusion while trying to prove it.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>State the theorem precisely</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Given → justified steps → conclusion</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">State the theorem precisely</text></svg>

steps.title: Recognise converse and corollary
steps.text: A converse swaps the condition and conclusion, so it needs its own justification. A corollary follows readily from an established theorem.
steps.why: A true statement does not automatically make its converse true.
steps.math: If P then Q; converse: if Q then P
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Recognise converse and corollary</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Given → justified steps → conclusion</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">If P then Q; converse: if Q then P</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Recognise converse and corollary</text></svg>

steps.title: Write a reason beside every claim
steps.text: For an angle calculation, a reason might be “straight-line angles total 180 degrees” or “alternate angles on parallel lines”.
steps.why: A diagram suggests a relationship; reasons establish it generally.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Write a reason beside every claim</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><rect id="row0" x="30" y="25" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num0" x="48" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">01</text><text id="math0" x="95" y="64" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Definition → meaning; axiom → accepted starting fact</text><rect id="row1" x="30" y="97" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num1" x="48" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">02</text><text id="math1" x="95" y="136" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Given → justified steps → conclusion</text><rect id="row2" x="30" y="169" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#f4f7f9" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num2" x="48" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#60798b" text-anchor="start">03</text><text id="math2" x="95" y="208" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">If P then Q; converse: if Q then P</text><rect id="row3" x="30" y="241" width="700" height="60" rx="10" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="none" stroke-width="2"/><text id="num3" x="48" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">04</text><text id="math3" x="95" y="280" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">Claim + reason, at every step</text><text id="caption0" x="35" y="355" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="21" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Write a reason beside every claim</text></svg>

quiz.question: What is a converse?
options: The statement with condition and conclusion swapped
quiz.hint: Think “if P then Q” changed to “if Q then P”.
quiz.explanation: A converse reverses the implication and requires its own justification.

quiz.question: Which is a valid proof reason?
quiz.hint: Use an established geometric fact.
quiz.explanation: Vertically opposite angles being equal is a theorem, unlike a visual estimate.

lessons.takeaway: A proof explains why every valid configuration works.
lessons.mistake: Treating one accurate drawing as proof of a general claim.

lessons.title: Prove vertically opposite angles equal
lessons.goal: Use two straight-line totals and eliminate their common angle.

steps.title: Label the angles at a crossing
steps.text: Two straight lines intersect. Name one angle α, its neighbour β, and the angle opposite α as γ.
steps.why: The crossing gives two useful straight-line pairs.
steps.math: α next to β; γ opposite α
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the first straight line
steps.text: Angles α and β together make 180 degrees.
steps.why: Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="beta" x="490" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">β</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the second straight line
steps.text: Angles β and γ also make 180 degrees. The same β appears in both equations.
steps.why: A second straight line supplies another angle total.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Two straight-line equations share β.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="ab" x1="150" y1="90" x2="610" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="cd" x1="150" y1="310" x2="610" y2="90" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="o" x="380" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text id="alpha" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="beta" x="490" y="210" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle">β</text><text id="gamma" x="380" y="285" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">γ</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Two straight-line equations share β.</text></svg>

steps.title: Subtract the shared angle
steps.text: Both α and γ equal 180 degrees minus β. Therefore they are equal, regardless of the drawing’s orientation.
steps.why: Subtracting equal quantities from equal quantities gives equal results.

quiz.question: Two vertically opposite angles are labelled 3x + 5 and 65 degrees. Find x.
quiz.hint: Set vertically opposite angles equal.

quiz.question: Which fact starts a proof that vertically opposite angles are equal?
quiz.hint: The proof compares two adjacent pairs.
quiz.explanation: Both pairs form straight angles, so each total is 180 degrees.

lessons.takeaway: Two equal totals minus the same adjacent angle leave equal opposite angles.
lessons.mistake: Confusing vertically opposite angles with adjacent angles.

lessons.title: Prove the isosceles angle rule and its converse
lessons.goal: Use triangle congruence to connect equal sides with equal opposite angles.

steps.title: State the equal-side assumption
steps.text: In triangle ABC, suppose AB = AC. The angles opposite those equal sides are angle C and angle B.
steps.why: Match a side to its opposite angle, not an adjacent one.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text></svg>

steps.title: Compare the triangle with reversed labels
steps.text: Compare ABC with the same triangle read backwards, ACB. Matching sides in that order: AB with AC, AC with AB, and BC with CB — all equal. So the triangles are congruent by SSS.
steps.why: All three corresponding sides are equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/></svg>

steps.title: Read the corresponding angles
steps.text: The congruence matches B with C, so the base angles are equal. This proves the equal-sides direction.
steps.why: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="base1" x="255" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text><text id="base2" x="450" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text></svg>

steps.title: Prove the converse separately
steps.text: Now assume the two base angles are equal. Compare ABC and ACB using those angles and their shared included side BC; ASA gives AB = AC.
steps.why: The converse follows from a different congruence argument, not from merely reversing words.
steps.math: Equal base angles → equal opposite sides
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Read the marked sides and angles, not the apparent shape.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="triangle" points="150,300 610,300 380,70" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="vertex0" x="125" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="vertex1" x="625" y="320" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="vertex2" x="395" y="90" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><line id="equal1" x1="220" y1="225" x2="230" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="equal2" x1="530" y1="225" x2="540" y2="235" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="base1" x="255" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text><text id="base2" x="450" y="278" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">equal</text></svg>

quiz.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle A = 40°. Find angle B.
quiz.hint: The two base angles share the remaining 140 degrees.

quiz.question: In triangle ABC, if angle B equals angle C, which sides are equal?
quiz.hint: Match each angle with the side opposite it.
quiz.explanation: The side opposite B is AC; the side opposite C is AB.

lessons.takeaway: Equal sides face equal angles; equal angles face equal sides.
lessons.mistake: Pairing equal sides with the wrong opposite angles.

lessons.title: Connect parallel lines and equal angles
lessons.goal: Understand both directions of the parallel-line angle tests.

steps.title: Start with parallel lines
steps.text: A transversal crosses parallel lines l and m. An alternate-angle pair is equal by the parallel-line angle fact.
steps.why: Parallelism is the stated assumption.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="line1" x1="75" y1="110" x2="690" y2="110" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="line2" x1="75" y1="260" x2="690" y2="260" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="transversal" x1="210" y1="350" x2="490" y2="30" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="l" x="710" y="118" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">l</text><text id="m" x="710" y="268" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">m</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Connect alternate and corresponding positions
steps.text: At either crossing, vertically opposite angles are equal. Combining that fact with alternate angles gives equality of corresponding angles.
steps.why: Equality can be transferred through a third angle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><line id="line1" x1="75" y1="110" x2="690" y2="110" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="line2" x1="75" y1="260" x2="690" y2="260" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="4"/><line id="transversal" x1="210" y1="350" x2="490" y2="30" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="4"/><text id="l" x="710" y="118" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">l</text><text id="m" x="710" y="268" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">m</text><circle id="angle1" cx="454" cy="85" r="24" fill="#fff3dd" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="alpha" x="454" y="94" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">α</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Use the converse test
steps.text: Suppose the alternate angles are equal but l ∥ m is not yet known. Through the point where the transversal meets m, draw the line parallel to l. By the parallel-line fact it makes an alternate angle equal to the one on l, which is exactly the angle m already makes there. Only one line through that point makes that angle, so the parallel is m itself: l ∥ m.
steps.why: Only one ray from the crossing makes a given angle with the transversal on that side, so the drawn parallel must be the second line itself.

steps.title: Get the corresponding-angle converse
steps.text: Replace one corresponding angle by its vertically opposite angle to obtain equal alternate angles. The converse test then proves parallelism.
steps.why: This links theorem 5 to the alternate-angle result and theorem 1.

quiz.question: A transversal makes equal corresponding angles with two lines. What follows?
quiz.hint: Use the converse corresponding-angle test.
quiz.explanation: Equal corresponding angles show that the two lines are parallel.

quiz.question: To infer equality of alternate angles, what fact must be given or proved?
options: The lines are the same length
The diagram is drawn to scale
quiz.hint: The rule depends on the relation between the crossed lines.
quiz.explanation: Parallel crossed lines guarantee equality of alternate angles.

lessons.takeaway: Parallelism gives angle equalities, and the appropriate equalities can prove parallelism.
lessons.mistake: Applying parallel-line angle facts before proving or being given parallelism.

lessons.title: Prove parallelogram diagonals bisect each other
lessons.goal: Use angle relationships and congruence to establish equal half-diagonals.

steps.title: Name the intersection
steps.text: In parallelogram ABCD, diagonals AC and BD meet at E. We want to prove AE = CE and BE = DE.
steps.why: Bisect means divide into two equal lengths.
steps.math: Goal: AE = CE and BE = DE
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,275 500,275 620,105 260,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="p0" x="115" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="p1" x="515" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="p2" x="635" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="p3" x="235" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">D</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Choose opposite small triangles
steps.text: Compare triangles AEB and CED. AB = CD because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
steps.why: Choose triangles containing the half-diagonals you want to compare.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Use a stated fact to justify each step.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="quad" points="140,275 500,275 620,105 260,105" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text id="p0" x="115" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">A</text><text id="p1" x="515" y="290" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">B</text><text id="p2" x="635" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">C</text><text id="p3" x="235" y="120" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">D</text><line id="ac" x1="140" y1="275" x2="620" y2="105" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="bd" x1="500" y1="275" x2="260" y2="105" stroke="#7650a0" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="centre" cx="380" cy="190" r="5" fill="#173349" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text id="e" x="384" y="218" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">E</text><text id="caption0" x="40" y="370" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="20" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">Use a stated fact to justify each step.</text></svg>

steps.title: Match two angle pairs
steps.text: Because AB ∥ CD, the transversal AC gives ∠EAB = ∠ECD and the transversal BD gives ∠EBA = ∠EDC (alternate angles). The equal side AB = CD lies between these angles, so the triangles are congruent by ASA.
steps.why: The equal side lies between the two matched angles.

steps.title: Read off the half-diagonals
steps.text: Corresponding sides now give AE = CE and BE = DE. This proves both diagonals are bisected at E.
steps.why: Congruence transfers equality to all corresponding sides.

quiz.question: A parallelogram diagonal AC is 18 cm long and meets the other diagonal at E. Find AE.
quiz.hint: Diagonals bisect each other.
quiz.explanation: AE is half of AC, so 18/2 = 9 cm.

quiz.question: Does a general parallelogram necessarily have equal diagonals?
options: No; bisection does not imply equal total lengths
Yes, because its opposite sides are parallel
quiz.hint: Distinguish equal halves from equal complete diagonals.
quiz.explanation: Each diagonal is bisected, but the two full diagonal lengths need not equal one another.

lessons.takeaway: Both diagonals are halved; they need not have the same full length.
lessons.mistake: Confusing “bisect each other” with “are equal”.

lessons.title: Why similar triangles have proportional sides
lessons.goal: Connect equal angles, a parallel construction and corresponding side ratios.

steps.title: Match the equal angles
steps.text: Triangles ABC and PQR have equal corresponding angles: A with P, B with Q, C with R. Suppose AB is the longer matching base.
steps.why: The correspondence determines the order of the side ratios.
steps.math: AB ↔ PQ; AC ↔ PR; BC ↔ QR

steps.title: Make a matching small triangle
steps.text: Choose D on AB so that AD = PQ. Through D draw DE parallel to BC, meeting AC at E.
steps.why: Parallel lines preserve the corresponding angles of the small triangle.

steps.title: Use congruence for the constructed triangle
steps.text: In triangles ADE and PQR: ∠A = ∠P (given), AD = PQ (construction) and ∠ADE = ∠ABC = ∠Q (corresponding angles, DE ∥ BC). ASA gives AE = PR and DE = QR.
steps.why: Equal-angle triangles become congruent when a corresponding side is also fixed.

steps.title: Apply parallel-line proportionality
steps.text: The parallel-line proportionality theorem gives AD/AB = AE/AC; applying the same argument from another vertex includes DE/BC. Replace the small-triangle sides by PQ, PR and QR.
steps.why: This proof uses the parallel-line proportionality result studied further in Chapter 16.

quiz.question: Two similar triangles have matching sides 4 and 10. Another side in the smaller triangle is 6. Find its matching larger side.
quiz.hint: The length scale factor is 10/4.

quiz.question: Why must corresponding sides be matched in the same order?
options: Every ratio must compare matching sides in the same direction
Ratios only work for right-angled triangles
quiz.hint: Keep larger/smaller or smaller/larger consistent.
quiz.explanation: Mixing opposite directions produces inconsistent scale factors.

lessons.takeaway: Equal corresponding angles lead to one consistent length scale factor.
lessons.mistake: Pairing sides by their position on the page instead of their opposite angles.

lessons.title: Prove the converse of Pythagoras
lessons.goal: Use a constructed right-angled triangle and SSS to test an unknown triangle.

steps.title: Put the longest side in the correct role
steps.text: Suppose a triangle has sides a, b and longest side c, with c² = a² + b². We want to show it is right-angled.
steps.why: The conclusion must not be assumed in the starting triangle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>Begin with a triangle whose angle has not yet been proved right.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="original" points="145,300 590,300 275,80" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text id="given-a" x="175" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">a</text><text id="given-b" x="460" y="180" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">b</text><text id="given-c" x="365" y="340" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start">c</text><text id="unknown" x="380" y="45" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#b96a12" text-anchor="middle">Angle unknown: do not assume 90°.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct a comparison triangle
steps.text: Construct a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides have lengths a and b. Call its hypotenuse d.
steps.why: A right-angled triangle with those perpendicular sides can be constructed independently.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><title>A comparison triangle supplies the right angle without assuming the conclusion.</title><rect width="760" height="400" fill="#fff"/><polygon id="comparison" points="170,290 570,290 170,100" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square1" x1="170" y1="265" x2="195" y2="265" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><line id="square2" x1="195" y1="265" x2="195" y2="290" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="3"/><text id="perpendicular side-a" x="125" y="205" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">a</text><text id="perpendicular side-b" x="365" y="335" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start">b</text><text id="hyp" x="370" y="170" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="29" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start">d</text><text id="reason" x="380" y="50" font-family="Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle">Constructed right-angled triangle</text></svg>

steps.title: Compare all three lengths
steps.text: The given equality and Pythagoras show d² = c². Positive side lengths therefore give d = c. The two triangles have all three sides equal.
steps.why: Positive square roots are unique, and SSS establishes congruence.
steps.math: d = c → triangles congruent by SSS

steps.title: Transfer the right angle
steps.text: The angle opposite c in the original triangle matches the right angle of the constructed triangle, so it is 90°. For sides 5, 12 and 13: 25 + 144 = 169 = 13², so the angle opposite 13 is a right angle.
steps.why: Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.
