quiz.question: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue counters. One red is drawn and kept out. What is P(red next)?
quiz.hint: Update both the red count and the total count.
quiz.explanation: Three red remain among five counters, giving 3/5.

quiz.question: Two independent events have probabilities 1/3 and 1/2. What is P(both)?
quiz.hint: Independence allows the second chance to remain unchanged.
quiz.explanation: (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6. Without independence, a conditional second probability is needed.

lessons.takeaway: Multiply along a path; update the branch probabilities when the situation changes.
lessons.mistake: Without replacement, do not reuse the original denominator or assume independence.

reference.name: Equally likely outcomes
reference.note: Use this counting rule only when the individual outcomes are equally likely.

reference.name: Complement
reference.note: An event and its complement exhaust all possibilities.

reference.name: Expected frequency
reference.formula: Expected count = number of trials × P(E)
reference.note: An expectation is a prediction, not a guarantee.

reference.name: Either event
reference.formula: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
reference.note: Subtract the overlap counted twice.

reference.name: Two-stage path
reference.formula: P(A then B) = P(A) × P(B given A)
reference.note: Use the probability appropriate after the first event.

toolkit.strategy: First decide whether you are counting equally likely outcomes, reading data, filling regions or following a tree. Define the event before choosing a denominator.

methods.title: Organise a sample space
methods.when: Several choices or stages form one outcome.
methods.rule: Total = n₁n₂… when every earlier choice has the stated number of next choices.
steps: Name each stage and preserve order where it matters.
List a table or tree systematically.
Multiply stage counts only after checking restrictions.
methods.example: 3 badge colours and 4 numbers give 12 badges; if two colours allow only 2 numbers, count 4 + 2 + 2 = 8.
methods.check: Count the complete list and check that no outcome is repeated.
methods.trap: Restricted choices can invalidate a blind multiplication.

methods.title: Use the probability scale and complement
methods.when: The opposite event is easier to count.
steps: Define E precisely.
Identify its complete complement.
Subtract from 1 and simplify.
methods.example: If P(at least one success) = 7/12, P(no successes) = 5/12.
methods.trap: “Not both” includes exactly one and neither; it does not mean neither only.

methods.title: Count equally likely outcomes
methods.when: A fair die, an item chosen at random or equal-sized sectors are specified.
methods.rule: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes.
steps: List all individual outcomes.
Select those satisfying every condition.
Form and simplify the fraction.
methods.example: Choose an integer from 1 to 12 at random: P(multiple of 3) = 4/12 = 1/3.
methods.check: The favourable list is 3, 6, 9, 12.
methods.trap: Two named categories need not be equally likely.

methods.title: Change a mixture and its denominator
methods.when: Counts are given as a ratio, then objects are added or removed.
methods.rule: A:B = a:b ⇒ A = ak, B = bk. After adding g, new total = old total + g.
steps: Represent counts with a common multiplier.
Use the given total or share to find the multiplier.
Write the new probability with the new total.
Solve for an unknown addition before recalculating other chances.
methods.example: 18 red and 30 blue; add g green with green probability 1/4: g/(48 + g) = 1/4, so g = 16 and P(blue) = 30/64.
methods.check: 16/64 = 1/4; all three counts total 64.
methods.trap: A new 25% share means g is one quarter of the final total, not the original total.

methods.title: Combine weighted independent events
methods.when: Repeated trials are independent but their outcomes may be biased.
methods.rule: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) under independence; add mutually exclusive complete path products.
steps: Label branches with their actual probabilities, not automatically 1/2.
Distinguish ordered outcomes and list every favourable path.
Multiply along each path, then add separate paths.
For “at least one”, consider 1 − P(none).
methods.example: If independent tosses have P(H)=3/5, exactly two heads in three tosses uses HHT, HTH, THH: 3(3/5)²(2/5)=54/125.
methods.check: All eight complete path probabilities add to 1.
methods.trap: Independence does not imply fair outcomes; three head-count categories are not equally likely.

methods.title: Count repeated faces, not just distinct labels
methods.when: A die repeats numbers or a spinner has unequal sectors.
methods.rule: Probability follows equally likely physical faces or sector angles, not the number of different names.
steps: Count the physical faces carrying each label.
Use those counts for the branch probabilities.
For independent rolls use a product; use the complement for at least one occurrence.
methods.example: A fair die labelled 1,1,2,2,2,6 has P(6)=1/6 and P(2)=1/2. In two independent rolls, P(at least one 2)=1−(1/2)²=3/4.
methods.check: The label probabilities 2/6+3/6+1/6 total 1.
methods.trap: The three distinct labels do not each have probability 1/3.

methods.title: Estimate and predict from data
methods.when: Observed trials are used to estimate future counts.
methods.rule: Estimated probability = successes/trials; expected count = future trials × probability.
steps: Use all recorded trials as the denominator.
Convert the count to a proportion.
Multiply by future trials under comparable conditions.
Describe the result as an expectation.
methods.example: 42 successes in 70 trials give 0.6; expected successes in 150 comparable trials = 90.
methods.check: The predicted count is between 0 and 150 and has the same proportion.
methods.trap: An expected count is neither guaranteed nor a claim that conditions will remain unchanged.

methods.title: Fill two- and three-set regions
methods.when: Totals overlap, and the question says only, both, exactly or neither.
methods.rule: n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B). For three sets: n(A∪B∪C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)−n(A∩B)−n(A∩C)−n(B∩C)+n(A∩B∩C).
steps: Put the triple overlap in first.
Subtract it from each inclusive pair count.
Subtract the known overlap regions from each set total.
Add the disjoint regions; subtract the union from the universal total.
methods.example: If n(A)=18, n(A∩B)=7, n(A∩C)=6 and the triple is 2: A∩B only = 5, A∩C only = 4, so A only = 18−5−4−2 = 7.
methods.check: Reassemble each complete set from its separate regions.
methods.trap: Pair intersections include the triple unless the question says “A and B only”.

methods.title: Read logical words as events
methods.when: The question contrasts at least one, exactly one, both or neither.
methods.rule: “Or” means union; “and” means intersection; “exactly one” selects only single-set regions.
steps: Translate the words into regions.
Add only those disjoint regions.
Divide by the full selection population.
methods.example: In three sets, “at least two” includes all three pair-only regions plus the triple region.
methods.check: Compare the chosen region list with the wording before calculating.
methods.trap: Adding inclusive pair intersections counts the triple three times.

methods.title: Update conditional tree branches
methods.when: Selection without replacement or a first event changes the second chance.
methods.rule: P(A then B) = P(A)P(B given A).
steps: Write the first-stage counts.
Update both colour count and total on every second-stage branch.
Multiply along a complete path.
Add disjoint favourable paths and compare with the complement if useful.
methods.example: 4 red and 3 blue, two draws without replacement: P(RB or BR) = (4/7)(3/6)+(3/7)(4/6)=4/7.
methods.trap: Do not keep the original denominator after removing a counter.

checks: Every probability lies from 0 to 1; complementary probabilities total 1.
Every person or outcome belongs to exactly one disjoint region.
At each tree split the conditional branch probabilities total 1.
State whether selection is random, outcomes equally likely, and replacement used.
Use the updated total after objects are removed or added.

challenges.title: Three clubs, eight separate regions
challenges.question: A group has 60 pupils. Rugby R has 30, music M has 25 and chess C has 20. The inclusive pair counts are R∩M = 12, R∩C = 8 and M∩C = 7; 4 pupils do all three. A pupil is chosen at random. (a) Find all seven regions inside the sets and the number outside. (b) Find the probability of exactly one activity. (c) Find the probability of at least two activities.
hints: Start with the triple and subtract it from each pair count.
Exactly one uses the three single-set regions; at least two uses the pair-only regions and the triple once.

solution.title: Separate the pairs
solution.math: RM only = 8; RC only = 4; MC only = 3; triple = 4
solution.reason: Inclusive pair counts contain the triple.

solution.title: Find single activities
solution.math: R only = 14; M only = 10; C only = 9
solution.reason: Subtract all the disjoint overlap regions from each set total.

solution.title: Complete the population
solution.reason: Disjoint regions count every pupil once.

solution.title: Find exactly one
solution.reason: Only the single-set regions qualify.

solution.title: Find at least two
solution.reason: The triple is included once, not three times.

challenges.answer: R only 14, M only 10, C only 9; RM only 8, RC only 4, MC only 3, triple 4, outside 8. Probabilities: 11/20 and 19/60.
challenges.check: The eight regions total 60; reconstruct R = 14+8+4+4 = 30, M = 10+8+3+4 = 25 and C = 9+4+3+4 = 20.

challenges.title: Add a new colour without losing the old counts
challenges.question: A bag initially contains 48 counters, red and blue in ratio 3:5. Green counters are then added until the probability that a counter chosen at random is green is 25%. (a) Find the original red and blue counts. (b) Find the number of green counters added. (c) Find the new probability of blue and compare it with the original probability.
hints: Find the size of one ratio part first.
Let g be the added count and use g/(48+g)=1/4.

solution.title: Recover the counts
solution.reason: Both ratio parts refer to the original total.

solution.title: Model the final share
solution.reason: The denominator must include the added counters.

solution.title: Solve the addition
solution.reason: Equivalent equation operations find the required count.

solution.title: Compare blue chances
solution.reason: The blue count stays fixed but the total grows.

solution.title: Measure the change
solution.reason: The fall is 5/32, about 15.6 percentage points; blue does not simply lose the 25% that green now holds.

challenges.answer: 18 red, 30 blue; add 16 green. Blue probability changes from 5/8 to 15/32, a decrease of 5/32.
challenges.check: The final probabilities are 18/64+30/64+16/64=1 and green is exactly 1/4.

challenges.title: Compare replacement rules
challenges.question: A bag contains 4 red and 3 blue counters. Two are selected randomly. (a) Without replacement, find the probability of one of each colour and of two matching colours. (b) With replacement and remixing, find the probability of one of each. (c) Which procedure makes one of each more likely, and by how much? (d) For 140 repetitions of the without-replacement experiment, resetting the bag each time, predict the number with one of each.
hints: Use two paths for one of each: RB and BR.
Without replacement the second denominator is 6; with replacement it is 7.

solution.title: Use the updated branches
solution.reason: The first counter changes the second draw.

solution.title: Add and complement
solution.reason: The two events exhaust all outcomes.

solution.title: Replace and remix
solution.reason: The original colour proportions are restored.

solution.title: Compare exactly
solution.reason: Use a common denominator.

solution.title: Predict a count
solution.reason: Expected frequency is number of repetitions times probability.

challenges.answer: Without replacement: one of each 4/7, matching 3/7. With replacement: one of each 24/49. Without replacement is higher by 4/49. Expected count 80.
challenges.check: Directly count matching paths without replacement: (4/7)(3/6)+(3/7)(2/6)=3/7, agreeing with the complement.

challenges.title: A biased coin: paths and a shortcut
challenges.question: A biased coin has P(heads)=3/5 on every toss; successive tosses are independent. (a) Find P(exactly one head in two tosses). (b) List the favourable paths and find P(exactly two heads in three tosses). (c) Find P(at least one head in three tosses) using a complement. (d) Predict the number of exactly-two-heads results in 250 independent repetitions of the three-toss experiment.
hints: Use 3/5 for H and 2/5 for T at every branch.
For part (b), list HHT, HTH and THH. For part (c), the only excluded path is TTT.

solution.title: Two-toss paths
solution.reason: HT and TH are disjoint and have equal products.

solution.title: List three-toss paths
solution.math: Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH
solution.reason: Order creates three different complete outcomes.

solution.title: Add their products
solution.reason: Independence permits multiplication; mutually exclusive paths permit addition.

solution.title: Use the complement
solution.reason: The complement is no heads, namely TTT.

solution.title: Predict a count
solution.reason: Expected frequency multiplies repetitions by probability, without guaranteeing the result.

challenges.answer: 12/25; favourable paths HHT, HTH, THH with total 54/125; at least one head 117/125; expected exactly-two-heads count 108.
challenges.check: For three tosses, P(0H), P(1H), P(2H), P(3H) are 8/125, 36/125, 54/125, 27/125; their sum is 1.

title: Simultaneous equations
intro: Find the values that make two equations true at the same time.
prerequisites: Multiplying every term in an equation

lessons.title: Eliminate one unknown, then find the other
lessons.goal: Scale complete equations, eliminate a variable and check both answers.

steps.title: Read the pair together
steps.text: Solve 2x + 3y = 17 and 3x − 2y = 6. A solution must satisfy both equations, not just one.
steps.why: Each equation is a separate constraint on the same pair.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2x + 3y = 17</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3x − 2y = 6</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Two unknowns need two independent equations.</text></svg>

steps.title: Scale the whole equations
steps.text: Choose multipliers 2 and 3 so the y-coefficients will become opposites. Put each whole left side in brackets and multiply the right side too.
steps.why: Multiplying both sides by the same non-zero number preserves equality.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(2x + 3y) = 2(17)</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3(3x − 2y) = 3(6)</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Scale BOTH sides: first equation ×2, second equation ×3.</text></svg>

steps.title: Make opposite y-coefficients
steps.text: Multiply the first whole equation by 2 and the second whole equation by 3. The y-coefficients become +6 and −6.
steps.why: Opposite coefficients, +6 and −6, cancel when the equations are added.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">4x + 6y = 34</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">9x − 6y = 18</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">EVERY term is multiplied, including the right-hand sides.</text></svg>

steps.title: Add the complete equations
steps.text: Adding cancels the y-terms. The remaining equation is 13x = 52, so x = 4.
steps.why: Equal quantities can be added to equal quantities.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">13x + 0y = 52</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x = 4</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Add the two rows: +6y and −6y cancel.</text></svg>

steps.title: Back-substitute
steps.text: Use x = 4 in the first original equation. Eight plus three y equals seventeen, giving y = 3.
steps.why: Substitution turns the two-variable equation into a one-variable equation.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(4) + 3y = 17</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3y = 9 → y = 3</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Back-substitute x = 4 into an original equation.</text></svg>

steps.title: Check both original equations
steps.text: The pair (4, 3) gives 17 in the first equation and 6 in the second. A check in just one equation would be incomplete.
steps.why: The pair is simultaneous only when both conditions hold.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the entire equation balanced"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the entire equation balanced</text><rect id="equation0" x="65" y="95" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row0" x="380" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2(4) + 3(3) = 17 ✓</text><rect id="equation1" x="65" y="195" width="630" height="76" rx="12" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2" /><text id="row1" x="380" y="245" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="31" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">3(4) − 2(3) = 6 ✓</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">The same pair works in BOTH original equations.</text></svg>

quiz.question: Solve x + y = 9 and x − y = 3. What is (x, y)?
quiz.hint: Add the equations to eliminate y.
quiz.explanation: 2x = 12 gives x = 6; then y = 3. Both equations check.

quiz.question: Multiply 2x − 3y = 7 by 4. Which equation results?
quiz.hint: The multiplier applies to every term on both sides.

lessons.takeaway: Match coefficients, eliminate, substitute back, then check both originals.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying only the variable you want to eliminate changes the equation.

lessons.title: See the solution where lines meet
lessons.goal: Interpret a simultaneous solution as an intersection and model a word problem.

steps.title: Turn a story into two equations
steps.text: At a school event, an adult ticket costs x euro and a child ticket y euro. One adult plus one child costs €11; two adults plus one child cost €18.
steps.why: The same ticket prices must fit both purchases.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="The story sets two constraints"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">The story sets two constraints</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">1 adult + 1 child = €11</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2 adults + 1 child = €18</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x + y = 11; 2x + y = 18</text></svg>

steps.title: Plot the first equation
steps.text: Write y = 11 − x and plot two points such as (3, 8) and (9, 2). Join them with a straight line.
steps.why: Every point on the line satisfies the first purchase.

steps.title: Add the second line
steps.text: The second equation is y = 18 − 2x; plot (4, 10) and (8, 2) and join them. The two lines cross at (7, 4).
steps.why: An intersection belongs to both lines, so it satisfies both equations.

steps.title: Know what other graph shapes mean
steps.text: Distinct parallel lines never meet, so there is no common solution. Coincident lines describe the same constraint and have infinitely many shared points.
steps.why: A pair of equations need not always determine a unique pair.
steps.math: Crossing: one; parallel: none; same line: infinitely many
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Count common points, not just equations"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Count common points, not just equations</text><line id="line-auto-1" x1="65" y1="145" x2="235" y2="285" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><line id="line-auto-2" x1="65" y1="285" x2="235" y2="145" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><circle id="circle-auto-1" cx="150" cy="215" r="6" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="150" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">One solution</text><line id="line-auto-3" x1="295" y1="145" x2="455" y2="265" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><line id="line-auto-4" x1="295" y1="190" x2="455" y2="310" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-2" x="375" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">No solution</text><line id="line-auto-5" x1="525" y1="145" x2="695" y2="285" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="8" /><line id="line-auto-6" x1="525" y1="145" x2="695" y2="285" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-3" x="610" y="330" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Same line</text></svg>

quiz.question: A pair of line graphs intersects at (−2, 5). What is the simultaneous solution?
quiz.hint: Coordinates are ordered as x then y.
quiz.explanation: The intersection gives x = −2 and y = 5.

quiz.question: How many solutions do y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 have?
quiz.hint: Compare the slopes and the intercepts.
quiz.explanation: They have the same slope but different intercepts, so they are distinct parallel lines and never meet.

lessons.takeaway: A graphical solution is a point satisfying both equations.
lessons.mistake: A line intersection may be approximate; substitute or solve algebraically to confirm exact values.

reference.name: Equivalent equations
reference.formula: Multiply both sides, and every term, by the same non-zero number.
reference.note: The solution set does not change.

reference.name: Elimination
reference.formula: Match coefficients, then add or subtract whole equations.
reference.note: Choose the operation that cancels one unknown.

reference.name: Graphical solution
reference.note: Parallel distinct lines have no common solution; the same line has infinitely many.

toolkit.strategy: Define two unknowns with units. Translate two independent facts, then choose elimination or substitution; a numerical solution must also fit the original story.

methods.title: Clear fractions before elimination
methods.when: Each equation contains fractional terms.
methods.rule: Multiply each whole equation by the least common multiple of its denominators; denominators must be non-zero.
steps: Choose an LCM separately for each equation.
Multiply every term, including constants.
Match one coefficient, add or subtract, then back-substitute.
methods.check: Original checks: 4+1=5 and 2−1/2=3/2.
methods.trap: Clearing only the variable fractions changes the equation.

methods.title: Choose elimination or substitution
methods.when: One variable is easy to isolate, or coefficients can be matched simply.
methods.rule: Equivalent equation operations preserve the common solution set.
steps: Use substitution when a variable has coefficient 1 or is already isolated.
Use elimination when coefficients are equal/opposite or simple multiples.
Find the second unknown in an original equation.
Check both.
methods.example: x+y=11 and 2x+y=18: subtract to obtain x=7, then y=4.
methods.trap: A value that satisfies only one equation is not a simultaneous solution.

methods.title: Model wages and two kinds of items
methods.when: Two purchases or shifts use the same two unknown rates.
methods.rule: Total = quantity₁ × rate₁ + quantity₂ × rate₂.
steps: Define each unknown rate and its units.
Translate each total separately.
Solve and interpret the rates.
methods.example: Example wages: 6r+2s=108, 4r+5s=138 ⇒ r=€12/h, s=€18/h.
methods.check: Both wage totals recompute correctly.
methods.trap: The numbers of hours are coefficients, not the unknown rates.

methods.title: Recover fixed and daily costs
methods.when: A price has a one-off part and a repeating daily/unit part.
methods.rule: C=F+nd; two distinct n-values identify F and d.
steps: Subtract two totals to remove F.
Divide the cost difference by the unit difference.
Back-substitute for F.
Use the model for a new duration; round down an affordable whole-day count.
methods.example: Example hire: 3 days €86 and 7 days €158 ⇒ d=€18/day, F=€32; 10 days €212.
methods.trap: Do not charge the fixed cost once per day.

methods.title: Translate ages and changed fractions
methods.when: The story changes the same quantities by adding or subtracting fixed amounts.
methods.rule: Age k years ago: x−k. Changed fraction: (n+a)/(d+b), with d+b≠0.
steps: Define present ages or original numerator and denominator.
Apply each change to the correct quantity.
Cross-multiply valid fractions or expand age relations.
Solve, then check the changed situations.
methods.example: Ages x+y=42 and x−6=2(y−6) give x=26, y=16. A changed denominator affects the whole denominator.
methods.check: Six years ago the ages were 20 and 10, and their current sum is 42.
methods.trap: “Twice the age six years ago” means 2(y−6), not 2y−6.

methods.title: Model folded rectangles
methods.when: A fold halves one dimension and a new perimeter is supplied.
methods.rule: P=2(L+W); after halving W, the folded perimeter is 2L+W.
steps: Name the original dimensions.
State which dimension the fold halves.
Write each perimeter using its actual dimensions.
Solve and check the original and folded rectangles.
methods.example: Original perimeter 50 and W-halved perimeter 40: 2L+2W=50, 2L+W=40 ⇒ W=10, L=15.
methods.trap: A fold does not generally halve the perimeter.

methods.title: Interpret intersections and exceptional systems
methods.when: A question asks about a common point or number of solutions.
methods.rule: Crossing lines: one pair; distinct parallel lines: none; coincident lines: infinitely many.
steps: Rearrange where useful to compare slopes and intercepts.
Solve algebraically for an exact point.
Interpret a contradiction or identity after elimination.
methods.example: 2x+2y=8 and x+y=5 give 0=−2, so no common point.
methods.check: The two equivalent slope forms have equal slopes but different intercepts.
methods.trap: Two written equations do not automatically give a unique answer.

checks: Multiply every term on both sides when clearing fractions or matching coefficients.
Use the same unknown consistently in both equations.
Check both original equations, including their original fractions.
Reject impossible ages, lengths, counts or denominators.
State units and whether an answer must be a whole number.

challenges.title: Fractions first, simultaneous equations second
challenges.question: Solve x/2 + y/3 = 5 and x/4 − y/6 = 3/2. (a) Clear the denominators, showing what multiplies every term. (b) Solve the system. (c) Verify the answer in the two original fractional equations.
hints: The LCMs are 6 and 12.
After clearing, the y coefficients are opposites.

solution.title: Clear the first equation
solution.reason: The multiplier applies to every term.

solution.title: Clear the second
solution.reason: The constant is multiplied too.

solution.title: Eliminate
solution.reason: Adding cancels y.

solution.title: Back-substitute
solution.reason: Use either equivalent equation.

solution.title: Check originals
solution.reason: Both fractional equations are satisfied.

challenges.answer: x=8 and y=3; cleared equations 3x+2y=30 and 3x−2y=18.
challenges.check: Direct substitution gives 5 and 3/2, independently confirming the transformed system.

challenges.title: Find ordinary and overtime rates
challenges.question: A part-time job pays one hourly rate for ordinary hours and a higher rate for overtime hours. A shift of 6 ordinary hours and 2 overtime hours pays €108. Another shift of 4 ordinary hours and 5 overtime hours pays €138. (a) Define the rates and form two equations. (b) Find both rates. (c) Calculate the pay for 9 ordinary hours and 3 overtime hours.
hints: Let r be the ordinary hourly rate and s the overtime hourly rate.
Multiply the first equation by 5 and the second by 2 to eliminate s.

solution.title: Model both shifts
solution.reason: Each total is hours times its corresponding rate.

solution.title: Match overtime
solution.reason: Whole equations are scaled.

solution.title: Subtract
solution.reason: The overtime terms cancel.

solution.title: Find overtime
solution.reason: Substitute into an original shift.

solution.title: Price the new shift
solution.reason: Apply the same two rates.

challenges.answer: Ordinary €12/hour; overtime €18/hour; new shift €162.
challenges.check: 4×12+5×18=138 and 6×12+2×18=108, checking both supplied shifts.

challenges.title: A hire quote and a maximum budget
challenges.question: A bicycle-hire company charges a fixed fee plus a constant fee per complete day. Three days cost €86 and seven days cost €158. (a) Find the fixed and daily fees. (b) Price ten days. (c) Find the greatest number of complete days affordable with €250 and prove the next day is unaffordable.
hints: Subtract the two quotes to isolate four daily fees.
After finding the fixed fee, subtract it from the budget before dividing by the daily fee.

solution.title: Write the model
solution.reason: The fixed fee is paid once in each quote.

solution.title: Find the repeating fee
solution.reason: Subtracting removes F.

solution.title: Find the fixed fee
solution.reason: Use a supplied quote.

solution.title: Extrapolate
solution.reason: Ten days use ten daily fees.

solution.title: Use the budget
solution.reason: Only complete days are allowed.

solution.title: Check the boundary
solution.reason: Test the last allowed and first disallowed integer.

challenges.answer: Fixed fee €32; daily fee €18; ten days €212; maximum 12 complete days.
challenges.check: The recovered model also gives 7 days = €158; testing 12 and 13 proves the budget maximum.

challenges.title: Recover an original fraction
challenges.question: An original fraction has positive integer numerator n and denominator d. Increasing only the numerator by 2 makes the fraction 1/2. Increasing only the denominator by 4 makes the original fraction 1/3. (a) Form two equations. (b) Find n and d. (c) Simplify the original fraction and check both changes using the original counts.
hints: Cross-multiplication gives d=2n+4 and d=3n−4.

solution.title: Translate the changes
solution.reason: Only the specified part changes in each situation.

solution.title: Clear valid denominators
solution.reason: Positive denominators allow cross-multiplication.

solution.title: Eliminate d
solution.reason: Both expressions describe the same denominator.

solution.title: Recover d
solution.reason: Substitute and then simplify the original fraction.

solution.title: Check both changes
solution.reason: The conditions refer to original counts, not the simplified numerator and denominator.

challenges.answer: n=8, d=20; original fraction 8/20=2/5.
challenges.check: Using the reduced counts 2 and 5 would fail the stated changes; 8 and 20 pass both.

title: Coordinate Geometry — The Line
intro: Use coordinates to measure, describe and connect straight lines.

lessons.title: Measure a segment and locate its midpoint
lessons.goal: Use coordinate differences for length and coordinate averages for midpoint.

steps.text: Take A(−2, 1) and B(4, 9). Read x horizontally and y vertically; do not swap them.
steps.why: Coordinates identify positions, not distances by themselves.

steps.title: Make a right-angled triangle
steps.text: The horizontal change is 4 − (−2) = 6. The vertical change is 9 − 1 = 8. These are the two perpendicular sides of a right-angled triangle.
steps.why: Coordinate-grid directions meet at right angles.

steps.title: Use Pythagoras for the distance
steps.text: Square both changes, add, and take the positive square root. The length is 10 units.
steps.why: The segment is the hypotenuse of the constructed right-angled triangle.

steps.title: Substitute with brackets
steps.text: Put 5 in place of y₁, 2 in place of x₁ and 3 in place of m. Brackets protect the whole x-difference.
steps.why: The slope multiplies the entire change in x.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Place known values into the template"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Place known values into the template</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">y − 5 = 3(x − 2)</text></svg>

steps.title: Expand and rearrange
steps.text: Multiply 3 by both terms in the bracket, then add 5 to both sides. The result is y = 3x − 1.
steps.why: Equivalent equation operations keep the same line.

steps.title: Use slope to move from the intercept
steps.text: Starting at (0, 3), move right 1 and up 2 to (1, 5). Repeat to get (2, 7).
steps.why: Slope 2 means a rise of 2 for a run of 1.

steps.title: Rearrange before reading
steps.text: For 2x + 3y = 12, first isolate y. Subtract 2x, then divide every term by 3.
steps.why: The x-coefficient is the slope only in the form y = mx + c.

steps.title: Check intercept and direction
steps.text: This line crosses the y-axis at (0, 4) and falls from left to right. Moving right 3 lowers y by 2.
steps.why: Negative slope matches a falling graph.

quiz.question: What are the slope and y-intercept of y = −4x + 7?
quiz.hint: Match with y = mx + c.
quiz.explanation: The x-coefficient is −4 and the constant is 7.

quiz.question: What is the slope of 3x + 2y = 8?
quiz.hint: Isolate y first.
quiz.explanation: y = −(3/2)x + 4, so the slope is −3/2.

lessons.takeaway: Isolate y, then read its x-coefficient and constant.
lessons.mistake: Find the y-intercept by setting x to zero, not y to zero.

lessons.title: Recognise parallel and perpendicular lines
lessons.goal: Compare slopes and handle horizontal or vertical exceptions.

steps.title: Compare slopes
steps.text: The lines y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 rise at the same rate. Different intercepts keep them separate.
steps.why: Distinct non-vertical parallel lines have equal slopes.

steps.title: Take a negative reciprocal
steps.text: A line perpendicular to slope 2 has slope −1/2. Their slope product is −1.
steps.why: For non-vertical perpendicular lines, m₁m₂ = −1.

steps.text: A perpendicular line through (4, 1) satisfies y − 1 = −(1/2)(x − 4). Simplify it to y = −x/2 + 3.
steps.why: A point and slope determine a non-vertical line.

quiz.question: Which slope is perpendicular to 3/4?
quiz.hint: Use the negative reciprocal.

quiz.question: Which pair is parallel and distinct?
quiz.hint: Look for equal slopes and different intercepts.
quiz.explanation: Both have slope 3 and different intercepts.

lessons.takeaway: Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular slopes are usually negative reciprocals.
lessons.mistake: The negative reciprocal of 3/4 is −4/3, not −3/4.

lessons.goal: Find intercepts, plot accurately and verify a third point.

steps.title: Join and check
steps.text: Join the two points with a straight line. Check (1, 4): two times one plus four equals six.
steps.why: Two distinct points determine a straight line.

steps.title: Read special equations
steps.text: The equation x = 3 fixes x but allows any y: it is vertical. The equation y = −2 fixes y and is horizontal.
steps.why: An equation may fix only one coordinate.

quiz.question: What is the x-intercept of 3x + 2y = 12?
quiz.hint: Set y = 0.
quiz.explanation: 3x = 12 gives x = 4, so the intercept is (4, 0).

quiz.question: Which point is on y = −3?
quiz.hint: Check the second coordinate.
quiz.explanation: (7, −3) has y-coordinate −3.

lessons.takeaway: Use two exact points and check a third.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse x = k with y = k.

lessons.title: Find where two lines intersect
lessons.goal: Equate two expressions for y, solve, and check both coordinates.

steps.title: Set the rules equal
steps.text: At the intersection of y = x + 2 and y = −2x + 8, the two expressions must give the same y-value.
steps.why: The intersection belongs to both lines.

steps.title: Find the shared x
steps.text: Add 2x to both sides and subtract 2. This gives 3x = 6, so x = 2.
steps.why: Equal operations preserve equality.

steps.title: Complete the coordinate pair
steps.text: Substitute x = 2 into y = x + 2. Then y = 4 and the intersection is (2, 4).
steps.why: A point requires both coordinates.

steps.title: Verify with the other rule
steps.text: The second rule gives −2(2) + 8 = 4. Both original equations agree.
steps.why: Checking both originals catches sign errors.

quiz.question: Where do y = 2x and y = x + 3 intersect?
quiz.hint: Set 2x = x + 3.
quiz.explanation: x = 3; then y = 6.

quiz.question: Why is finding only x insufficient?
quiz.hint: Recall the form of a coordinate pair.
quiz.explanation: An intersection is written (x, y), so both values are needed.

lessons.takeaway: Equate y-values, then use an original equation to find y.
lessons.mistake: Do not stop at x when the question asks for a point.

lessons.title: Give a slope real-world units
lessons.goal: Interpret rates and starting values in a straight-line model.

steps.title: Read the axes
steps.text: A taxi fare C euro is modelled by C = 2d + 5, where d is kilometres. The slope unit is euro per kilometre.
steps.why: Units identify the meaning of a rate.

steps.title: Interpret the intercept
steps.text: At zero kilometres, the model gives a cost of €5. This is the fixed starting charge.
steps.why: At zero input the variable term vanishes.

steps.title: Calculate the rate
steps.text: Cost rises from €7 to €13 as distance rises from 1 km to 4 km. Six euro over three kilometres gives €2/km.
steps.why: A line has constant change per unit input.

steps.title: Use the model
steps.text: A 6 km journey costs 2(6) + 5 = €17 in this example. Keep the fixed and variable charges separate.
steps.why: The model combines starting amount and accumulated change.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Fixed cost plus distance cost"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Fixed cost plus distance cost</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Fixed charge: €5</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">6 km × €2 per km = €12</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Total: €5 + €12 = €17</text></svg>

quiz.question: Volume falls from 80 L to 50 L in 6 min. What is the rate of change?
quiz.hint: Use final minus initial divided by time.

quiz.question: For C = 4n + 12, what does 12 represent?
quiz.hint: Set n to zero.
quiz.explanation: When n = 0, C = 12. It is the fixed cost.

lessons.takeaway: Slope is a rate with units; intercept is the value at zero input.
lessons.mistake: Do not confuse total cost with cost per unit.

reference.name: Distance
reference.note: Distance is non-negative.

reference.name: Midpoint
reference.note: Average each coordinate separately.

reference.name: Slope
reference.note: A vertical line has undefined slope.

reference.name: Point–slope equation
reference.note: Use one known point and a defined slope.

reference.name: Slope–intercept form
reference.note: c is the y-value when x = 0.

reference.name: Parallel / perpendicular
reference.note: The product rule applies to non-vertical lines; horizontal and vertical lines are perpendicular.

toolkit.strategy: Mark known points and the unknown target. Use differences for lengths and slopes, averages for midpoints, equations for whole lines and simultaneous equations for intersections.

methods.title: Measure a direct or multi-leg route
methods.when: A map asks for distance directly or via named points.
methods.rule: AB=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²]; via C means AC+CB.
steps: Calculate horizontal and vertical changes for each leg.
Apply Pythagoras separately to each required segment.
Add segment lengths for a route; compare with the direct distance.
methods.check: A broken route cannot be shorter than the straight segment joining its endpoints.
methods.trap: Do not add coordinate differences and call the result the direct distance.

methods.title: Find or reverse a midpoint
methods.when: A segment’s centre or an unknown endpoint is required.
methods.rule: M=((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2); missing endpoint B=2M−A coordinate by coordinate.
steps: Average corresponding coordinates for a midpoint.
For a missing endpoint, double the midpoint then subtract the known endpoint.
Check the midpoint again.
methods.trap: Distance uses differences; midpoint uses sums.

methods.title: Calculate a slope and classify exceptions
methods.when: Two points determine the line’s direction.
methods.rule: m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), provided x₂≠x₁; horizontal m=0; vertical slope undefined.
steps: Choose one point order and use it twice.
Check the denominator before dividing.
Interpret the sign from left to right.
methods.check: Swapping both point orders gives the same ratio.
methods.trap: A vertical line has undefined slope, not zero.

methods.title: Build a line from one point and slope
methods.when: You know a point and a finite slope, possibly found from other information.
methods.rule: y−y₁=m(x−x₁).
steps: Substitute the point with brackets.
Expand and collect to the requested form.
Check the original point.
methods.check: At x=−1 the equation gives y=5.
methods.trap: Subtracting a negative coordinate becomes addition.

methods.title: Read slope and intercept only after isolating y
methods.when: A line is given as ax+by+c=0 or y=mx+c.
methods.rule: For b≠0, ax+by+c=0 ⇒ m=−a/b and y-intercept −c/b.
steps: Isolate y before reading the x-coefficient.
Set x=0 for the y-intercept.
Handle b=0 as a vertical line separately.
methods.check: The point (0,4) satisfies the original form.
methods.trap: The x-coefficient in an unrearranged equation is not automatically the slope.

methods.title: Construct parallel and perpendicular lines
methods.when: A new line must have a stated relation to another line.
methods.rule: Parallel finite slopes: m₁=m₂. Perpendicular finite slopes: m₁m₂=−1. Horizontal y=k has slope 0; vertical x=k has undefined slope; a horizontal–vertical pair is perpendicular.
steps: Find the original slope.
Use the same slope for a parallel or the negative reciprocal for a perpendicular.
Insert the new point in point–slope form.
For a horizontal/vertical pair, write y=k or x=k directly.
methods.example: Perpendicular to y=−2x+3 through (4,5): m=1/2, y=x/2+3.
methods.check: (−2)(1/2)=−1 and (4,5) lies on the new line.
methods.trap: The product test cannot include an undefined vertical slope.

methods.title: Plot a line with checks
methods.when: A graph, intercepts or a drawn route is needed.
methods.rule: x-intercept: y=0; y-intercept: x=0.
steps: Find two distinct points, using intercepts if convenient.
Plot with labelled equal numerical steps on each axis.
Join with a straight line and check a third point.
methods.example: 2x+y=8 has intercepts (4,0),(0,8), with check point (1,6).
methods.trap: If both intercept calculations give the origin, choose another point instead of plotting one point twice.

methods.title: Find an exact intersection
methods.when: Two routes meet or a perpendicular reaches a given line.
methods.rule: At the intersection, both line equations hold.
steps: Equate two expressions for y or use elimination.
Solve for x, then find y.
Check both equations.
methods.example: y=−2x+3 and y=x/2+3 meet at (0,3).
methods.check: Both give y=3 at x=0.
methods.trap: A graph reading is approximate unless the coordinates are confirmed algebraically.

methods.title: Interpret a linear rate and its domain
methods.when: Coordinates represent cost, time, volume or another measured quantity.
methods.rule: y=mx+c: m=change in y/change in x; c is the value at x=0.
steps: Name both quantities and units.
Find the slope from two observations.
Find c and state the valid range of inputs.
Interpret predictions in context.
methods.example: A tank changes from 80 L at 0 min to 50 L at 6 min: V=80−5t; V=20 at t=12 min.
methods.check: The slope has units L/min, and both observed points fit.
methods.trap: A linear model should not be extended to physically impossible negative volume.

checks: Keep the same subtraction order in both parts of a slope.
An ordered pair is (x,y); an intercept includes its zero coordinate.
Keep square roots exact until the final requested rounding.
Check a derived line with both its slope and a supplied point.
Substitute an intersection into both line equations and attach map units.

challenges.title: Direct route or the boundary path?
challenges.question: On a coordinate map, one unit represents 100 m. A=(−2,1), B=(4,9) and C=(4,1). (a) Find the direct distance AB and the route AC then CB, in metres. (b) What percentage longer is the route via C than the direct route? (c) Find the midpoint of AB. (d) At a constant 5 km/h, how many minutes would each route take?
hints: The horizontal and vertical changes from A to B are 6 and 8.
Compare the extra route length with the direct length, not the longer length.

solution.title: Calculate the direct distance
solution.reason: Coordinate differences form perpendicular sides.

solution.title: Add the boundary legs
solution.reason: A route via a point uses a sum of segment lengths.

solution.title: Compare percentages
solution.reason: The direct distance is the reference amount.

solution.title: Locate the midpoint
solution.reason: Average corresponding coordinates.

solution.title: Convert distance to time
solution.reason: Use kilometres with km/h, then multiply hours by 60.

challenges.answer: 1000 m direct; 1400 m via C; 40% longer; midpoint (1,5); times 12 min and 16.8 min.
challenges.check: The direct segment is the hypotenuse of a 6–8–10 triangle; 1000 m divided by 12/60 h gives 5 km/h.

challenges.answer: M=(3,0), N=(1,2); MN ∥ BC; MN=2√2 and BC=4√2, so MN is half BC; line MN is y=−x+3.

challenges.title: A perpendicular access route
challenges.question: A straight path passes through T=(−2,5) and U=(4,−1). A base is at P=(4,5). A direct access route from P meets the path perpendicularly at I. One coordinate unit is 200 m. (a) Find equations of the path and the access line. (b) Find I. (c) Compare the exact distance PI with the alternative route P→U→I, in metres. (d) State the extra distance of the alternative route.
hints: The path has slope −1, so the access line has slope 1.
After finding I, calculate PU and UI separately for the alternative route.

solution.title: Find the path
solution.reason: Two points determine its slope and equation.

solution.title: Find the access line
solution.reason: Use a perpendicular slope and point P.

solution.title: Find the foot
solution.reason: Solve the two lines simultaneously.

solution.title: Find exact lengths
solution.math: PI=3√2 units; PU=6 units; UI=3√2 units
solution.reason: The coordinate differences determine each segment.

solution.title: Convert and compare
solution.reason: One unit is 200 m.

solution.title: Find the extra distance
solution.reason: The shared exact surd cancels.

challenges.answer: Path y=−x+3; access y=x+1; I=(1,2); direct 600√2 m; via U 1200+600√2 m; extra 1200 m.
challenges.check: I satisfies both lines and the slopes multiply to −1. PU is a vertical 6-unit segment, independently explaining the extra 1200 m.

title: Ratio — Time — Speed
intro: Keep units consistent while comparing shares, durations and journeys.

lessons.title: Share a total in a ratio
lessons.goal: Find equal parts and distinguish direct from inverse proportion.

steps.text: A ratio of 2 m to 50 cm must first become 200 cm to 50 cm. It simplifies to 4:1.
steps.why: A ratio compares like units.

quiz.question: Share €84 in the ratio 3:4. What is the smaller share?
quiz.hint: There are seven parts.
quiz.explanation: €84/7 = €12; three parts give €36.

quiz.question: For a fixed distance, speed doubles. What happens to time?
quiz.hint: Use time = distance/speed.
quiz.explanation: With distance unchanged, doubling speed halves the time.

lessons.takeaway: Find one equal part before finding each share.
lessons.mistake: A 2:3 split gives two fifths and three fifths, not two thirds and one third.

lessons.title: Work with clock time and elapsed time
lessons.goal: Convert time units and calculate durations across hours or midnight.

steps.title: Separate a reading from a duration
steps.text: 18:45 is a clock time. A duration of 1 hour 30 minutes equals 90 minutes or 1.5 hours.
steps.why: Hours contain 60 minutes, not 100.

steps.text: A bus leaves at 14:47 and arrives at 16:12. First count 13 minutes to 15:00.
steps.why: Whole-hour boundaries simplify subtraction.

steps.text: From 15:00 to 16:00 is 60 minutes; then add 12 minutes. Total: 13 + 60 + 12 = 85 minutes.
steps.why: Adjacent intervals add to the total.

steps.title: Cross midnight deliberately
steps.text: From 23:40 to 00:15 the next day is 20 minutes to midnight and 15 minutes afterwards. The duration is 35 minutes.
steps.why: Include the day change rather than subtracting clock readings blindly.

quiz.question: Express 2 h 45 min in decimal hours.
quiz.hint: Divide the minutes by 60.

quiz.question: A train leaves at 09:38 and arrives at 11:05. How long is the journey?
quiz.hint: Count to 10:00, then 11:00, then five more minutes.

lessons.takeaway: Convert minutes using 60; split awkward intervals at whole hours or midnight.
lessons.mistake: 1 h 30 min is not 1.30 decimal hours.

lessons.title: Choose speed, distance or time
lessons.goal: Rearrange the journey relationship and calculate average speed.

steps.title: Match the units
steps.text: A cyclist covers 18 km in 45 minutes. Convert the time to 0.75 hours before calculating kilometres per hour.
steps.why: Time units must match the speed unit.

steps.title: Divide distance by time
steps.text: Speed is 18 divided by 0.75, giving 24 km/h. Always include the unit.
steps.why: Speed means distance per unit time.

steps.text: At 8 m/s for 15 s, distance is 120 m. For 120 m at 8 m/s, time is 15 s. Convert m/s to km/h by multiplying by 3.6.
steps.why: Inverse operations rearrange d = vt.
steps.math: d = vt; t = d/v; 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h

quiz.question: A runner covers 400 m in 80 s. What is the average speed?
quiz.hint: Divide total distance by total time.

quiz.question: Convert 10 m/s to km/h.
quiz.hint: Multiply by 3.6.

lessons.takeaway: Average speed is total distance divided by total elapsed time.
lessons.mistake: Do not simply average two speeds when their durations differ.

reference.name: Share in ratio a:b
reference.note: Convert to matching units first.

reference.name: Direct proportion
reference.note: The ratio y/x stays constant.

reference.name: Inverse proportion
reference.note: The product stays constant.

reference.name: Journey formulae
reference.formula: v = d/t; d = vt; t = d/v
reference.note: Use compatible units.

toolkit.strategy: Put quantities into compatible units first. Decide whether the situation fixes a ratio, a product, a total amount of work, or a journey distance before choosing the calculation.

methods.title: Share a total or reconstruct it from one share
methods.when: A ratio and either the total or one participant’s share is given.
methods.rule: A:B=a:b ⇒ A=aN/(a+b), B=bN/(a+b) for total N. If A is known, one part=A/a and N=(a+b)A/a (a≠0).
steps: Convert units if needed.
Find the value of one part from the information actually given.
Multiply by each required number of parts.
methods.example: If A:B=3:5 and A=€72, one part is €24; B=€120 and total=€192.
methods.check: 72:120 simplifies to 3:5.
methods.trap: Dividing the known share by a+b treats it incorrectly as the total.

methods.title: Mix quantities with different ratios
methods.when: Two jugs or batches have unequal sizes and different ingredient ratios.
methods.rule: Ingredient amount = batch volume × ingredient parts/total parts.
steps: Convert every volume to the same unit.
Find the actual amount of each ingredient in each batch.
Add matching ingredient amounts, then simplify the final ratio.
methods.example: 1.5 L at 2:3 gives 0.6 L juice; 2 L at 3:7 gives 0.6 L juice. Mixed juice:water = 1.2:2.3 = 12:23.
methods.check: Ingredient amounts sum to the combined volume 3.5 L.
methods.trap: Do not average the two ratios when the volumes differ.

methods.title: Identify direct or inverse proportion
methods.when: Changing one quantity changes another under a fixed condition.
methods.rule: Direct: y=kx. Inverse: xy=k. For identical workers, workers × time = fixed work.
steps: Name what stays fixed.
Find the constant ratio or product.
Use the same constant for the new situation.
methods.example: 6 equal workers need 15 days: 90 worker-days; 9 such workers need 10 days.
methods.trap: Worker-time is inverse only under comparable productivity and divisible work with no added bottleneck.

methods.title: Update a partly completed work problem
methods.when: The number of workers changes after some work is done.
methods.rule: Remaining worker-days = total worker-days − completed worker-days.
steps: Calculate the total work in worker-days.
Subtract work already completed.
Divide the remainder by the new number of equal workers.
Add elapsed time if total time is requested.
methods.example: 6 workers need 15 days. After 4 days, 66 worker-days remain; 11 workers need 6 more days, 10 days total.
methods.trap: Do not restart the entire original workload when the team changes.

methods.title: Read durations across midnight
methods.when: A journey passes an hour boundary, midnight or a connection.
methods.rule: 1 h=60 min; 1 day=24 h. Duration=finish−start on one continuous timeline; add 24 h to a next-day clock time before subtracting.
steps: Separate clock times from durations.
Count to midnight and onward, or convert to a continuous minute timeline.
Include waiting times once.
methods.check: Adding 95 minutes to 23:42 reaches 01:17.
methods.trap: 01:17 is not earlier in the journey just because its clock number is smaller.

methods.title: Use compatible speed units
methods.when: A distance, speed or time is unknown.
methods.rule: v=d/t; d=vt; t=d/v; 1 m/s=3.6 km/h.
steps: Identify the requested quantity.
Convert units to match before substituting.
Calculate and include the compound speed unit.
methods.check: 24 km/h for 3/4 h gives 18 km.
methods.trap: 45 minutes is 0.75 hours, not 0.45 hours.

methods.title: Average a whole journey
methods.when: Different legs have different speeds or durations.
methods.rule: Average speed = total distance / total elapsed time; use moving time only if explicitly asked.
steps: Find each leg’s distance or time as needed.
Add all relevant distances.
Add all relevant times, including stops for an overall average.
Divide totals.
methods.example: 72 km/h for 40 min and 48 km/h for 35 min: 76 km in 1.25 h gives 60.8 km/h.
methods.check: The total distance reconstructed from the average and total time is 76 km.
methods.trap: The arithmetic mean of speeds works only for equal time durations.

checks: Ratio quantities must use matching units.
Preserve the actual amount of each ingredient when mixing.
Convert minutes to hours by dividing by 60, not 100.
Average speed is total distance divided by the relevant total time.
State equal-productivity assumptions in worker-time questions and include stops if overall speed is requested.

challenges.title: Unequal legs and a rest stop
challenges.question: A coach travels at 72 km/h for 40 minutes and then 48 km/h for 35 minutes. (a) Find the total distance. (b) Find its average speed while moving. (c) If a 15-minute stop occurs between the two legs, find the overall average speed including the stop. Explain why averaging 72 and 48 is unsuitable.
hints: Turn each duration into hours before finding its distance.
The stop adds time but no distance.

solution.title: Find leg distances
solution.reason: Each distance is speed times its own duration.

solution.title: Combine distance
solution.reason: Add the two legs.

solution.title: Average while moving
solution.reason: Use total distance over total moving time.

solution.title: Include the stop
solution.reason: The 15-minute stop contributes only time.

solution.title: Explain the weighting
solution.math: (72+48)/2=60 km/h is not the moving average
solution.reason: The two speeds lasted for unequal durations, so an unweighted mean is inappropriate.

challenges.answer: 76 km; moving average 60.8 km/h; overall average 50⅔ km/h with the stop.
challenges.check: 60.8×1.25=76 and (152/3)×1.5=76; including a stop lowers the average as expected.

challenges.title: Mix two different jugs
challenges.question: Jug A contains 1500 ml of juice and water in ratio 2:3. Jug B contains 2 L in ratio 3:7. They are mixed. (a) Find the amount of juice and water in each jug, in litres. (b) Find the ratio of juice to water in the mixture. (c) How much pure juice must be added to make the final mixture half juice?
hints: Calculate actual ingredient volumes before combining the ratios.
For the final step, (1.2+x)/(3.5+x)=1/2.

solution.title: Convert and split A
solution.math: 1500 ml=1.5 L; juice=0.6 L, water=0.9 L
solution.reason: Use 2/5 and 3/5 of the same volume.

solution.title: Split B
solution.reason: The second jug uses ten total parts.

solution.title: Combine
solution.reason: Add like ingredients, not ratio numbers.

solution.title: Model added juice
solution.reason: The added juice increases both numerator and total.

solution.title: Solve and check
solution.math: x=1.1 L; final juice=2.3 L and water=2.3 L
solution.reason: Equal ingredient volumes give a half-juice mixture.

challenges.answer: A: 0.6 L juice, 0.9 L water; B: 0.6 L juice, 1.4 L water. Mixed ratio 12:23. Add 1.1 L pure juice.
challenges.check: The initial component volumes total 3.5 L; after adding, 2.3/4.6=1/2.

challenges.title: A team changes after work has begun
challenges.question: Six equally productive workers can complete a job in 15 working days. Assume the work is divisible and the productivity per worker remains constant. (a) How long would nine workers need from the start? (b) Instead, six workers work for four days, then eleven workers take over the remaining work. Find the remaining time and the total completion time. (c) Explain which assumption makes this method valid.
hints: Measure work in worker-days.
Subtract 6×4 from the total before dividing by 11.

solution.title: Quantify the job
solution.reason: Each identical worker contributes the same daily amount.

solution.title: Change the starting team
solution.reason: The same work is divided among nine workers.

solution.title: Find the remainder
solution.reason: Only unfinished work remains for the new team.

solution.title: Find completion time
solution.reason: Add the elapsed and remaining periods.

solution.title: State the model condition
solution.math: Constant equal productivity and divisible work
solution.reason: Extra workers must not introduce unmodelled delays or change individual output.

challenges.answer: Nine workers: 10 days. Changed-team plan: 6 further days, 10 days total, under the stated constant-productivity assumptions.
challenges.check: The changed-team output is 6×4+11×6=90 worker-days, exactly the original workload.

challenges.title: A midnight connection and two averages
challenges.question: A bus leaves at 23:42 and reaches a connection at 01:17 the next day after 114 km. After an 18-minute wait, a second bus travels 78 km in 65 minutes. (a) Find the first journey duration and the final arrival time. (b) Find each bus’s average speed. (c) Find the overall average speed for the 192 km journey, including waiting, to 1 decimal place. (d) Compare it with the average while travelling only.
hints: Count the first duration through midnight; put the second departure at 01:35.
Elapsed time includes both journeys plus 18 minutes; moving time excludes the wait.

solution.title: Read the timeline
solution.math: First leg=95 min; second departure=01:35; arrival=02:40
solution.reason: Count 18 min to midnight and 77 min after it; the clock resetting at 00:00 does not make the duration negative.

solution.title: Find each speed
solution.reason: Use hours in the denominator.

solution.title: Add elapsed time
solution.reason: The waiting period is included once.

solution.title: Find overall speed
solution.reason: Round only the final quotient.

solution.title: Find moving average
solution.reason: Both moving legs use 72 km/h; waiting lowers the overall rate.

challenges.answer: First leg 95 min; final arrival 02:40 next day. Each bus averages 72 km/h; overall 64.7 km/h; moving average 72 km/h.
challenges.check: From 23:42 to 02:40 is 2 h 58 min=178 min; 72×160/60=192 km checks the moving total.

steps.title: Convert a share to an angle
steps.text: Rugby is 10 out of 20, exactly half. Its angle is half of 360°, or 180°.
steps.why: Angles preserve the same proportions as frequencies.

steps.title: Calculate every sector
steps.text: Football gives 6/20 × 360° = 108°. Other gives 4/20 × 360° = 72°. Draw each angle at the centre, starting where the previous sector ends.
steps.why: The sectors do not overlap and together fill the circle, so their angles must add to 360°.

steps.title: Check and work backwards
steps.text: The three angles total 360°. A 72° sector in a group of 20 represents 72/360 × 20 = 4 pupils.
steps.why: Reverse the proportional relationship to recover a count.

quiz.question: A category has frequency 15 out of 60. What is its pie-chart angle?
quiz.hint: Find its fraction of the whole turn.

quiz.question: A sector is 120° in a chart of 45 people. How many people does it represent?
quiz.hint: 120° is what fraction of 360°?

lessons.takeaway: Frequency/total and sector angle/360° express the same proportion.
lessons.mistake: Do not multiply a raw frequency by 360° without dividing by the total.

lessons.title: Make histogram areas tell the truth
lessons.goal: Interpret continuous classes and use density when widths differ (extension: JC exam histograms use equal widths).

steps.why: Non-overlapping class boundaries assign each value once.

steps.text: Time is continuous and the classes meet at their boundaries, so histogram bars touch. Category bars in a bar chart usually have gaps.
steps.why: A histogram represents intervals of continuous values.

quiz.question: A histogram class has width 5 and frequency 20. What is its frequency density?
quiz.hint: Divide frequency by class width.

quiz.question: In 10 ≤ t < 20, which value belongs to the class?
quiz.hint: Read which endpoint is included.
quiz.explanation: 10 is included by ≤; 20 is excluded by <.

lessons.takeaway: For unequal class widths, frequency is represented by area, not height.
lessons.mistake: A wider class can contain more observations without having a taller bar.

lessons.title: Read stem-and-leaf plots
lessons.goal: Preserve data values, interpret a key and compare two groups.

quiz.question: The key says 4 | 6 means 4.6 kg. What does 5 | 2 mean?
quiz.hint: Use the place value shown in the key.
quiz.explanation: The stem is whole kilograms and the leaf tenths, so it means 5.2 kg.

quiz.question: A stem row is 3 | 1 1 5 8. How many observations are in that row?
quiz.hint: Count leaves, including repeats.
quiz.explanation: There are four leaves, so four observations.

lessons.takeaway: A stem-and-leaf plot keeps individual values; its key determines place value.
lessons.mistake: Never delete a repeated leaf as if it were an accidental duplicate: each leaf is one observation.

steps.text: The increase is 110 − 100 = 10. Compared with the original 100, this is 10%, not 100%.
steps.why: Percent change uses the original amount as denominator.
