quiz.question: Solve (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0.
quiz.hint: Set each factor to zero.
quiz.explanation: x − 5 = 0 gives 5; x + 2 = 0 gives −2.

quiz.question: Why can you not set each factor to zero in (x − 1)(x + 2) = 6?
quiz.hint: Check the condition of the zero-product rule.
quiz.explanation: The rule applies only when the product equals zero; first rearrange the equation into zero form.

lessons.takeaway: Zero on one side → factorise → set each factor to zero → check both roots.
lessons.mistake: Do not lose the second root, and remember that the factor (x − 4) gives the root +4, not −4.

lessons.title: Use the quadratic formula carefully
lessons.goal: Identify signed coefficients and evaluate both formula branches.

steps.title: Identify a, b and c
steps.text: For 2x² + x − 6 = 0, a = 2, b = 1 and c = −6. An x written without a number in front has coefficient 1. If the x-term is absent, b = 0.
steps.why: Standard form records all signed coefficients.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the signed coefficients together"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the signed coefficients together</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">2x² + x − 6 = 0: a = 2, b = 1, c = −6</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate the discriminant
steps.text: Compute b² − 4ac using brackets for negative c. It is 1 − 4(2)(−6) = 49.
steps.why: The discriminant determines the real-root cases.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the signed coefficients together"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the signed coefficients together</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2x² + x − 6 = 0: a = 2, b = 1, c = −6</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">D = 1² − 4(2)(−6) = 49</text></svg>

steps.title: Substitute into the formula
steps.text: The whole numerator is divided by 2a = 4. Since √49 = 7, the two choices are −1 + 7 and −1 − 7.
steps.why: The fraction bar applies to the whole numerator.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the signed coefficients together"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the signed coefficients together</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2x² + x − 6 = 0: a = 2, b = 1, c = −6</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">D = 1² − 4(2)(−6) = 49</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x = (−1 ± √49)/4 = (−1 ± 7)/4</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate and verify both branches
steps.text: The plus branch gives 3/2; the minus branch gives −2. Both satisfy the original. A negative discriminant would mean no real roots; zero would give one repeated root.
steps.why: The ± symbol represents two calculations.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Keep the signed coefficients together"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Keep the signed coefficients together</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">2x² + x − 6 = 0: a = 2, b = 1, c = −6</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">D = 1² − 4(2)(−6) = 49</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x = (−1 ± √49)/4 = (−1 ± 7)/4</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x = 6/4 = 3/2 or x = −8/4 = −2</text></svg>

quiz.question: For 3x² − 5x − 2 = 0, what is b?
quiz.hint: Include the sign attached to the x-term.
quiz.explanation: The x-term is −5x, so b = −5.

quiz.question: A quadratic has discriminant −9. How many real roots does it have?
quiz.hint: A negative number has no real square root.
quiz.explanation: D < 0 means the quadratic has no real roots.

lessons.takeaway: Write signed a, b, c first; calculate the discriminant; evaluate both ± branches.
lessons.mistake: Do not divide only part of the numerator by 2a.

lessons.title: Build a quadratic from a word problem
lessons.goal: Translate a rectangle’s dimensions, solve and reject impossible values.

steps.title: Define the unknown
steps.text: A rectangle has area 40 m² and length 3 m more than its width. Let the width be x metres; the length is x + 3.
steps.why: A clear variable definition keeps the units and quantities consistent.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Turn the dimensions into an equation"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Turn the dimensions into an equation</text><rect id="rectangle" x="110" y="110" width="320" height="200" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="270" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Area = 40 m²</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="72" y="220" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="270" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x + 3</text></svg>

steps.title: Translate the area rule
steps.text: Area is length times width. Therefore x(x + 3) = 40, or x² + 3x − 40 = 0.
steps.why: The area rule converts the story into a product.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Turn the dimensions into an equation"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Turn the dimensions into an equation</text><rect id="rectangle" x="110" y="110" width="320" height="200" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="270" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Area = 40 m²</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="72" y="220" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="270" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x + 3</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="590" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x(x + 3) = 40</text></svg>

steps.title: Solve the equation
steps.text: Factorise as (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0. The algebraic solutions are x = −8 and x = 5.
steps.why: The zero-product rule gives candidate roots.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Turn the dimensions into an equation"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Turn the dimensions into an equation</text><rect id="rectangle" x="110" y="110" width="320" height="200" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="270" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Area = 40 m²</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="72" y="220" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="270" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x + 3</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="590" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x(x + 3) = 40</text><text id="text-auto-5" x="590" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x = 5 or −8</text></svg>

steps.title: Return to the situation
steps.text: A width cannot be negative, so choose x = 5 m. The length is 8 m; 5 × 8 = 40 checks the area and 8 − 5 = 3 checks the difference.
steps.why: A mathematical root must also satisfy the real-world restrictions.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Turn the dimensions into an equation"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Turn the dimensions into an equation</text><rect id="rectangle" x="110" y="110" width="320" height="200" rx="0" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="270" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="30" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Area = 40 m²</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="72" y="220" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">5 m</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="270" y="350" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">8 m</text><text id="text-auto-4" x="590" y="145" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x(x + 3) = 40</text><text id="text-auto-5" x="590" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#173349" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">x = 5 or −8</text><text id="text-auto-6" x="590" y="300" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Use x = 5</text></svg>

quiz.question: A rectangle has width x and length x + 4, with area 60. Which equation models it?
quiz.hint: Area is a product of the dimensions.
quiz.explanation: Width times length gives x(x + 4) = 60.

quiz.question: A length problem gives candidate widths 6 cm and −9 cm. Which width is valid?
quiz.hint: A physical length must be positive.
quiz.explanation: 6 cm is valid; a negative width is not physically meaningful.

lessons.takeaway: Define → translate → solve → interpret → check the original story.
lessons.mistake: Do not keep a negative length simply because it solves the algebraic equation.

lessons.title: Form an equation from its roots
lessons.goal: Turn each root into a factor and expand to a monic quadratic.

steps.title: Start with the required roots
steps.text: Find a monic quadratic whose roots are 2 and −5. Monic means the coefficient of x² is 1.
steps.why: The equation is built backwards: each given root must make the finished equation true.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Build factors that vanish at the given roots"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Build factors that vanish at the given roots</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Roots: 2 and −5</text></svg>

steps.title: Create one zero factor per root
steps.text: The factor x − 2 vanishes at 2. The factor x + 5 vanishes at −5.
steps.why: x − r is zero exactly when x = r.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Build factors that vanish at the given roots"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Build factors that vanish at the given roots</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Roots: 2 and −5</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Factors: (x − 2) and (x + 5)</text></svg>

steps.title: Set their product equal to zero
steps.text: The product is zero whenever either required root is used. Write (x − 2)(x + 5) = 0.
steps.why: A zero factor makes the whole product zero.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Build factors that vanish at the given roots"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Build factors that vanish at the given roots</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Roots: 2 and −5</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Factors: (x − 2) and (x + 5)</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">(x − 2)(x + 5) = 0</text></svg>

steps.title: Expand and check
steps.text: Multiply every term to obtain x² + 5x − 2x − 10, hence x² + 3x − 10 = 0. Substituting either root gives zero.
steps.why: Expansion preserves the roots while changing the form.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Build factors that vanish at the given roots"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Build factors that vanish at the given roots</text><rect id="row-0" x="35" y="68" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-0" x="380" y="106" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Roots: 2 and −5</text><rect id="row-1" x="35" y="137" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-1" x="380" y="175" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Factors: (x − 2) and (x + 5)</text><rect id="row-2" x="35" y="206" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#eef2f5" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-2" x="380" y="244" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">(x − 2)(x + 5) = 0</text><rect id="row-3" x="35" y="275" width="690" height="58" rx="12" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2" /><text id="eq-3" x="380" y="313" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="26" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">x² + 3x − 10 = 0</text></svg>

quiz.question: A monic quadratic has roots 3 and −4. Which equation is correct?
quiz.hint: Build (x − 3)(x + 4).
quiz.explanation: (x − 3)(x + 4) expands to x² + x − 12.

quiz.question: Which factor corresponds to root x = −7?
quiz.hint: The factor must equal zero when x is −7.
quiz.explanation: x + 7 becomes −7 + 7 = 0.

lessons.takeaway: Root r gives factor (x − r); multiply the factors and set the product to zero.
lessons.mistake: The sign in a factor is opposite to the root’s sign.

reference.name: Standard form
reference.note: Move every term to one side before using the formula.

reference.name: Zero-product rule
reference.note: This requires the product to equal zero.

reference.name: Quadratic formula
reference.note: Use the signs of a, b and c exactly as written.

reference.name: Discriminant
reference.note: D > 0: two real roots; D = 0: one repeated root; D < 0: no real roots.

reference.name: Equation from roots
reference.note: This gives a monic quadratic; non-zero multiples have the same roots.

toolkit.strategy: Put the equation in zero form, then decide whether factorisation is practical or the formula is safer. Keep both algebraic roots until the context has been checked.

methods.title: Rearrange and factorise a quadratic
methods.when: The expression can be written as a product of linear factors.
methods.rule: uv=0 ⇒ u=0 or v=0; this rule requires the product to equal zero.
steps: Rearrange to ax²+bx+c=0.
Remove a common factor if useful and factorise completely.
Set each factor equal to zero.
Check each root in the original equation.
methods.trap: Do not set factors separately to zero when their product equals a non-zero number.

methods.title: Use the formula for a non-monic quadratic
methods.when: Factorisation is awkward or a reliable general method is needed.
steps: Write a,b,c with their signs.
Compute the discriminant without rounding.
Evaluate both branches and simplify exactly where possible.
Use calculator brackets around the whole numerator and denominator.
methods.trap: An x written alone has coefficient 1; an absent x-term has coefficient 0.

methods.title: Read what the discriminant permits
methods.when: The number or nature of real roots is requested.
methods.rule: D=b²−4ac: D>0 gives two distinct real roots; D=0 a repeated real root; D<0 no real roots.
steps: Put the equation in zero form.
Calculate D from the signed coefficients.
State the number of real roots before evaluating the formula.
methods.example: x²−6x+9=0 has D=0 and repeated root 3.
methods.check: (x−3)² expands to the original expression.
methods.trap: A negative discriminant means no real roots, not that both roots are negative.

methods.title: Model a uniform border
methods.when: A border of width x surrounds every side of a rectangle.
methods.rule: Outer dimensions are L+2x and W+2x; border area=(L+2x)(W+2x)−LW.
steps: Sketch and label one border strip on each side.
Decide whether the given area is total outer area or border area only.
Form and solve the quadratic.
Reject roots that cannot represent the stated width.
methods.example: An 8 m by 5 m garden has outer area 88 m²: (8+2x)(5+2x)=88 ⇒ x=1.5 or −8; use 1.5 m.
methods.check: Outer dimensions 11 m and 8 m give 88 m².
methods.trap: Adding x just once to each dimension misses the border on the opposite side.

methods.title: Translate and validate a word problem
methods.when: Dimensions or other related quantities are expressed using one unknown.
methods.rule: Translate the original relation first; then solve and apply the domain.
steps: Define the unknown with units and restrictions.
Express all other quantities in terms of it.
Form the equation from the stated area or other relation.
Test every algebraic root against the original statement.
methods.example: A rectangle of width x and length x+3 has area 40: x²+3x−40=0 gives 5 and −8; width 5 m, length 8 m.
methods.trap: Do not discard a root merely because it is inconvenient; name the restriction it violates.

methods.title: Solve a target that may have two valid answers
methods.when: A quadratic profit or output model is set equal to a target.
methods.rule: Solve model expression = target, not automatically =0; then rearrange to zero.
steps: Substitute the requested target.
Move all terms to one side.
Solve both roots.
Check both in the original model and against the allowed input range.
methods.example: For P(n)=−2n²+36n−80, P=64 gives n²−18n+72=0, so n=6 or 12.
methods.check: P(6)=P(12)=64; both may satisfy a non-negative integer domain.
methods.trap: The smaller root is not automatically the only realistic one.

methods.title: Form an equation from specified roots
methods.when: Roots are supplied and the equation is required.
methods.rule: Roots r,s ⇒ a(x−r)(x−s)=0 for a≠0. Monic form: x²−(r+s)x+rs=0; with leading coefficient a, expand to ax²−a(r+s)x+ars=0.
steps: Turn each root into a factor that vanishes at it.
Multiply by the required leading coefficient.
Expand and collect.
Check each given root.
methods.example: Roots −3 and 4 give (x+3)(x−4)=0 ⇒ x²−x−12=0; leading coefficient 4 gives 4x²−4x−48=0.
methods.check: Substitution of −3 and 4 makes each product zero.
methods.trap: A negative root produces a plus sign in its factor.

checks: Move every term to one side before applying the zero-product rule or quadratic formula.
Use signed a,b,c from ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0.
A square root in the formula gives both the plus and minus branches.
Check both roots in the original equation before applying context restrictions.
A physical length must be positive; a contextual quadratic may still have two valid positive solutions.

challenges.title: A border around every side
challenges.question: A rectangular garden is 8 m long and 5 m wide. A uniform path of width x metres is laid outside all four sides. The combined area of garden and path is 88 m². (a) Write the outer dimensions and form an equation. (b) Solve for x, keeping both algebraic roots. (c) Choose the valid width and find the area of the path alone.
hints: Each outer dimension gains x at both ends.
After expanding, simplify to 2x²+13x−24=0.

solution.title: Label the outside
solution.reason: The border appears on opposite sides of each dimension.

solution.title: Translate the total area
solution.reason: The supplied area includes the garden.

solution.title: Solve
solution.reason: The discriminant is 13²+192=361.

solution.title: Apply the domain
solution.reason: A path width must be positive, so the negative root does not describe this construction.

solution.title: Find path area
solution.reason: Subtract the original garden area from the outer area.

challenges.answer: Outer dimensions (8+2x)m and (5+2x)m; algebraic roots 1.5 and −8; valid width 1.5 m; path area 48 m².
challenges.check: The final outside rectangle is 11 m by 8 m, area 88 m²; subtracting the 40 m² garden leaves 48 m².

challenges.title: Use the formula and verify the factorisation
challenges.question: Solve 3x²−5x−2=0. (a) Identify a,b,c and the discriminant. (b) Use the quadratic formula to obtain both exact roots. (c) Use the roots to write an integer-coefficient factorisation of 3x²−5x−2 and expand it as a check.
hints: Include the minus signs in b and c.
The denominator is 2a=6; one root is a fraction.

solution.title: Identify coefficients
solution.reason: Read the equation in zero form.

solution.title: Calculate the discriminant
solution.reason: Subtracting the negative product adds 24.

solution.title: Evaluate both branches
solution.reason: The plus/minus produces two roots.

solution.title: Build the factors
solution.reason: Each root makes one factor zero, and the leading coefficient is 3.

solution.title: Expand to verify
solution.reason: Expansion checks both coefficients and the constant.

challenges.answer: a=3, b=−5, c=−2; D=49; roots 2 and −1/3; factorisation (x−2)(3x+1).
challenges.check: Direct substitution gives 12−10−2=0 and 1/3+5/3−2=0.

challenges.title: One profit target, two feasible quantities
challenges.question: An invented classroom profit model is P(n)=−2n²+36n−80 euro, where n is a whole number of items and 0≤n≤15. (a) Find all n for which profit is €64. (b) Check which roots satisfy the allowed range. (c) Calculate P(9) and compare it with the target. Explain why the smaller target root must not automatically be selected.
hints: Set the expression equal to 64, then bring the 64 to the left.
Divide by −2 to obtain n²−18n+72=0.

solution.title: Set the target
solution.reason: The desired profit is not zero.

solution.title: Rearrange and factor
solution.reason: Moving the target and dividing by −2 gives an equivalent equation.

solution.title: Check the domain
solution.math: n=6 or n=12; both are integers in [0,15]
solution.reason: Both algebraic solutions meet the stated restrictions.

solution.title: Verify the target
solution.reason: Check in the original model.

solution.title: Compare a third input
solution.math: P(9)=−162+324−80=82, which is €18 above the target
solution.reason: A quadratic can reach the same target at two different inputs; the question asks for all valid ones.

challenges.answer: n=6 and n=12 both give €64 and both are valid. P(9)=€82, which is €18 above the target.
challenges.check: Both target quantities are 3 away from n = 9, the axis of symmetry, and direct substitution confirms that each gives €64.

challenges.title: Build from roots, then change the right-hand side
challenges.question: (a) Form the monic quadratic equation with roots −3 and 4. (b) Form an equivalent equation with leading coefficient 4. (c) Now solve x²−x−12=18. Explain why the roots from part (a) cannot simply be reused.
hints: Use factors x+3 and x−4 for the given roots.
For part (c), move 18 to the left before factorising.

solution.title: Build the monic equation
solution.reason: A factor must vanish at each required root.

solution.title: Scale the whole equation
solution.reason: A non-zero multiple has the same zero set.

solution.title: Change the target correctly
solution.reason: The new equation has a different constant in zero form.

solution.title: Solve the new equation
solution.reason: The constants −6 and +5 multiply to −30 and add to −1.

solution.title: Check and explain
solution.reason: The old roots made the expression zero, not eighteen.

challenges.answer: (a) x²−x−12=0. (b) 4x²−4x−48=0. (c) x=6 or −5; changing the target changes the roots.
challenges.check: −3 and 4 give zero in x²−x−12, while 6 and −5 give eighteen, confirming the distinction.

title: Geometry 2 — Similar Triangles, Circles and Theorems
intro: Match shapes and arcs carefully, and attach a reason to every geometric step.

lessons.title: Use similar triangles to find lengths
lessons.goal: Match corresponding vertices and apply one consistent scale factor.

steps.title: Identify the same shape
steps.text: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. Their sizes may differ; congruent triangles also have equal size.
steps.why: Similarity fixes angles but allows uniform scaling.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Match corresponding sides, not screen positions"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Match corresponding sides, not screen positions</text><polygon id="small" points="85,310 245,310 85,190" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><polygon id="large" points="435,310 675,310 435,130" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="63" y="256" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">3</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="390" y="225" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">4.5</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Same shape; corresponding angles match.</text></svg>

steps.title: Find the scale factor
steps.text: A side of length 3 corresponds to 4.5. Going small to large, the scale factor is 4.5/3 = 1.5.
steps.why: Corresponding sides define the scale factor.

steps.title: Apply it to the matching side
steps.text: The side of length 5 corresponds to the unknown large side. Multiply 5 by 1.5.
steps.why: All lengths scale by the same factor.

steps.title: Check every available pair
steps.text: The missing side is 7.5. The other pairs also have ratio 1.5: 6/4 and 4.5/3.
steps.why: A consistent ratio checks the vertex matching.

quiz.question: A triangle is enlarged by scale factor 2.5. A side is 4 cm. What is its image length?
quiz.hint: Multiply the length by the scale factor.

quiz.question: Which condition guarantees two triangles are similar?
quiz.hint: The third angle is then fixed by the triangle sum.
quiz.explanation: Two pairs of equal angles force the third pair to be equal, giving AA similarity.

lessons.takeaway: Match the vertices, then use one scale factor for all corresponding lengths.
lessons.mistake: A rotated triangle still has the same correspondences; do not match sides only by their position on the page.

lessons.title: Use a parallel cut through a triangle
lessons.goal: Distinguish part-to-whole from part-to-part ratios.

steps.title: Spot the parallel lines
steps.text: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB and E on AC, with DE parallel to BC. Triangle ADE has the same angles as ABC.
steps.why: Parallel-line angle facts give AA similarity.

steps.title: Choose a consistent ratio
steps.text: AD = 6 and AB = 15, so every side of the small triangle is 6/15 = 2/5 of the matching side of the large one. AB is the whole side, not just DB.
steps.why: Matching ratios must use matching portions.

steps.title: Find the corresponding length
steps.text: AC = 25, so AE/25 = 2/5. Multiply 25 by 2/5.
steps.why: Similarity preserves the side ratio.

steps.text: AE = 10. Therefore EC = 25 − 10 = 15. The whole is the sum of its two parts.
steps.why: A full segment equals its component segments.

quiz.question: In triangle ABC, D lies on AB and E on AC, with DE ∥ BC. AD = 4, AB = 10 and AC = 15. Find AE.
quiz.hint: Use AD/AB = AE/AC.

quiz.question: E lies on the segment AC. AE = 6 and AC = 15. Find EC.
quiz.hint: Subtract the smaller segment from the whole side.

lessons.takeaway: Use small/whole on both sides, or part/part on both sides—never mix them.
lessons.mistake: Check whether the question asks for the matching part or the remaining part.

lessons.title: Choose the right circle-angle fact
lessons.goal: Use centre, circumference, semicircle and cyclic-quadrilateral facts correctly.

steps.text: Both the central angle AOB and circumference angle ACB stand on the same arc AB. The points A and B must match.
steps.why: The theorem compares angles subtending one specified arc.

steps.title: Recognise a semicircle
steps.text: If AB is a diameter, the central angle is 180°. The circumference angle standing on the diameter is 90°.
steps.why: A diameter makes a central straight angle.

steps.text: All four vertices of a cyclic quadrilateral lie on a circle. Opposite angles add to 180°; if one is 85°, its opposite is 95°.
steps.why: Opposite cyclic angles subtend arcs that sum to a full circle.

steps.why: Taking half of the same angle gives equal results.

lessons.takeaway: Check same arc, diameter or cyclic conditions before choosing a circle theorem.
lessons.mistake: Angles standing on different arcs are not automatically equal.

lessons.title: Prove the triangle-angle sum
lessons.goal: Use a parallel line to move the three angles onto a straight line.

steps.title: Name the three angles
steps.text: In triangle ABC, label the angles at B, C and A as alpha, beta and gamma. We want their sum, without assuming its value.
steps.why: A proof states the target before using it.

steps.text: Draw a line through A parallel to BC. This is an auxiliary construction: it creates useful angle relationships without changing the triangle.
steps.why: An auxiliary parallel line creates a bridge to known facts.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary line helps prove the triangle-angle sum?
options: A line through a vertex parallel to the opposite side
A random line outside the triangle
quiz.hint: It should create alternate-angle relationships.
quiz.explanation: A parallel through a vertex transfers the two other angles onto one straight line.

quiz.question: Why are the transferred angles equal to the base angles?
options: They are alternate angles between parallel lines.
quiz.hint: Name the theorem that justifies the equality.
quiz.explanation: Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal; appearance alone is not a proof.

lessons.takeaway: Construction + alternate angles + straight angle = a proof of the triangle sum (Theorem 4).
lessons.mistake: Do not use the triangle sum as an assumption in its own proof.

lessons.title: Prove the exterior-angle theorem
lessons.goal: Compare two expressions for 180° and remove the shared angle.

steps.title: Extend one side
steps.text: Extend BC beyond C and label the exterior angle theta. The two interior opposite angles are alpha at B and beta at A.
steps.why: Extending a side creates an exterior angle.
steps.math: Exterior θ; interior opposite α and β

steps.text: The exterior angle theta and adjacent interior angle gamma form a straight angle. Thus theta plus gamma is 180°.
steps.why: Adjacent straight-line angles are supplementary.

steps.title: Use the triangle sum
steps.text: The three interior angles add to 180°. Therefore alpha plus beta plus gamma has the same value as theta plus gamma.
steps.why: The already-proved triangle-angle sum applies.

steps.title: Subtract the shared angle
steps.text: Subtract gamma from both expressions. What remains is theta = alpha + beta.
steps.why: Subtracting equal quantities from equals preserves equality.

quiz.question: Two interior opposite angles are 48° and 67°. Find the exterior angle.
quiz.hint: Add the two interior opposite angles.

quiz.question: Which angle is excluded from the remote-angle sum?
options: The interior angle adjacent to the exterior angle
quiz.hint: Remote means not touching the exterior angle at that vertex.
quiz.explanation: The adjacent interior angle forms a straight line with the exterior angle; the other two are remote.

lessons.takeaway: Theorem 6: an exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite (remote) angles.
lessons.mistake: Do not include the adjacent interior angle in that sum.

lessons.title: Prove opposite parallelogram parts are equal
lessons.goal: Use a diagonal and ASA congruence rather than assuming the result.

steps.title: Start from the definition
steps.text: ABCD is a parallelogram: AB is parallel to CD and BC is parallel to AD. We aim to prove opposite sides and angles equal.
steps.why: The definition supplies parallelism, not the desired conclusion.

steps.title: Draw a diagonal
steps.text: Draw AC. It forms triangles ABC and CDA, sharing the side AC.
steps.why: An auxiliary diagonal creates triangles to compare.

steps.title: Use alternate angles and ASA
steps.text: AC is a transversal of the parallel lines AB and CD, so the alternate angles BAC and ACD are equal. Likewise BC ∥ AD gives angle BCA equal to CAD. With the common side AC between these angles, the triangles are congruent by ASA.
steps.why: ASA establishes congruence from two angles and their included side.

steps.title: Match the corresponding parts
steps.text: Congruence gives AB = CD, BC = AD and angle B = angle D. Adding the paired angles at the diagonal also gives angle A = angle C.
steps.why: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
steps.math: Opposite sides and opposite angles are equal

quiz.question: Which side is shared when diagonal AC splits parallelogram ABCD?
quiz.hint: The diagonal belongs to both triangles.
quiz.explanation: Both triangles contain AC.

quiz.question: What justifies the equal angle pairs used in this proof?
options: Alternate angles from opposite parallel sides
The diagonal always bisects every angle
quiz.hint: Use the defining parallel sides.
quiz.explanation: The diagonal is a transversal through the parallel pairs, giving equal alternate angles.

lessons.takeaway: A diagonal turns the parallelogram proof (Theorem 9) into an ASA triangle-congruence proof.
lessons.mistake: A general parallelogram diagonal does not necessarily bisect its angles.

lessons.title: Prove Pythagoras using similarity
lessons.goal: Split a right-angled triangle, compare matching sides, and add the results.

steps.title: Identify the hypotenuse
steps.text: Triangle ABC has a right angle at A. Therefore BC is the hypotenuse, and the target is AB² + AC² = BC².
steps.why: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Proof: Pythagoras from similar triangles"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Proof: Pythagoras from similar triangles</text><polygon id="ABC" points="320,83.35680867601536 120,320 600,320" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="330" y="88.35680867601536" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">A</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="101" y="347" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">B</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="610" y="347" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">C</text><polyline id="rightA" points="305.80,100.16 322.60,114.36 336.80,97.56" fill="none" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" /><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Right angle at A; BC is the hypotenuse.</text></svg>

steps.title: Drop a perpendicular to BC
steps.text: Draw AD perpendicular to the hypotenuse, with D on BC. Each smaller triangle shares an acute angle with the original and also has a right angle.
steps.why: Two equal angles establish triangle similarity.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img" aria-label="Proof: Pythagoras from similar triangles"><rect id="rect-auto-1" x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="18" fill="#f8fbfc" stroke="none" stroke-width="2" /><text id="diagram-title" x="28" y="38" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Proof: Pythagoras from similar triangles</text><polygon id="ABC" points="320,83.35680867601536 120,320 600,320" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3" /><text id="text-auto-1" x="330" y="88.35680867601536" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">A</text><text id="text-auto-2" x="101" y="347" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">B</text><text id="text-auto-3" x="610" y="347" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">C</text><polyline id="rightA" points="305.80,100.16 322.60,114.36 336.80,97.56" fill="none" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" /><line id="altitude" x1="320" y1="83.35680867601536" x2="320" y2="320" stroke="#7650a0" stroke-width="3" stroke-dasharray="6 4" /><polygon id="rightD" points="320,300 340,300 340,320" fill="none" stroke="#7650a0" stroke-width="2" /><text id="text-auto-4" x="313" y="347" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#7650a0" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">D</text><text id="diagram-footer" x="380" y="378" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" fill="#6d8190" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Draw AD perpendicular to BC.</text></svg>

steps.title: Write the matching side ratios
steps.text: From similarity, AB/BC = BD/AB, giving AB² = BC·BD. Similarly AC/BC = DC/AC gives AC² = BC·DC.
steps.why: Proportional corresponding sides give the squared-length equations.

AC² = BC · DC.</text></svg>

steps.title: Add and combine the hypotenuse parts
steps.text: Add the two equations and take out BC. Since BD + DC = BC, the sum becomes BC².
steps.why: Segment addition and the distributive law complete the proof.

quiz.question: In this proof, why is AD drawn perpendicular to BC?
options: To create two right-angled triangles similar to the original
To force D to be the midpoint
To turn the triangle into a square
quiz.hint: Look at the angle pairs in the smaller triangles.
quiz.explanation: The perpendicular creates right angles, and each small triangle shares an acute angle with the original.

quiz.question: Which equality finishes the proof after factoring out BC?
quiz.hint: D lies on the hypotenuse segment.
quiz.explanation: The two adjoining segments BD and DC add to the full segment BC.

lessons.takeaway: Two similarity ratios give two squared lengths; adding them proves Pythagoras (Theorem 14).
lessons.mistake: The altitude foot is not necessarily the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

lessons.title: Prove the centre-angle theorem
lessons.goal: Use equal radii and exterior angles to establish the factor of two.

steps.title: Join the radii
steps.text: A, B and C lie on a circle with centre O. Join OA, OB and OC. The triangles AOC and BOC have two equal sides because their sides are radii.
steps.why: Radii of a circle are equal.

steps.title: Split the circumference angle
steps.text: Extend CO to meet the circle again at D, and let ∠ACO = α and ∠OCB = β, so ∠ACB = α + β. Because OA = OC and OB = OC, the base angles match: ∠OAC = α and ∠OBC = β.
steps.why: Isosceles triangles have equal base angles.

steps.text: Angle AOD is an exterior angle of AOC, so it equals 2α. Similarly angle DOB equals 2β.
steps.why: An exterior angle equals the sum of its interior opposite angles.

steps.title: Combine the two parts
steps.text: Add to get angle AOB = 2α + 2β = 2(angle ACB). In other configurations the corresponding proof subtracts parts; the same-arc condition remains essential.
steps.why: The distributive law gives the factor two; the selected arc determines which central angle is intended.

quiz.question: A, B and C lie on a circle with centre O. Why are triangles AOC and BOC isosceles?
options: OA, OB and OC are radii of one circle.
Every triangle inside a circle is equilateral.
quiz.hint: Identify the equal lengths supplied by the circle.
quiz.explanation: Radii of the same circle are equal, giving two equal sides in each triangle.

quiz.question: A circumference angle is 38°. Find the centre angle on the same arc.
quiz.hint: Double the circumference angle.

lessons.takeaway: Theorem 19: equal radii → equal base angles → exterior-angle sums → the factor of two.
lessons.mistake: Use the central angle subtending the same arc, which may be a reflex angle in another configuration.

reference.name: Similar triangles
reference.formula: Corresponding angles equal; corresponding lengths in one ratio
reference.note: Match vertices before forming ratios.

reference.name: Parallel cut in a triangle
reference.formula: AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC when DE ∥ BC
reference.note: D lies on AB and E on AC.

reference.name: Circle angles
reference.formula: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
reference.note: Theorem 19: both angles must stand on the same arc.

reference.name: Semicircle and cyclic quadrilateral
reference.formula: Angle in semicircle = 90°; opposite cyclic angles sum to 180°
reference.note: Corollaries 3 and 5: the vertices lie on the circle; the semicircle angle stands on a diameter.

reference.name: Parallelogram
reference.formula: Opposite sides and opposite angles are equal
reference.note: A diagonal creates congruent triangles.

reference.name: Pythagoras
reference.note: Theorem 14: BC is the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle.

toolkit.strategy: Mark the givens before using a theorem. Establish equal angles or congruence, match corresponding vertices, then form ratios or equations. Every proof line needs a reason.

methods.title: Establish similarity and match sides
methods.when: Two triangles have matching angles but may differ in size or orientation.
methods.rule: AA similarity: two equal angle pairs suffice. If ΔABC∼ΔDEF, then AB/DE=BC/EF=AC/DF (Theorem 13); corresponding angles are equal and all corresponding lengths use one scale.
steps: Name both equal angle pairs and their reasons.
Write the triangles in matching vertex order.
Choose one known corresponding pair to find scale.
Apply the same scale to the requested side.
methods.example: If ΔABC∼ΔDEF and AB/DE=3/5, then AC=9 and DF=15 are consistent.
methods.check: Check a second corresponding side ratio if available.
methods.trap: Matching is based on angles and vertices, not the apparent left-to-right positions.

methods.title: Use a parallel cut through a triangle
methods.when: D lies on AB, E on AC and DE is parallel to BC.
methods.rule: AD/AB=AE/AC=DE/BC (Theorem 13, similar triangles); also AD/DB=AE/EC (Theorem 12) when all denominators are non-zero.
steps: Prove the small and whole triangles similar using parallel-line angles.
Choose either small/whole or part/part consistently.
Solve the proportion.
Subtract from the whole if the question asks for a remaining segment.
methods.example: AD=4, AB=10, AC=15 ⇒ AE=6 and EC=9.
methods.trap: DB is a remaining part, whereas AB is the whole side.

methods.title: Handle crossing triangles and indirect widths
methods.when: Two straight lines cross and a parallel pair forms triangles on opposite sides.
methods.rule: Vertically opposite angles are equal; a parallel pair supplies a second equal angle pair, giving AA similarity.
steps: State which points are collinear and which sides parallel.
Match the crossing vertex with itself.
Use corresponding distances from the crossing vertex.
Convert units and distinguish horizontal width from slant distance.
methods.example: If OA/OC=6/9 and OB=8, then OD=12 when ΔAOB∼ΔCOD.
methods.check: 6/9=8/12; the larger triangle must have all corresponding sides scaled by 3/2.
methods.trap: A rotated or reversed triangle still needs matching corresponding sides.

methods.title: Combine shadow similarity with Pythagoras
methods.when: Equal sun angles or sight lines give similar right-angled triangles, but a slant length is requested.
methods.rule: Under parallel sun rays on level ground, height/shadow is constant. For a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse c satisfies c²=a²+b²; c=√(a²+b²), a=√(c²−b²).
steps: Convert every measurement to one unit.
Use similarity to find a missing vertical or horizontal length.
Use Pythagoras only after identifying the perpendicular sides.
Keep the slant distinct from the width or height.
methods.example: A 1.2 m pole casts a 0.9 m shadow; a 6 m shadow gives height 8 m and slant √(8²+6²)=10 m.
methods.check: The height/shadow ratios are both 4/3.
methods.trap: A line-of-sight distance is usually a hypotenuse, not the perpendicular width.

methods.title: Choose the circle-angle fact with its conditions
methods.when: Angles lie on a circle, perhaps with a diameter or cyclic quadrilateral.
methods.rule: Same arc: centre angle=2×circumference angle (Theorem 19). Same segment: circumference angles equal (Corollary 2). Diameter: circumference angle=90° (Corollary 3). Cyclic opposite angles sum to 180° (Corollary 5).
steps: Identify the shared endpoints and the arc that the angle subtends.
Check that a stated diameter passes through the centre.
For a cyclic quadrilateral check all four vertices lie on the circle.
Write the chosen relation before solving.
methods.example: Centre angle 138° gives circumference angle 69° on the same arc; cyclic opposite to 112° is 68°.
methods.check: Verify the doubled or supplementary relation.
methods.trap: The other arc can require a reflex central angle; shared endpoints alone do not settle which angle is intended.

methods.title: Prove the triangle-angle sum
methods.when: A proof of the 180° triangle-angle sum is required.
methods.rule: Theorem 4: the three angles of any triangle sum to 180°, so α+β+γ=180°.
steps: Through the top vertex draw a line parallel to the opposite side.
Use alternate angles to transfer the two base angles to that line.
The transferred angles and the top angle fill a straight angle, hence total 180°.
methods.example: Base angles α and β reappear beside γ on the auxiliary parallel: α+γ+β=180°.
methods.check: The proof uses a straight angle and parallel-angle facts, not the triangle sum itself.
methods.trap: Do not assume the theorem you are trying to prove.

methods.title: Prove the exterior-angle theorem
methods.when: One triangle side is extended and an exterior angle θ is considered.
methods.rule: Theorem 6: exterior angle θ equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, θ=α+β.
steps: Let γ be the adjacent interior angle.
Use the straight line to write θ+γ=180°.
Use the proved triangle sum to write α+β+γ=180°.
Subtract γ from the equal totals.
methods.example: θ+γ=α+β+γ ⇒ θ=α+β.
methods.trap: The adjacent interior angle is excluded from the remote-angle sum.

methods.title: Prove opposite parallelogram parts equal
methods.when: ABCD is a parallelogram and opposite-side/angle equality needs proof.
methods.rule: Theorem 9: AB∥CD and BC∥AD; diagonal AC gives ΔABC≅ΔCDA by ASA, so opposite sides and angles are equal.
steps: Draw AC.
Use alternate angles: BAC=ACD and BCA=CAD.
Use common included side AC to obtain ASA congruence.
Match sides AB=CD, BC=AD and opposite angles; add diagonal angle parts for angles A and C.
methods.example: Parallel pairs + two angle pairs + shared diagonal ⇒ opposite sides and angles equal.
methods.check: The correspondence A↔C, B↔D, C↔A matches all claimed parts.
methods.trap: A parallelogram diagonal need not bisect each angle.

methods.title: Prove Pythagoras using an altitude
methods.when: Triangle ABC has a right angle at A and the theorem needs a proof.
methods.rule: Theorem 14 (Pythagoras): AB²+AC²=BC², with BC the hypotenuse.
steps: Drop AD perpendicular to BC, with D on BC.
Use AA to obtain ΔABD∼ΔCBA and ΔACD∼ΔBCA.
Form AB/BC=BD/AB and AC/BC=DC/AC; cross-multiply.
Add AB²=BC·BD and AC²=BC·DC; use BD+DC=BC.
methods.example: AB²+AC²=BC(BD+DC)=BC².
methods.check: The hypotenuse pieces are lengths whose sum is BC; no midpoint assumption is needed.
methods.trap: The altitude foot D is not generally the midpoint.

methods.title: Prove the centre-angle theorem
methods.when: A,B,C lie on a circle with centre O; angles stand on the same arc AB.
methods.rule: Theorem 19: the angle at the centre standing on arc AB is twice ∠ACB, the angle at the circle on the same arc.
steps: Join OA, OB and OC; extend CO to the circle again at D.
Equal radii make AOC and BOC isosceles. Name the two angle parts at C as α and β.
Exterior angles give AOD=2α and DOB=2β.
When the diameter lies inside ∠ACB, add: AOB=2α+2β=2(α+β); in an outside configuration subtract corresponding parts instead.
methods.example: Two equal-radius triangles turn the circumference angle parts into doubled central parts.
methods.check: Check the same-arc choice, including a reflex central angle if that arc requires one.
methods.trap: Do not double an angle while silently switching to the other arc.

methods.title: Use isosceles and equilateral structure
methods.when: Equal sides or a 60° angle appear inside a parallelogram or similar-triangle problem.
methods.rule: Isosceles: angles opposite equal sides are equal. Equilateral: all sides equal and each angle is 60°. A parallelogram has equal opposite sides/angles and adjacent angles summing to 180°.
steps: Mark the equal sides supplied or already proved.
Use the triangle sum to determine the remaining angles.
Conclude equilateral only when all three sides or all three angles are equal.
Use an equilateral altitude through the midpoint to form two right-angled triangles if a length is needed.
methods.example: AB=AD=8 and ∠BAD=60° make ΔABD equilateral, so BD=8; its altitude is √(8²−4²)=4√3.
methods.check: The two base angles are (180°−60°)/2=60°; Pythagoras checks the altitude.
methods.trap: Equal adjacent parallelogram sides alone make a rhombus, not necessarily equilateral triangles; the angle condition matters.

checks: Use a common unit before forming a length ratio.
Write corresponding triangles in matching vertex order.
Do not mix part/whole with part/part in one ratio.
Circle the relevant right angle or mark the same arc before choosing a formula.
A diagram suggests relationships; only the givens and proved facts justify them.

challenges.title: A shadow gives a height and a slant
challenges.question: On level ground, a vertical pole 1.2 m high casts a 90 cm shadow. At the same time a vertical tree casts a 6 m shadow. Treat the sun rays as parallel. (a) Explain why the triangles are similar. (b) Find the tree’s height. (c) Find the straight-line distance from the tree top to the tip of its shadow.
hints: Convert 90 cm to metres before forming the ratio.
First find height by similarity; then use height and shadow as Pythagoras perpendicular sides.

solution.title: Identify the angles
solution.math: Both have a right angle and the same sun-ray angle
solution.reason: Parallel rays and horizontal ground provide a second equal angle, so AA similarity applies.

solution.title: Match the units
solution.reason: Corresponding length ratios require matching units.

solution.title: Use similarity
solution.reason: The height-to-shadow ratio is common.

solution.title: Find the slant
solution.reason: The slant is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle.

challenges.answer: AA similarity; tree height 8 m; slant distance 10 m.

challenges.title: Match triangles across a crossing
challenges.question: A,O,C are collinear in that order, and B,O,D are collinear in that order. AB∥CD. Given OA=6 cm, OC=9 cm, OB=8 cm and AB=10 cm: (a) prove triangles AOB and COD are similar, naming the angle reasons; (b) find OD and CD; (c) find the complete lengths AC and BD.
hints: The angles at O are vertically opposite.
Match A with C and B with D; the scale from AOB to COD is 9/6.

solution.title: Prove AA similarity
solution.reason: The first pair is vertically opposite; the second follows from AB∥CD and transversal AC.

solution.title: Match corresponding sides
solution.reason: The larger triangle is COD.

solution.title: Find the unknown sides
solution.reason: All corresponding lengths share one scale factor.

solution.title: Add collinear parts
solution.reason: O lies between each named pair of endpoints.

challenges.answer: ΔAOB∼ΔCOD by AA; OD=12 cm, CD=15 cm, AC=15 cm, BD=20 cm.
challenges.check: The small triangle has 6²+8²=10² and the large one 9²+12²=15²; all side ratios are 2:3.

challenges.title: Measure a canal without crossing it
challenges.question: A,B,C lie in that order along a straight canal bank with AB=20 m and BC=10 m. T is across the canal directly opposite A, so AT is perpendicular to the bank. On the land side, CD is drawn perpendicular to the bank, with CD=6 m. T,B,D are collinear. (a) Explain why triangles TAB and DCB are similar. (b) Find the perpendicular canal width AT. (c) Find the exact and 3-significant-figure line-of-sight distance TB.
hints: Each triangle has a right angle; the angles at B are vertically opposite.
AT matches CD, while AB matches CB. After finding AT, TB is the hypotenuse.

solution.title: Establish similarity
solution.reason: The right angles and vertically opposite angles establish AA.

solution.title: Match the ratio
solution.reason: The perpendicular widths correspond, as do the bank segments.

solution.title: Find the canal width
solution.reason: Similarity transfers the scale factor.

solution.title: Find the sight line
solution.reason: AT and AB are the perpendicular sides.

solution.title: Round the requested length
solution.reason: Round the exact root only at the end.

challenges.answer: ΔTAB∼ΔDCB by AA; canal width 12 m; TB=4√34 m≈23.3 m.
challenges.check: The smaller sight segment BD has length √(10²+6²)=2√34, exactly half TB, independently confirming the similarity scale.

challenges.title: From a parallelogram to two equilateral triangles
challenges.question: ABCD is a convex parallelogram with AB=AD=8 cm and ∠DAB=60°. (a) Find angles ABC and BCD, giving reasons. (b) Prove triangle ABD is equilateral and find BD. (c) Prove triangle BCD is also equilateral. (d) Let E be the midpoint of BD. Use the altitudes of the two equilateral triangles and Pythagoras to find AC exactly.
hints: The equal sides AB and AD make triangle ABD isosceles; its remaining angles share 120°.
In an equilateral triangle, the altitude from the opposite vertex meets the midpoint of the base. BE=4 cm.

solution.title: Find parallelogram angles
solution.reason: Adjacent angles between parallel sides sum to 180°, and opposite parallelogram angles are equal.

solution.title: Prove ABD equilateral
solution.math: AB=AD and ∠BAD=60° ⇒ the other two angles are 60°; BD=8 cm
solution.reason: The isosceles base angles share the remaining 120°, so all angles and sides are equal.

solution.title: Prove BCD equilateral
solution.reason: Opposite parallelogram sides are equal, giving three equal sides.

solution.title: Use the common midpoint
solution.reason: In each equilateral triangle, SSS congruence of the two half-triangles makes the midpoint line perpendicular to the base.

solution.title: Find the altitudes
solution.reason: Each half-triangle has hypotenuse 8 and one perpendicular side 4.

solution.title: Add the correct segments
solution.reason: A and C are on opposite sides of BD; their perpendiculars pass through the same midpoint E.

challenges.answer: Angles ABC=120°, BCD=60°; both ABD and BCD are equilateral; BD=8 cm; AC=8√3 cm.
challenges.check: A coordinate check is A(0,0), B(8,0), D(4,4√3), C(12,4√3): AC²=12²+(4√3)²=192, giving 8√3.

title: Cylinder – Sphere
intro: Turn curved shapes into familiar areas, volumes and rates.

lessons.title: Build a cylinder from layers
lessons.goal: Find volume and reverse the formula to find a missing dimension.

steps.title: Identify the radius and height
steps.text: A cylindrical container has radius 3 centimetres and height 8 centimetres. Its circular cross-section stays the same all the way up.
steps.why: Volume counts equal layers stacked through the height.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="210" y="100" width="270" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="480" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="405" y="87" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Find one circular layer
steps.text: Square the radius before multiplying by pi. Keep pi in the calculation until the end.
steps.why: The circle formula supplies an area in square centimetres.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="210" y="100" width="270" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="480" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="405" y="87" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="345" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text></svg>

steps.title: Stack the layers
steps.text: Multiply the base area by the height of eight centimetres. Squared length times length gives cubed length.
steps.why: Each one-centimetre layer has the same cross-sectional area.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="210" y="100" width="270" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="480" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="405" y="87" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="345" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text><text id="layers" x="345" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#3175ba">8 layers, each 1 cm high</text></svg>

steps.title: Round and reverse if needed
steps.text: The volume is about 226.2 cubic centimetres. If volume and radius were known instead, divide volume by the circular base area to find height.
steps.why: Undo multiplication by the base area using division.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="210" y="100" width="270" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="480" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="405" y="87" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text><text id="base-formula" x="345" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#087f75">base area = 9π cm²</text><text id="layers" x="345" y="248" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="22" fill="#3175ba">8 layers, each 1 cm high</text><text id="result" x="380" y="360" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="28" fill="#087f75">V = 72π cm³ ≈ 226.2 cm³</text></svg>

quiz.question: A cylinder has radius 2 cm and height 5 cm. Its volume is…
quiz.hint: Square the radius, then multiply by height.
quiz.explanation: π × 2² × 5 = 20π cm³.

quiz.question: A cylinder has volume 54π cm³ and radius 3 cm. Its height is…
quiz.hint: Divide the volume by πr².

lessons.takeaway: A cylinder’s volume is circular base area times perpendicular height.
lessons.mistake: Using the diameter where the formula needs the radius.

lessons.title: Unroll the surface
lessons.goal: Choose curved, open or closed surface area correctly.

steps.title: Separate the surfaces
steps.text: A closed cylinder has one curved side and two circular ends. Decide which parts are present before calculating area.
steps.why: Surface area counts exposed faces, not the space inside.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="body" x="210" y="100" width="270" height="200" rx="0" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><ellipse id="base" cx="345" cy="300" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><ellipse id="top" cx="345" cy="100" rx="135" ry="42" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><line id="radius" x1="345" y1="100" x2="480" y2="100" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="3"/><text x="405" y="87" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#087f75">r = 3 cm</text><line id="height" x1="535" y1="100" x2="535" y2="300" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><text x="620" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">h = 8 cm</text></svg>

steps.title: Unroll the curved side
steps.text: Imagine cutting the side vertically and laying it flat. It becomes a rectangle whose width is the circumference of the base.
steps.why: One full wrap around the circle has length two pi times radius.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="curved" x="190" y="110" width="340" height="170" rx="8" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba">curved surface</text><text x="360" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">width = 2πr</text><text x="580" y="201" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#173349">h</text></svg>

steps.title: Count the circular ends
steps.text: Add one circle for an open-topped can, or two circles for a closed can. An end has area pi times radius squared.
steps.why: An absent lid contributes no area.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><rect id="curved" x="190" y="110" width="340" height="170" rx="8" fill="#edf4fc" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="360" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#3175ba">curved surface</text><text x="360" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#3175ba">width = 2πr</text><text x="580" y="201" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="27" fill="#173349">h</text><circle id="end1" cx="108" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><circle id="end2" cx="652" cy="195" r="52" fill="#e8f5f1" stroke="#087f75" stroke-width="2"/><text x="108" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text><text x="652" y="202" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#087f75">πr²</text></svg>

steps.title: Calculate the closed total
steps.text: For radius 3 centimetres and height 8 centimetres, the curved side is 48 pi square centimetres and the two ends total 18 pi. Add those areas.
steps.why: The area units must match before addition.
