quiz.question: To find θ from cos θ = 0.8, use…
quiz.hint: You know the ratio and want the angle.
quiz.explanation: Inverse cosine reverses cosine: θ = cos⁻¹(0.8) ≈ 36.87° in degree mode.

quiz.question: In a triangle question, sin⁻¹(0.5) in degree mode is…
quiz.hint: Which acute angle has sine one half?
quiz.explanation: sin 30° = 0.5, so inverse sine of 0.5 is 30°. A calculator left in radian mode shows 0.5236, which is the same angle measured in radians, not 0.52 degrees.

lessons.takeaway: Ratio known → inverse trig; angle known → ordinary trig. Check DEG mode.
lessons.mistake: Reading sin⁻¹ as one divided by sin.

lessons.title: Find a side in the numerator
lessons.goal: Rearrange a trigonometric ratio when the unknown is on top.

steps.title: Mark the known angle and side
steps.text: A right-angled triangle has a thirty-degree angle and hypotenuse twelve centimetres. Find the side opposite that angle.
steps.why: The opposite–hypotenuse pair selects sine.

steps.title: Undo division by twelve
steps.text: Multiply both sides by twelve to isolate x. This is ordinary equation solving, not a new trig trick.
steps.why: Multiplication cancels the denominator beneath the unknown.

Lengths are in the same units.</text></svg>

steps.title: Evaluate in degree mode
steps.text: Sine thirty degrees is one half. Half of twelve is six centimetres.
steps.why: The trig ratio is a scale factor relating the two sides.

steps.title: Check against the hypotenuse
steps.text: Six is less than twelve, as a shorter side must be. If asked for the other shorter side, use cosine with the same hypotenuse.
steps.why: A geometric size check catches many wrong-ratio errors.

quiz.question: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 and angle 30°. Opposite side?
quiz.hint: Use opposite = hypotenuse × sine.

quiz.question: If cos 40° = x/9, then x is…
quiz.hint: Multiply both sides by 9.
quiz.explanation: x = 9 cos 40°. The unknown is in the numerator.

lessons.takeaway: Write the ratio, then multiply to undo a denominator under the unknown.
lessons.mistake: Memorising “finding a side always means multiply”.

lessons.title: Find a side in the denominator
lessons.goal: Move an unknown denominator before dividing by the ratio.

steps.title: Choose the relevant ratio
steps.text: The side opposite a thirty-degree angle is six centimetres. Find the hypotenuse, now called h.
steps.why: Opposite and hypotenuse still select sine, even when the unknown changes.

steps.title: Multiply away the unknown denominator
steps.text: Multiply both sides by h. This moves h out of the fraction and next to the sine ratio.
steps.why: Multiplying both sides by h keeps the equation balanced and removes the fraction; multiplying one side only would not.

steps.title: Divide by the known ratio
steps.text: Divide by sine thirty degrees to isolate h. Dividing six by one half gives twelve.
steps.why: An unknown denominator leads to a different rearrangement from an unknown numerator.

steps.title: Use the longest-side check
steps.text: The hypotenuse must exceed six centimetres. Multiplying six by one half would give three, which cannot be the hypotenuse.
steps.why: The geometry provides a quick reasonableness check.

quiz.question: If cos 60° = 5/h, what is h?
quiz.hint: Multiply by h, then divide by cos 60°.

quiz.question: If tan 35° = 7/a, then a is…
quiz.hint: The unknown is underneath the known side.
quiz.explanation: a tan 35° = 7, so a = 7/tan 35°.

lessons.takeaway: Unknown underneath: multiply it out, then divide by the known trig ratio.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by a trig ratio when the unknown is the denominator.

lessons.title: Model a real situation as a right-angled triangle
lessons.goal: Choose a right-angled triangle and interpret the final length.

steps.title: Draw the situation and mark the right angle
steps.text: A straight ladder rests against a vertical wall on level ground. Its foot is four metres from the wall, and it makes a sixty-degree angle with the ground.
steps.why: A vertical wall and level ground create the required right angle.

steps.title: Name the required height
steps.text: The wall height reached by the ladder is opposite the marked ground angle. Opposite and adjacent select tangent.
steps.why: The ladder itself is the hypotenuse, not the required vertical height.

steps.title: Calculate the height
steps.text: Multiply four by tangent sixty degrees. The height reached is approximately six point nine three metres.
steps.why: The triangle equation gives vertical height above ground level.

steps.title: Interpret any extra height in the question
steps.text: If an angle is measured from an observer’s eyes instead of ground level, add the eye height when the requested total height includes it. Never add an extra height without a reason.
steps.why: The triangle measures the difference in vertical levels between its endpoints.
steps.math: total height = rise above eyes + eye height

quiz.question: A ladder makes 45° with level ground, and its foot is 3 m from a vertical wall. Height reached?
quiz.hint: Use tan 45° = height/3.
quiz.explanation: tan 45° = 1, so height = 3 metres.

quiz.question: An observer’s eye height is 1.6 m. A trig calculation gives a rise of 8 m above eye level to a tower top. Total height on level ground?
quiz.hint: The triangle starts at eye level.
quiz.explanation: Add the eye height: 8 + 1.6 = 9.6 metres.

lessons.takeaway: Model first, solve second, interpret the units and reference level last.
lessons.mistake: Confusing the sloping line of sight with vertical height.

reference.name: Pythagoras
reference.note: Right-angled triangles only; h is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle), a and b are the two shorter sides.

reference.name: Sine
reference.note: Name sides relative to θ.

reference.name: Cosine
reference.note: The adjacent side is not the hypotenuse.

reference.name: Tangent
reference.note: Only use the two shorter sides.

reference.name: Find an angle
reference.note: Use inverse trig in degree mode; this does not mean reciprocal.

reference.name: Find a length
reference.formula: Write the ratio equation, then rearrange
reference.note: An unknown denominator usually requires division, not multiplication.

toolkit.strategy: Draw and label a right-angled triangle first. Identify the requested quantity and its reference angle, then choose Pythagoras or the ratio using the two relevant sides.

methods.title: Pythagoras: forward and reverse
methods.when: Two side lengths in a right-angled triangle are known.
methods.rule: h²=a²+b²; a=√(h²−b²), with h the hypotenuse and h>b>0.
steps: Mark the right angle and hypotenuse.
Add squares to find h; subtract to find a shorter side.
Take the positive square root and retain an exact surd if appropriate.
methods.example: Shorter sides 5 and 2√6 give h=√(25+24)=7.
methods.trap: Subtracting in the wrong order or squaring only the coefficient of a surd.

methods.title: Use a rectangle’s diagonal and aspect ratio
methods.when: A screen or rectangle is described by diagonal D and width:height = p:q.
methods.rule: width=pk, height=qk, k=D/√(p²+q²); area=D²pq/(p²+q²).
steps: Introduce the common ratio scale k.
Use Pythagoras on the diagonal.
Find width and height, then compare areas using unrounded values.
methods.example: A 20-unit diagonal with ratio 4:3 gives k=4, width 16, height 12, area 192.
methods.trap: Assuming the longer diagonal always means the larger area for different aspect ratios.

methods.title: Name sides relative to the chosen angle
methods.when: A right-angled triangle has an acute reference angle θ.
methods.rule: sinθ=O/H; cosθ=A/H; tanθ=O/A. O and A depend on θ; H does not.
steps: Mark θ.
Name opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from that angle.
Choose the ratio containing exactly the known side and required side.
methods.example: For O=9 and A=12, tanθ=9/12=3/4.
methods.check: Switching to the other acute angle swaps O and A.
methods.trap: Calling the bottom side adjacent without looking at the angle.

methods.title: Find an angle with inverse trig
methods.when: Two relevant side lengths are known and an acute angle is required.
methods.rule: θ=sin⁻¹(O/H), cos⁻¹(A/H) or tan⁻¹(O/A), in degree mode.
steps: Form the correct side ratio.
Use the matching inverse-trig key.
State degrees and check the result lies between 0° and 90°.
methods.trap: Reading sin⁻¹ as 1/sin or using radian mode.

methods.title: Keep special-angle values exact
methods.when: An exact answer uses 30°, 45° or 60° in a right-angled triangle.
steps: Recognise the 1:√3:2 or 1:1:√2 side ratio.
Substitute the exact ratio rather than its rounded decimal.
Simplify surds and round only if the question asks.
methods.example: An opposite side with hypotenuse 10 and angle 60° is 10(√3/2)=5√3.
methods.check: (5√3)²+5²=100 verifies the corresponding 30°–60° triangle.
methods.trap: Replacing √3 by 1.7 before later calculations.

methods.title: Find a side above a fraction bar
methods.when: The chosen ratio has the unknown in its numerator.
methods.rule: If sinθ=x/H, then x=H sinθ; similarly for cosine or tangent.
steps: Write the ratio as an equation.
Multiply both sides by the known denominator.
Calculate in degrees, then use a size check.
methods.example: If cos40°=a/9, then a=9cos40°≈6.89.
methods.check: The adjacent side is shorter than the hypotenuse 9.
methods.trap: Choosing multiplication from memory without first writing the equation.

methods.title: Find a side below a fraction bar
methods.when: The chosen ratio has an unknown denominator.
methods.rule: If sinθ=O/h, then h=O/sinθ; if tanθ=O/a, then a=O/tanθ.
steps: Multiply by the unknown denominator.
Divide by the known non-zero ratio.
Check the hypotenuse or relative side lengths.
methods.check: 14 is greater than the known side 7.
methods.trap: Multiplying 7 by sin30° when the unknown is underneath.

methods.title: Find horizontal distance from another shape
methods.when: A sight-line problem gives circumference, diameter or other geometry instead of direct distance.
methods.rule: C=2πr; r=C/(2π). The right-angled triangle needs horizontal distance, not curved boundary length.
steps: Use the other shape’s formula to recover the needed straight distance.
Decide whether the sight line spans a radius, diameter or a sum of distances.
Use that distance as the appropriate triangle side.
methods.example: A circular court of circumference 30π m has radius 15 m; centre-to-edge is 15 m and across it is 30 m.
methods.check: Twice the radius must recover the diameter and circumference formula.
methods.trap: Using the circumference as the triangle’s horizontal side.

methods.title: Convert a rise into total height
methods.when: An observer sights a top from eye level on level ground.
methods.rule: H=e+d tanθ when e is eye height and d is horizontal distance; adjust the vertical reference if ground levels differ.
steps: Draw a horizontal line from the eyes to the object.
Calculate the rise above that line.
Add the eye height only when the required height starts at the same ground level.
methods.check: Subtracting e must return d tanθ.
methods.trap: Adding eye height twice or confusing a sloping sight line with d.

methods.title: Link right-angled triangles without rounding early
methods.when: Two right-angled triangles share a side or a calculated length.
methods.rule: Carry the shared side exactly; (a√b)²=a²b. Each triangle needs its own right angle and reference angle.
steps: Solve the triangle containing enough known data.
Transfer the shared side to the second triangle.
Use exact surds or fractions until the final step.
If combining angles, establish whether the shared ray lies between the others.
methods.example: A shared side √(8²+6²)=10 can then be the hypotenuse of a second triangle with a 6-unit side, giving its other shorter side 8.
methods.check: Check Pythagoras separately in both triangles.
methods.trap: Adding angles without checking the rays’ order.

methods.title: Use two observation positions
methods.when: Two angles look at one top from different known horizontal positions.
methods.rule: Same vertical rise gives d tanβ=(d+s)tanα when the farther observer is s farther away, at the same eye level.
steps: Define d as the nearer horizontal distance.
Write the same rise using both triangles.
Solve for d, find the rise, then add any eye height.
methods.example: With α=30°,β=45°, separation s: d=s/(√3−1).
methods.check: Both tangent expressions must give the same rise.
methods.trap: Treating the distance between observers as either complete triangle base.

checks: Set the calculator to degree mode; inverse trig returns an angle.
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and must be the longest side.
Keep surds and full calculator precision until the final requested rounding.
Check whether a triangle measures total height or only the rise above eye level.
Compare the quantity actually asked for: diagonal, height and area are different.

challenges.title: A sight line across a circular field
challenges.question: A level circular field has circumference 88π m. A vertical pole stands at a point on its boundary. An observer at the centre has eye height 1.7 m and sees the pole top at elevation 35°. (a) Find the field radius. (b) Find the pole height to the nearest 0.1 m. (c) A second observer with the same eye height stands on the opposite end of the diameter through the pole. Find that observer’s angle of elevation to the nearest 0.1°. Use degree mode.
hints: Convert circumference into radius before using trigonometry.
The first horizontal distance is r; the second is 2r. Both observers see the same rise above eye level.

solution.title: Find the horizontal distances
solution.reason: The first observer is at the centre, while the second is at the opposite boundary.

solution.title: Calculate the rise and height
solution.reason: The tangent triangle measures only the rise above the eyes.

solution.title: Use the second position
solution.reason: Use the unrounded rise rather than rounded total height.

solution.title: Find the new angle
solution.reason: The farther observer has the smaller elevation angle.

challenges.check: Using the unrounded φ gives 88tanφ=44tan35°, so both triangles agree on the rise.

challenges.title: Compare screens by area
challenges.question: Screen A has diagonal 50 inches and width:height ratio 16:9. Screen B has diagonal 48 inches and width:height ratio 4:3. Both screens are exact rectangles. (a) Express each screen’s width and height using one scale factor and find that factor. (b) Find each area to the nearest square inch. (c) Which screen has greater area, and by what percentage relative to the smaller area? Keep exact expressions until the final rounding.
hints: Use width=16k and height=9k for A, rather than dividing the diagonal in the ratio 16:9.
The diagonal gives (16k)²+(9k)²=50². For B, the ratio triangle is 3–4–5.

solution.title: Find A’s dimensions
solution.reason: The diagonal is the hypotenuse.

solution.title: Find B’s dimensions
solution.reason: The 4:3 ratio has diagonal multiplier 5.

solution.title: Compare unrounded areas
solution.reason: Multiply the actual width and height, not the diagonal.

solution.title: Calculate relative difference
solution.reason: Screen B is larger despite its shorter diagonal.

challenges.answer: (a) k=50/√337, j=9.6. (b) A≈1068 in²; B≈1106 in². (c) B is larger by about 3.53%.
challenges.check: For B, 38.4²+28.8²=48²; for A, the symbolic dimensions square to a total of 2500.

challenges.title: A shared side carries exact information
challenges.question: Triangle ABC is right-angled at B, with AB=6 cm and BC=6√3 cm. Triangle ACD is right-angled at C, with CD=5 cm. D lies on the opposite side of AC from B, as shown. (a) Find AC and AD exactly. (b) Find ∠BAC exactly. (c) Find ∠CAD to the nearest 0.1°. (d) Hence find ∠BAD to the nearest 0.1°, explaining whether the angles add or subtract.
hints: Solve triangle ABC first; its hypotenuse becomes a shorter side of ACD.
In ACD, AD is the hypotenuse. The ray AC lies inside angle BAD in the stated configuration.

solution.title: Find the shared side
solution.reason: Square both the coefficient and the surd correctly.

solution.title: Solve the second triangle
solution.reason: The right angle in ACD is at C.

solution.title: Find the two angles
solution.reason: Each ratio is relative to its own angle at A.

solution.title: Combine using the configuration
solution.reason: B and D lie on opposite sides of AC, so AC separates the two angle parts.

challenges.answer: (a) AC=12 cm, AD=13 cm. (b) 60°. (c) 22.6°. (d) 82.6°, adding the two angles.
challenges.check: The second triangle is a 5–12–13 right-angled triangle; its complementary acute angles sum to 90°.

challenges.title: Two observations, one unknown height
challenges.question: An observer on level ground sights a vertical mast at elevation 30°. The observer walks 20 m directly towards its foot and sights the top at 45°. Eye height is 1.5 m at both positions. (a) Define the nearer horizontal distance d and write the rise above eye level in two ways. (b) Find d exactly as a surd. (c) Find the mast height exactly and to the nearest 0.1 m. (d) Verify the farther triangle.
hints: At 45°, the rise equals the nearer horizontal distance.
Use d=(d+20)/√3, then rationalise the denominator if needed.

solution.title: Model both triangles
solution.reason: Both observations share the same vertical rise.

solution.title: Solve the shared-rise equation
solution.reason: Multiplying numerator and denominator by √3+1 preserves the fraction.

solution.title: Restore the eye height
solution.reason: The tangent triangles start at eye level.

solution.title: Check the farther view
solution.reason: The farther triangle gives exactly the same rise as the nearer one.

challenges.answer: (a) rise=d=(d+20)/√3. (b) d=10(√3+1) m. (c) H=11.5+10√3 m≈28.8 m. (d) Both triangles give rise d.
challenges.check: d≈27.32 m and farther distance≈47.32 m; their rise-to-run ratios are 1 and 1/√3 respectively.

quiz.question: Which point lies on y = 3x − 2?
quiz.hint: Substitute the first coordinate into the rule.
quiz.explanation: At x = 2, y = 6−2 = 4, so (2,4) lies on the line.

quiz.question: The y-intercept of y = −2x + 5 is…
quiz.hint: At the y-axis, x = 0.
quiz.explanation: Putting x = 0 gives y = 5.

lessons.takeaway: Table → ordered pairs → plot; use the domain to decide whether to join.
lessons.mistake: Swapping x and y or joining a finite set of points without permission.

lessons.title: Sketch a quadratic with its turning point
lessons.goal: Use a symmetric table to plot a smooth parabola.

steps.title: Recognise the squared term
steps.text: Use y equals x squared minus twice x minus three. Its positive squared-term coefficient means the curve opens upwards.
steps.why: The squared term controls the parabola’s overall direction.

steps.title: Draw a smooth curve
steps.text: The turning point is (1,−4): the lowest output in the table, with matching outputs on either side. Draw a smooth U-shaped curve through the points instead of sharp corners.
steps.why: A quadratic graph is a parabola, not a sequence of straight segments.

steps.title: Check the key features
steps.text: The x-axis crossings are negative one and three. The y-axis crossing is negative three; the minimum output is negative four.
steps.why: Intercepts and the vertex provide several independent checks.

quiz.question: For y = (x − 2)² + 3, the minimum point is…
quiz.hint: The square is smallest when it is zero.
quiz.explanation: At x = 2, the square is zero and y = 3, so the vertex is (2,3).

quiz.question: If the coefficient of x² is negative, the parabola…
quiz.hint: Think of −x².
quiz.explanation: A negative leading coefficient turns the parabola downwards, giving a maximum rather than a minimum.

lessons.takeaway: Use symmetric points, a smooth curve and a clearly marked turning point.
lessons.mistake: Joining parabola points with a ruler as a broken zigzag.

lessons.title: Read solutions from intersections
lessons.goal: Solve equations by intersecting a function graph with a horizontal line.

steps.title: Translate the equation into a height
steps.text: Use the same quadratic graph and solve f of x equals negative three. We are asking where its output reaches height negative three.
steps.why: An equation f(x) equals k fixes a horizontal output level.

steps.title: Draw the target level
steps.text: Add the horizontal line y equals negative three. Look for every place it meets the parabola.
steps.why: An intersection satisfies both the curve rule and the line rule.

steps.title: Read both inputs
steps.text: The intersections occur at inputs zero and two. Both are solutions, because a U-shaped graph can reach the same output twice.
steps.why: Different inputs may share an output in a function.

steps.title: Check with algebra
steps.text: Moving negative three to the other side leaves x squared minus twice x equals zero. Factorising gives the same two solutions.
steps.why: Graphical and algebraic answers describe the same intersections.

quiz.question: To solve f(x) = 4 graphically, draw…
quiz.hint: The output value is the vertical coordinate.
quiz.explanation: Draw the horizontal line y = 4 and read the x-coordinates where it intersects f.

quiz.question: For f(x) = x², solving f(x) = 9 gives…
quiz.hint: The square graph reaches height 9 on both sides.
quiz.explanation: Both (−3)² and 3² equal 9.

lessons.takeaway: A target output is a horizontal line; read every matching input.
lessons.mistake: Reading the intersection’s y-coordinate when the question asks for x.

lessons.title: Compare two function graphs
lessons.goal: Use intersections to solve f(x) = g(x) and to read where f(x) < g(x).

steps.title: Write both rules
steps.text: Compare the parabola y equals x squared with the line y equals x plus two. We want inputs for which the outputs are equal.
steps.why: At an intersection, the point belongs to both graphs.

steps.title: Plot each rule on the same axes
steps.text: Keep the axes and scales identical. Reading the graph, the crossings appear to be at (−1,1) and (2,4).
steps.why: Comparing graphs requires a common coordinate system.

steps.title: Read the requested quantities
steps.text: The equation asks for inputs, so the solutions are negative one and two. If asked for intersection coordinates, include the corresponding outputs too.
steps.why: Input solutions and full points are different forms of answer.

steps.title: Confirm exactly, then read an inequality
steps.text: Bring all terms to one side and factorise. The two factors give exactly the values read from the graph. The same picture answers an inequality: the parabola is below the line only between the crossings, so x² < x + 2 exactly when −1 < x < 2.
steps.why: An exact algebraic check refines a visual estimate, and the crossings are the endpoints of the inequality’s solution set.

quiz.question: On the same graph, y = x² is below y = x + 2 for which inputs?
quiz.hint: The graphs cross at x = −1 and x = 2; test one input between them, such as x = 0.
quiz.explanation: At x = 0 the parabola gives 0 and the line gives 2, so the parabola is lower there. It is lower only between the crossings: −1 < x < 2.

quiz.question: Solve x² = 4x graphically or algebraically.
quiz.hint: Bring all terms to one side and take out the common factor x.
quiz.explanation: x²−4x = x(x−4) = 0 gives x = 0 or 4.

lessons.takeaway: Intersections solve equal-output equations; between or beyond them, read which graph is higher to solve an inequality.
lessons.mistake: Stopping after the first crossing: two graphs can meet more than once.

lessons.title: Interpret a quadratic ball-height graph
lessons.goal: Connect roots, maximum and domain to a real situation.

steps.title: Read the variables and units
steps.text: A simplified kicked-ball model gives height H in metres after time t in seconds. The rule is twenty t minus five t squared.
steps.why: This graph shows height against time, not the ball’s sideways path.

steps.title: Find ground-level times
steps.text: Set height equal to zero and factorise. The roots zero and four are launch and landing times in this model.
steps.why: A height of zero means the ball is at ground level.

steps.title: Locate the maximum
steps.text: The peak is halfway between the two equal-height ground points, at two seconds. Substitution gives a maximum height of twenty metres.
steps.why: The quadratic’s symmetry places the vertex halfway between its roots.

steps.title: Use the physical domain
steps.text: For this flight, time runs from zero to four seconds. Height fifteen metres occurs twice, once on the way up and once on the way down.
steps.why: The physical story restricts the portion of the mathematical curve we use.

quiz.question: For H(t) = 20t − 5t², the ball lands after launch at…
quiz.hint: Set H equal to zero and choose the positive later root.
quiz.explanation: 5t(4−t) = 0 gives t = 0 and t = 4; landing is at 4 seconds.

quiz.question: Why can H(t) = 15 have two solutions?
options: The rule is not a function
The ball reaches 15 m on the way up and down
Every quadratic has exactly two roots for every target
quiz.hint: A single output can come from different inputs.
quiz.explanation: The same height occurs at t = 1 and t = 3. This is still a function because each time has one height.

lessons.takeaway: Roots, vertex and domain must be interpreted in the story’s units.
lessons.mistake: Treating a height–time curve as the literal spatial path of a ball.

lessons.title: Graph exponential growth and decay
lessons.goal: Use multiplication and negative inputs to plot exponential rules.

steps.title: Build a table by multiplying
steps.text: For y equals two to the power x, moving one input step right doubles the output. At zero, the output is one.
steps.why: Any non-zero base raised to the power zero is one.

steps.title: Plot and draw the smooth growth curve
steps.text: The curve crosses the y-axis at one and gets increasingly steep to the right. It stays above the x-axis.
steps.why: Powers of a positive base remain positive.

steps.title: Compare a decay rule
steps.text: For one half raised to x, each step right halves the output. The curve still passes through (0,1) but decreases to the right.
steps.why: A base between zero and one causes multiplicative decay.

steps.title: Read values without expecting equal gaps
steps.text: Doubling makes the vertical differences grow; halving makes them shrink. The horizontal axis is approached but never reached by either positive-base exponential.
steps.why: Repeated multiplication is not the same as repeated addition.

quiz.question: The point at x = 0 on y = 3ˣ is…
quiz.hint: Any non-zero base to power zero is one.
quiz.explanation: 3⁰ = 1, so the graph passes through (0,1).

quiz.question: Which rule represents exponential decay as x increases?
quiz.hint: Look for a base between zero and one.
quiz.explanation: Multiplying by 1/3 for each unit increase makes the output decay.

lessons.takeaway: Exponential rules use a constant multiplier; negative powers give reciprocals.
lessons.mistake: Treating an exponential graph as a straight line with equal vertical gaps.

lessons.title: Move a function without rebuilding it
lessons.goal: Relate simple vertical and horizontal changes to coordinates.

steps.title: Start with a familiar graph
steps.text: Use the basic parabola y equals x squared. Its vertex is at the origin, and opposite inputs give equal outputs.
steps.why: A known graph provides a reference shape.

steps.title: Add outside to move vertically
steps.text: Adding three to the whole function raises every output by three. Every point keeps its input coordinate.
steps.why: An outside addition changes y after the original rule acts.

steps.title: Change inside to move horizontally
steps.text: Replacing x by x minus two moves the parabola two units right. The new square is zero when x is two.
steps.why: To reproduce an old output, x minus two must equal the old input, so x must be two larger: every point moves two to the right.

steps.title: Check a transformed point
steps.text: Combining both changes gives a vertex at (2,3). Check a nearby point as well, such as (3,4).
steps.why: Substitution verifies the direction and size of the movement.

quiz.question: The graph y = x² − 4 is y = x² moved…
quiz.hint: The change is outside the square.
quiz.explanation: Subtracting four changes every output by −4, shifting the graph down four.

quiz.question: The vertex of y = (x + 1)² + 2 is…
quiz.hint: Find the input that makes the bracket zero.
quiz.explanation: x + 1 = 0 when x = −1; then y = 2, so the vertex is (−1,2).

lessons.takeaway: Outside changes move outputs; inside changes move inputs in the opposite direction.
lessons.mistake: Reading x minus two as a shift left by two.

reference.name: Linear
reference.note: m is the slope (also called gradient); c is the y-intercept.

reference.name: Quadratic
reference.note: a > 0 opens upwards; a < 0 opens downwards.

reference.name: Axis of symmetry
reference.note: The vertex lies on this line.

reference.name: Solve graphically
reference.formula: f(x) = k: intersect with y = k
reference.note: Read all intersection x-coordinates; graph answers may be approximate.

reference.name: Two functions
reference.note: Each intersection satisfies both rules. Between or beyond the intersections, the higher graph has the larger output, which answers f(x) < g(x) or f(x) > g(x).

reference.name: Vertical translation
reference.formula: f(x) + k shifts up by k
reference.note: The x-coordinate of each point is unchanged.

reference.name: Horizontal translation
reference.formula: y = f(x − h): shift the graph h units right
reference.note: For negative h, the shift is left. Together, f(x − h) + k shifts right by h and up by k.

reference.name: Exponential function
reference.formula: y = aˣ, with a > 0 and a ≠ 1
reference.note: Passes through (0,1). It grows if a > 1 and decays if 0 < a < 1.

toolkit.strategy: Decide whether the rule is given or must first be built from the situation. State the domain, choose a sensible graph window, and translate every graph feature back into the requested quantity.

methods.title: Build and check a straight-line graph
methods.when: The rule is y=mx+c or linear data are supplied.
methods.rule: m=Δy/Δx for Δx≠0; c=f(0); y−y₁=m(x−x₁).
steps: Find m and c or evaluate a short table.
Plot two points and check a third.
Join continuously only over a real interval domain.
methods.check: At x=4 the rule returns 20.
methods.trap: Plotting the constant c on the x-axis.

methods.title: Recover a linear model from a table
methods.when: Costs or other outputs rise by a fixed amount per input step.
methods.rule: m=(output change)/(input change); fixed part c=y−mx.
steps: Use two rows, accounting for unequal input gaps.
Find the fixed amount with one row.
Check unused rows and any practical domain.
methods.example: €11 at 2 h and €20 at 5 h give m=9/3=3 and C=3h+5.
methods.check: C(5)=20 and the starting charge is €5.
methods.trap: Dividing total cost by hours when there is a fixed fee.

methods.title: Build a quadratic table and vertex
methods.when: The rule contains a non-zero squared term.
methods.rule: y=ax²+bx+c, a≠0; vertex x=−b/(2a), y=f(−b/(2a)); y=a(x−h)²+k has vertex (h,k).
steps: Find the symmetry line.
Choose inputs on both sides and evaluate them with brackets.
Draw a smooth curve; a>0 gives a minimum and a<0 a maximum.
methods.example: y=2(x−3)²−5 has vertex (3,−5), minimum −5 and symmetric outputs at 2 and 4.
methods.check: f(3−u)=f(3+u) in vertex form.
methods.trap: Drawing a quadratic as a broken straight-line graph.

methods.title: Find intercepts and translate their meaning
methods.when: The graph’s crossings or zeros are needed.
methods.rule: y-intercept: x=0; x-intercepts: f(x)=0. For a quadratic, factorise when possible and use the zero-product rule.
steps: Set the correct coordinate to zero.
Solve, then write full coordinate pairs if asked.
Interpret roots within the model’s domain.
methods.example: y=(x−2)(x+4) crosses at (2,0),(−4,0), and at (0,−8) on the y-axis.
methods.check: Each crossing gives the corresponding zero coordinate.
methods.trap: Calling a root (0,2) instead of (2,0).

methods.title: Solve a target output graphically
methods.when: An equation f(x)=k is given.
methods.rule: Draw the horizontal line y=k; read all intersection x-values.
steps: Plot the function accurately on a useful scale.
Draw the target level horizontally.
Read every crossing and check by substitution or algebra if possible.
methods.example: For f(x)=(x−1)², f(x)=9 gives x=−2 or 4.
methods.check: Both inputs are 3 units from the symmetry line x=1.
methods.trap: Drawing x=k or missing the second crossing.

methods.title: Solve equality of two functions
methods.when: Two graphs or rules must be compared: equal outputs, or one output below the other.
methods.rule: f(x)=g(x) at their intersections; f(x)<g(x) where the graph of f is below the graph of g.
steps: Plot on the same axes and scale.
Locate all crossings in the stated domain.
Give x-values for an equation, or full points for intersections; for an inequality, give the interval of x where the required graph is lower.
Check exact candidate inputs in both rules.
methods.check: Both rules give 1 and 9 at those inputs; at x=0, 0<3 confirms the inequality side.
methods.trap: Confusing an intersection of two functions with an x-axis root.

methods.title: Derive a constrained area model
methods.when: A fixed perimeter or fencing total links two unknown dimensions.
methods.rule: For three fenced sides with total L: length=L−2x; A=x(L−2x), with 0<x<L/2.
steps: Name the repeated side x.
Use the length constraint to express the other side.
Multiply to get area and state positive-length restrictions.
For a target area, solve and test all candidate dimensions.
methods.example: With 28 m of fence, A=28x−2x² and 0<x<14.
methods.check: 2x+length must return 28 and both dimensions must be positive.
methods.trap: Using a four-sided perimeter when one side is an existing wall.

methods.title: Find a maximum or minimum and interpret it
methods.when: The problem asks for greatest area, height or another quadratic output.
methods.rule: For A=ax²+bx+c, vertex input=−b/(2a); check domain endpoints when included. Three-side fencing: maximum L²/8 at x=L/4, length=L/2.
steps: Find the vertex by symmetry or completing the square.
Verify it lies in the allowed domain.
Evaluate the output and state the corresponding physical dimensions.
methods.example: A=28x−2x²=98−2(x−7)² has maximum 98 m² at x=7 m.
methods.check: Subtracting 2(x−7)², which is never negative, can only lower 98, so 98 is the maximum.
methods.trap: Giving the maximum’s input instead of the maximum output.

methods.title: Graph and estimate exponential values
methods.when: The input appears as a power rather than as a polynomial variable.
methods.rule: y=abˣ with a>0,b>0,b≠1; y(0)=a, y(x+1)/y(x)=b. b>1 gives growth; 0<b<1 gives decay; b⁻ⁿ=1/bⁿ.
steps: Make a table including zero and appropriate negative inputs.
Draw a smooth positive curve.
To estimate an input for output T, draw y=T and bracket it between known powers.
methods.example: For 3ˣ=20, 3²=9 and 3³=27 show 2<x<3; refine the graph or a value table.
methods.check: Substitute the estimated input and see whether its output is close to 20.
methods.trap: Expecting equal additive gaps or treating a graph estimate as exact.

methods.title: Transform a known graph
methods.when: The new rule changes f(x) without requiring a new shape from scratch.
methods.rule: f(x)+k: up k; f(x−h): right h; −f(x): reflect in x-axis; f(−x): reflect in y-axis. Combined g(x)=a f(x−h)+k maps (u,v) to (u+h,av+k).
steps: Identify inside changes separately from outside changes.
Transform a key point and the intercept/vertex where useful.
Check a second point by substitution.
methods.example: From y=x² to y=−(x−2)²+3, vertex (0,0) becomes (2,3) and the parabola opens down.
methods.check: Input 3 gives output 2, matching the transformed point (1,1)→(3,2).
methods.trap: Reading x−2 as a shift left instead of right.

checks: Every plotted point must satisfy its rule; check a spare point after drawing.
Use smooth curves for quadratic/exponential functions, not joined line segments.
Intersections answer equal-output questions; report x-values or full coordinates as requested.
A model’s maximum and roots must lie in its practical domain.
Graph estimates should be labelled approximate; preserve exact algebraic answers when available.

challenges.title: Forty metres of fencing
challenges.question: A rectangular pen uses an existing straight wall as one side. Exactly 40 m of fencing forms the other three sides. Let x metres be the width perpendicular to the wall. (a) Express the remaining fenced side and the area A in terms of x; state the domain for a non-degenerate pen. (b) Find both possible widths giving area 168 m², with the matching lengths. (c) Find the greatest possible area and its dimensions. (d) Explain why both solutions in (b) are physically admissible.
hints: The fence constraint is 2x+L=40.
For the maximum, write A=200−2(x−10)².

solution.title: Build the model and domain
solution.reason: Both width and length must be positive.

solution.title: Solve the target area
solution.reason: Both algebraic roots must be tested against the domain.

solution.title: Recover matching dimensions
solution.math: x=6 gives L=28; x=14 gives L=12
solution.reason: The two widths have different matching lengths.

solution.title: Find the maximum
solution.reason: The vertex lies within the allowed domain.

solution.title: Check admissibility
solution.reason: Each pair uses the correct total fence and produces positive dimensions.

challenges.answer: (a) L=40−2x, A=40x−2x², 0<x<20. (b) 6×28 m or 14×12 m. (c) Maximum 200 m² at 10×20 m. (d) Both satisfy the domain and fence constraint.
challenges.check: 6×28=14×12=168, while the vertex dimensions give 10×20=200.

challenges.title: Recover and compare hire charges
challenges.question: A hire company A charges €26 for 2 hours and €47 for 5 hours. Its cost is linear in duration h for 0≤h≤8. Company B charges C=10h+3 euro over the same domain. (a) Find A’s formula. (b) Find the duration and cost at which the companies agree. (c) State when A is cheaper. (d) With €61 available, what is the longest hire duration from A within the stated model?
hints: Use the change in total cost divided by the change in time.
The fixed fee comes from substituting one table row after the hourly rate is found.

solution.title: Find A’s rate and fee
solution.reason: The table determines the slope and intercept.

solution.title: Find the intersection
solution.reason: At the meeting point the same duration has equal cost.

solution.title: Compare over the domain
solution.reason: The sign of the difference decides which output is smaller.

solution.title: Reverse the budget
solution.reason: The budget bound and the model’s upper limit both apply.

challenges.check: A(5)=47 checks the original data; A(7)=61 uses the budget exactly.

challenges.title: Quadratic growth meets exponential growth
challenges.question: For 0≤x≤5, let f(x)=x² and g(x)=2ˣ. (a) Make a table for integer inputs 0 to 5. (b) Use the graphs to find their intersection coordinates in this interval, and check the integer inputs exactly. (c) Which output is larger at x=1,3,5? (d) Estimate the input for which g(x)=12 to the nearest 0.1. You may refine the graph with trial values of 2ˣ.
hints: Use the same axes for both functions. Equal outputs are intersections, not necessarily x-axis roots.
For part (d), 2³=8 and 2⁴=16; trial inputs near 3.5 and 3.6 refine the estimate.

solution.title: Make the table
solution.reason: Exponential growth doubles at each unit input step.

solution.title: Read and check the crossings
solution.math: Intersections shown are (2,4) and (4,16); f(2)=2²=4=2²=g(2) and f(4)=4²=16=2⁴=g(4)
solution.reason: The graph identifies the crossing locations; direct substitution verifies them exactly.

solution.title: Compare requested positions
solution.math: At x=1: g>f; x=3: f>g; x=5: g>f
solution.reason: Comparing one point does not establish which function is larger everywhere.

solution.title: Refine an inverse estimate
solution.reason: The output target lies between the trial outputs; the input is rounded only at the end.

challenges.answer: (a) Table above. (b) (2,4),(4,16). (c) g, f, g respectively. (d) x≈3.6.
challenges.check: 2^3.585≈12.0003 verifies the refined estimate; both integer crossing outputs match exactly.

challenges.title: One transformation, several graph questions
challenges.question: Consider g(x)=−(x−2)²+9. (a) Describe how to obtain its graph from y=x², and give its vertex and opening direction. (b) Find both x-intercepts and the y-intercept. (c) Solve g(x)=5. (d) Restrict the domain to 0≤x≤5. Find the greatest and least outputs on this interval and state where they occur.
hints: Read the bracketed square first: it is zero at x=2.
The restricted minimum need not be a turning point; test the included endpoints.

solution.title: Transform the basic parabola
solution.math: Shift right 2, reflect in the x-axis, then shift up 9; vertex (2,9), opening down
solution.reason: Inside and outside changes act on different coordinates.

solution.title: Find intercepts
solution.reason: Both square roots matter when solving a squared equation.

solution.title: Solve the target output
solution.reason: The graph reaches that height on both sides of its vertex.

solution.title: Apply the restricted domain
solution.math: g(0)=5, g(2)=9, g(5)=0; greatest 9 at x=2; least 0 at x=5
solution.reason: The downward vertex gives the maximum; compare both endpoints for the minimum.

challenges.answer: (a) Right 2, reflect in the x-axis, up 9; vertex (2,9), opens down. (b) (−1,0),(5,0),(0,5). (c) x=0 or 4. (d) Maximum 9 at 2, minimum 0 at 5.
challenges.check: On 0≤x≤5, −2≤x−2≤3, so 0≤(x−2)²≤9; hence 0≤g(x)≤9 with both limits attained.

title: Geometry 3: Transformations – Constructions
intro: Move shapes precisely and build new ones using geometric reasons.

lessons.title: Translate every point by the same move
lessons.goal: Use a translation vector and preserve shape.

steps.title: Specify the movement
steps.text: Translate a triangle three units right and one unit up. The same displacement applies to every vertex.
steps.why: A translation slides a shape without turning or resizing it. Exam papers often name one by a directed line segment, for example the translation that maps A to B.

quiz.hint: A slide preserves the shape itself.
quiz.explanation: Position changes, while lengths, angles, shape and orientation are preserved.

lessons.takeaway: Apply the same horizontal and vertical change to every vertex.
lessons.mistake: Moving different vertices by different amounts.

lessons.title: Axial symmetry: reflect in a mirror line
lessons.goal: Place reflected points at equal perpendicular distances.

steps.title: Identify the mirror line
steps.text: Reflect a triangle in the y-axis; exam papers call this axial symmetry in the y-axis. This vertical line acts as the mirror.
steps.why: A reflection reverses the side of the mirror while preserving distance from it.

steps.text: The point (1,0) is one unit to the right of the mirror. Its image is one unit to the left, at (−1,0).
steps.why: The mirror is the perpendicular bisector of the point–image segment.

steps.title: Join and check the mirror image
steps.text: The two triangles are congruent but face opposite ways. Each original point and image point lies on a line perpendicular to the mirror.
steps.why: Reflection preserves size but reverses orientation.
steps.math: distance to mirror = image distance to mirror

quiz.hint: Change x only.

quiz.question: Reflect (3,−2) in the x-axis.

lessons.takeaway: The mirror bisects each point–image segment at right angles.
lessons.mistake: Changing both coordinates for an axis reflection.

lessons.title: Recognise central and axial symmetry
lessons.goal: Distinguish a mirror reflection from a half-turn.

steps.title: Test an axis of symmetry
steps.text: A line is an axis of symmetry when reflecting the entire shape in it leaves the shape unchanged. Do not judge by one matching vertex alone.
steps.why: Every point of the shape must have its reflected partner.

steps.title: Test a centre of symmetry
steps.text: A centre of symmetry gives an unchanged shape after a half-turn. Every point and its partner lie opposite each other through the centre.
steps.why: The centre is the midpoint of each partner pair.

steps.text: For a half-turn about the origin, both coordinate signs reverse. A point (2,3) moves to (−2,−3).
steps.why: Opposite points have the origin as their midpoint.

steps.title: Separate the two tests
steps.text: A general parallelogram has a centre of symmetry at its diagonals’ intersection, but need not have any mirror axis. Symmetry of one type does not imply the other.
steps.why: A half-turn and a reflection are different transformations.
steps.math: centre symmetry does not imply an axis

quiz.question: A half-turn about the origin maps (4,−1) to…
quiz.hint: Both coordinates change sign.
quiz.explanation: A 180° turn maps (x,y) to (−x,−y), giving (−4,1).

quiz.question: A non-square rectangle has how many axes of symmetry?
quiz.hint: Test the two midlines and the diagonals.
quiz.explanation: Its horizontal and vertical midlines are axes; its diagonals are not, unless it is a square.

lessons.takeaway: An axis gives a reflection; a centre gives a half-turn.
lessons.mistake: Assuming a centre of symmetry must lie on a mirror axis.

lessons.title: Rotate around a specified centre
lessons.goal: Use centre, angle and direction to locate an image.

steps.title: State all three rotation instructions
steps.text: Rotate the triangle ninety degrees anticlockwise about the origin. The centre stays fixed during the turn.
steps.why: A rotation is incomplete without its centre, angle and direction.

steps.text: (1,0) lies one unit to the right of the origin. A quarter-turn anticlockwise places it one unit above, at (0,1).
steps.why: Rotation preserves distance from the centre.

steps.title: Use the coordinate rule
steps.text: For ninety degrees anticlockwise about the origin, swap coordinates and negate the old y-coordinate. Check each vertex independently.
steps.why: Check it on the axis points: (1,0) goes to (0,1) and (0,1) goes to (−1,0), so x along and y up become y to the left and x up.

quiz.hint: Use (x,y) → (−y,x).

quiz.hint: The image depends on where and which way you turn.

lessons.takeaway: Keep the centre fixed and preserve each point’s distance from it.
lessons.mistake: Rotating about the page origin when the stated centre is elsewhere.

lessons.title: Construct a perpendicular bisector
lessons.goal: Use equal-radius arcs to bisect a segment at right angles.

steps.title: Draw the given segment
steps.text: Draw segment AB and open the compass to more than half its length. Do not estimate the midpoint by eye.
steps.why: Two circles need to intersect above and below the segment.

steps.title: Draw arcs from A
steps.text: With the compass point on A, draw arcs above and below the segment. Keep the compass opening fixed.
steps.why: Every point on these arcs is the same distance from A.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="segment" x1="250" y1="210" x2="510" y2="210" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="250" y="243" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="510" y="243" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><circle id="arc-a" cx="250" cy="210" r="170" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Repeat from B at the same radius
steps.text: Draw matching arcs from B to create intersections P and Q. Both intersections are equally far from A and B.
steps.why: Equal compass openings establish equality of the paired distances.

steps.title: Join the intersections
steps.text: Draw the straight line through P and Q. It meets AB at its midpoint M and at a right angle; leave the arcs visible.
steps.why: Points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

quiz.question: Why must the compass opening stay the same for the two sets of arcs?
options: To make the intersections equidistant from A and B
quiz.hint: The proof depends on equal distances.
quiz.explanation: Equal radii make each intersection equally far from both endpoints, locating their perpendicular bisector.

quiz.question: A perpendicular bisector of AB…
quiz.hint: Both words in its name matter.
quiz.explanation: Bisector means equal halves, and perpendicular means a right angle.

lessons.takeaway: Same radius from both endpoints → two intersections → join them.
lessons.mistake: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints.

lessons.title: Construct an angle bisector
lessons.goal: Build the ray that splits an angle into two equal angles.

steps.title: Begin at the angle’s vertex
steps.text: Let V be the vertex of the angle. The required bisector must start at V, not at the middle of one side.
steps.why: An angle is formed by two rays sharing a vertex.

steps.title: Mark equal distances along the rays
steps.text: Centre the compass on V and draw one arc crossing both rays at A and B. These points are equally distant from V.
steps.why: A single compass circle has one fixed radius.

steps.title: Draw matching crossing arcs
steps.text: From A and B, draw equal-radius arcs inside the angle, meeting at P. Use the same opening for the pair.
steps.why: P is equally far from A and B, creating two matching triangles.

steps.text: Draw ray VP. Triangles VAP and VBP have three equal corresponding sides, so their angles at V are equal.
steps.why: SSS congruence proves that VP bisects the angle.

quiz.question: Which point must an angle bisector pass through?
quiz.hint: The two new angles share the original corner.
quiz.explanation: Both equal angles must begin at the original vertex.

quiz.question: A bisector divides a 74° angle into…
quiz.hint: Bisect means split into two equal parts.
quiz.explanation: 74 ÷ 2 = 37°, so both new angles measure 37°.

lessons.takeaway: Equal marks from the vertex, equal crossing arcs, then join to the vertex.
lessons.mistake: Joining the two side marks instead of joining the vertex to the arc intersection.

lessons.title: Construct a perpendicular at a point
lessons.goal: Use symmetric marks and crossing arcs to make a right angle.

steps.title: Locate the given point on the line
steps.text: The point P lies on a straight line. We want a new line through P at ninety degrees to the original.
steps.why: The new perpendicular must pass through the stated point.
steps.math: new line through P, perpendicular to l
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="line" x1="90" y1="220" x2="680" y2="220" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="point" cx="380" cy="220" r="5" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text x="380" y="254" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#b96a12">P</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Mark equally far points on both sides
steps.text: With centre P, mark A and B on the line using the same compass radius. P is now the midpoint of AB.
steps.why: Equal distances either side create a segment centred on P.

steps.title: Cross equal arcs from the marks
steps.text: Draw matching arcs from A and B above the line to meet at Q. Keep the compass opening the same for those arcs.
steps.why: Q lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

steps.text: Draw PQ and extend it as required. Since P is the midpoint of AB, this is the perpendicular bisector and so makes a right angle.
steps.why: A line through two points on the perpendicular bisector is that bisector.

quiz.question: If P is midway between A and B, and Q is equally far from A and B, then PQ is…
quiz.hint: Both P and Q lie on the perpendicular bisector.
quiz.explanation: The line through them is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

quiz.question: A constructed perpendicular makes an angle of…
quiz.hint: Perpendicular means a right angle.
quiz.explanation: A right angle measures 90°.

lessons.takeaway: Create equal marks around the point, then use equal arcs to locate the perpendicular.
lessons.mistake: Placing A and B at unequal distances from P.

lessons.title: Drop a perpendicular from an outside point
lessons.goal: Construct the perpendicular through a point that is not on the given line.

steps.title: Begin with the line and the outside point
steps.text: A point P lies above a line. The required perpendicular must pass through P and meet the line at a right angle.
steps.why: We need to locate a direction, not guess the nearest point by eye.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="80" y1="270" x2="680" y2="270" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="given" cx="380" cy="90" r="5" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text x="380" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12">P</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Equal distances from A and B locate their perpendicular bisector.</text></svg>

steps.title: Cut the line in two places
steps.text: With centre P, draw an arc large enough to cross the line at A and B. The two distances from P are equal because the compass opening stays fixed.
steps.why: Two points on one circle are equally far from its centre.

steps.title: Locate a second equidistant point
steps.text: With equal openings centred at A and B, draw two crossing arcs on the other side of the line. Label their intersection Q.
steps.why: Both P and Q are equally far from A and B.

steps.title: Join the two equidistant points
steps.text: Draw PQ. It is the perpendicular bisector of AB, so it meets the original line at a right angle while passing through P.
steps.why: The perpendicular bisector is the line of points equally distant from the endpoints.
steps.math: PQ ⟂ AB, with P on PQ

quiz.question: Why must the first arc from P cross the line twice?
options: To locate A and B equally far from P
quiz.hint: Both crossings belong to the same circle centred at P.
quiz.explanation: The intersections create A and B with PA = PB, placing P on their perpendicular bisector.

quiz.question: After equal arcs from A and B meet at Q, which line gives the required perpendicular?
quiz.hint: Use both points that are equally far from A and B.
quiz.explanation: P and Q both lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so joining PQ gives the required perpendicular.

lessons.takeaway: One arc from the outside point, matching arcs from its two crossings, then join the outside point to the new intersection.
lessons.mistake: Joining the outside point to just one crossing instead of to the intersection of the equal arcs.

lessons.title: Construct a parallel through a point
lessons.goal: Build two perpendiculars to obtain parallel lines.

steps.title: Identify the line and the new point
steps.text: A point P lies away from a given line. We want a new line through P that never meets the original.
steps.why: The required parallel must pass through the specified point.
steps.math: new line through P, parallel to l
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="90" y1="300" x2="680" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="p" cx="380" cy="170" r="5" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text x="402" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12">P</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct a perpendicular connection
steps.text: Construct a line through P perpendicular to the given line, using equal-distance compass arcs. This is a helper line.
steps.why: A perpendicular gives a precise reference direction.
steps.math: m ⟂ l; P lies on m
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="90" y1="300" x2="680" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><circle id="p" cx="380" cy="170" r="5" fill="#b96a12" stroke="#b96a12" stroke-width="2"/><text x="402" y="164" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#b96a12">P</text><line id="perpendicular" x1="380" y1="45" x2="380" y2="335" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><path id="right1" d="M 380 300 L 397 300 L 397 283 L 380 283" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct another perpendicular at P
steps.text: On the helper line, mark equal distances above and below P. Crossing arcs from those marks locate a perpendicular to the helper.
steps.why: The point-on-line perpendicular construction can be used a second time.

steps.title: Explain why the result is parallel
steps.text: The original line and the new line are both perpendicular to the same helper line. Therefore they are parallel.
steps.why: In a plane, two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel.

quiz.question: Two distinct lines in the same plane are each perpendicular to the same line. They are…
quiz.hint: Both make the same right-angle direction.
quiz.explanation: Distinct lines perpendicular to the same line in a plane are parallel.

quiz.question: What must be checked after constructing a parallel through P?
options: It passes through P and has the correct direction
quiz.hint: Both the position and direction are part of the instruction.
quiz.explanation: A line parallel to the original but missing P does not satisfy the construction.

lessons.takeaway: A perpendicular to a perpendicular gives the parallel direction.
lessons.mistake: Drawing a parallel-looking line that misses the given point.

lessons.title: Divide a segment into equal parts
lessons.goal: Use equal auxiliary marks and parallel lines.

steps.title: Choose the required number of parts
steps.text: Divide segment AB into five equal parts. Start by drawing a sloping auxiliary ray from A.
steps.why: The auxiliary ray lets us make equal steps without dividing AB numerically.
steps.math: AB is to be divided into 5 equal parts

steps.title: Step off five equal compass lengths
steps.text: Mark five equal intervals along the auxiliary ray, starting at A. The compass opening stays constant throughout.
steps.why: Equal auxiliary steps will correspond to equal shares of AB.

steps.title: Join the final mark to B
steps.text: Draw the line from the fifth auxiliary mark to B. This sets the direction for all the parallel helper lines.
steps.why: A, B and the fifth mark now form a triangle whose side along the ray is already cut into five equal steps.

steps.why: Parallel lines cut the sides of a triangle proportionally.

quiz.question: To divide AB into seven equal parts by this method, how many equal steps are marked on the auxiliary ray?
quiz.hint: One step represents each required part.
quiz.explanation: Mark seven equal steps, join the seventh mark to B, then draw parallels through the earlier six.

quiz.question: Why must the helper lines be parallel?
quiz.hint: The similar-triangle relationship depends on parallelism.
quiz.explanation: Parallel lines create similar triangles, transferring equal auxiliary steps into equal segment divisions.

lessons.takeaway: Equal steps on a helper ray become equal parts on AB through parallels.
lessons.mistake: Using unequal compass steps or non-parallel connectors.

lessons.title: Construct a triangle from three sides
lessons.goal: Locate the third vertex by intersecting two distance circles.

steps.title: Draw one known side
steps.text: Construct a triangle with sides eight, five and seven centimetres. Draw AB equal to eight centimetres as the base.
steps.why: One known side fixes the distance between two vertices.
steps.math: AB = 8 cm; AC = 5 cm; BC = 7 cm

steps.title: Set the distance from A
steps.text: With centre A and radius five centimetres, draw an arc above the base. The third vertex must lie somewhere on this arc.
steps.why: Every point on the arc is five centimetres from A.

steps.title: Set the distance from B
steps.text: With centre B and radius seven centimetres, draw an arc to cross the first. Label the chosen intersection C.
steps.why: The intersection satisfies both distance requirements at once.

steps.title: Complete and verify
steps.text: Join AC and BC, leaving the arcs visible. Check the side lengths and remember that the two shorter lengths must sum to more than the longest.
steps.why: SSS fixes the triangle’s shape, up to a mirror image.

quiz.question: Can lengths 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm form a triangle?
quiz.hint: The two shorter sides must reach past the longest.
quiz.explanation: 2 + 3 = 5, which is less than 6, so they cannot close into a triangle.

quiz.question: In an SSS construction, the third vertex is located by…
options: The intersection of two compass arcs
Drawing a vertical line from the midpoint only
quiz.hint: It must satisfy two given distances simultaneously.
quiz.explanation: One arc fixes distance from A and another fixes distance from B. Their intersection locates C.

lessons.takeaway: Base first; then intersect the two distance arcs.
lessons.mistake: Using the same compass radius for both arcs when the two given sides differ.

lessons.title: Construct from two sides and their included angle
lessons.goal: Use SAS in the correct order.

steps.title: Identify the included angle
steps.text: Construct AB of six centimetres, AC of four centimetres and angle A of sixty degrees. The given angle lies between the two known sides.
steps.why: SAS requires the angle included by the stated side pair.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="200" y1="300" x2="560" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 6 cm</text><text x="180" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">A</text><text x="580" y="325" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="24" fill="#173349">B</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Draw the base and angle ray
steps.text: Draw AB to scale, then draw a ray from A making sixty degrees with AB. Use the required protractor or compass method.
steps.why: The ray fixes the direction of the second known side.
steps.math: draw ray AC at 60° to AB

steps.title: Locate the second side length
steps.text: Measure four centimetres from A along that ray, or use a compass arc of radius four centimetres. Mark the point C.
steps.why: Direction plus distance identifies the vertex.

steps.title: Join the final side
steps.text: Connect C to B. The known sides and included angle now determine the triangle; no guess for the third side was needed.
steps.why: SAS determines a unique shape, up to reflection.

quiz.question: In SAS, the given angle must be…
quiz.hint: Included means lying between the two given sides.
quiz.explanation: The included angle is formed by the two specified sides.

quiz.question: After drawing a given side and the included-angle ray, how is the third vertex fixed?
options: By the second given side length
quiz.hint: The vertex lies on the ray at a specified distance.
quiz.explanation: Mark the second side’s given length along the ray from the angle vertex.

lessons.takeaway: Known side → included-angle ray → second side length → close the triangle.
lessons.mistake: Putting the given angle at the wrong endpoint.

lessons.title: Construct from a side and two angles
lessons.goal: Locate a third vertex by intersecting two rays.

steps.title: Read the endpoint information
steps.text: Draw base AB of six centimetres. The angles at A and B are fifty and sixty degrees respectively.
steps.why: The stated angles are attached to particular endpoints.

steps.title: Draw the first angle ray
steps.text: At A, draw a ray making fifty degrees with AB on the chosen side of the base.
steps.why: The third vertex must lie on this ray.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="180" y1="305" x2="540" y2="305" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="360" y="342" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">AB = 6 cm</text><line id="ray-a" x1="180" y1="305" x2="393.26265556273717" y2="50.8434640669264" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><path id="angle-a" d="M 221.1384070199385 255.97315564038541 A 64 64 0 0 1 244.0 305.0" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text x="278" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="23" fill="#3175ba">50°</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Draw the second ray inward
steps.text: At B, measure sixty degrees from BA, on the same side of AB as the first ray. The two rays meet at C.
steps.why: Each ray enforces one angle condition; their intersection enforces both.
steps.math: ray from B at 60° to BA

steps.title: Check the remaining angle
steps.text: The third angle is seventy degrees because triangle angles total one hundred and eighty. This provides a construction check.
steps.why: The triangle angle sum supplies the missing angle.

quiz.question: A triangle has angles 42° and 68°. Its third angle is…
quiz.hint: Subtract both known angles from 180°.

quiz.question: At endpoint B, the inside angle must be measured from…
options: The ray BA pointing towards A
quiz.hint: The triangle’s base side from B is BA.
quiz.explanation: Measure from BA into the triangle; using the outward continuation gives an exterior angle instead.

lessons.takeaway: Draw both interior-angle rays from the correct ends of the base.
lessons.mistake: Measuring the angle from the outward continuation of the base.

lessons.title: Construct a right-angled triangle from RHS
lessons.goal: Use the right angle, hypotenuse and one shorter side.

steps.title: Separate the hypotenuse from the given perpendicular side
steps.text: The triangle has a right angle at A, side AB of eight centimetres and hypotenuse BC of ten centimetres.
steps.why: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, so it is BC.

steps.title: Construct the right-angle ray
steps.text: Draw AB and construct a perpendicular through A. The third vertex C must lie on that perpendicular.
steps.why: The perpendicular guarantees the required right angle.

steps.title: Use the hypotenuse as a compass radius
steps.text: With centre B and radius ten centimetres, draw an arc to meet the perpendicular. Its intersection is C.
steps.why: Every point on that arc is the required hypotenuse distance from B.

steps.title: Join and check with Pythagoras
steps.text: Join B to C. The remaining side is six centimetres, since ten squared minus eight squared is thirty-six.
steps.why: Pythagoras checks a construction whose defining data were RHS.

quiz.question: In an RHS construction, the compass radius from the far endpoint of the known perpendicular side is…
quiz.hint: The third vertex must be a hypotenuse length away.
quiz.explanation: The arc centred at that endpoint uses the known hypotenuse length.

quiz.question: Can a right-angled triangle have hypotenuse 5 cm and another side 7 cm?
options: No, the hypotenuse must be longest
quiz.hint: Check the longest side before constructing.
quiz.explanation: A hypotenuse of 5 cm cannot be shorter than a perpendicular side of 7 cm.

lessons.takeaway: Known perpendicular side → perpendicular → hypotenuse arc → connect.
lessons.mistake: Using a shorter side as the hypotenuse arc radius.

lessons.title: Construct a rectangle
lessons.goal: Use equal heights on perpendiculars and check parallel sides.

steps.title: Draw the chosen base
steps.text: Construct a rectangle eight centimetres long and four centimetres wide. Draw the eight-centimetre base AB.
steps.why: A rectangle has four right angles and equal opposite sides.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="190" y1="300" x2="570" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">8 cm</text><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Construct perpendiculars at both ends
steps.text: Through A and B, construct perpendicular rays on the same side of AB.
steps.why: The two perpendiculars will be parallel to each other.
steps.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 400" role="img"><rect x="0" y="0" width="760" height="400" rx="0" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#ffffff" stroke-width="2"/><line id="base" x1="190" y1="300" x2="570" y2="300" stroke="#173349" stroke-width="3"/><text x="380" y="337" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="25" fill="#173349">8 cm</text><line id="left-ray" x1="190" y1="300" x2="190" y2="65" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><line id="right-ray" x1="570" y1="300" x2="570" y2="65" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="3"/><path id="rights" d="M 190 280 L 210 280 L 210 300 M 550 300 L 550 280 L 570 280" fill="none" stroke="#3175ba" stroke-width="2"/><text id="caption" x="380" y="383" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Segoe UI,Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#8ca1af">Leave construction arcs visible: they show how the result was obtained.</text></svg>

steps.title: Mark equal widths
steps.text: Mark D four centimetres from A and C four centimetres from B along those rays. Use a fixed compass opening to transfer the same length.
steps.why: Equal heights keep the top edge parallel to the base.

steps.title: Join the final side and check
steps.text: Connect D to C. Check the right angles, equal opposite sides and equal diagonals; do not assume a tilted quadrilateral is a rectangle just from appearance.
steps.why: The constructed perpendicular sides and equal widths establish the rectangle.
steps.math: AB ∥ DC; AD ∥ BC; AC = BD
