quiz.question: A rectangle’s diagonals are…
options: Always equal to its shorter side
quiz.hint: This holds for every rectangle, not only a square.
quiz.explanation: Both diagonals have length √(length² + width²), so they are equal.

quiz.question: A rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm. Its perimeter is…
quiz.hint: Add all four side lengths.

lessons.takeaway: Two perpendiculars, equal widths, then connect and verify.
lessons.mistake: Drawing the second perpendicular on the opposite side of the base.

reference.name: Translation
reference.note: Every point moves by the same vector (a,b).

reference.name: Axial symmetry (reflection) in the axes
reference.note: Each point and its image are equally far from the mirror line.

reference.name: Central symmetry
reference.note: A half-turn; the centre is the midpoint of every point–image pair.

reference.name: Rotation about origin
reference.note: State centre, angle and direction.

reference.name: Construct a bisector
reference.formula: Equal-radius arcs locate equally distant points
reference.note: Do not change the compass opening between matched arcs.

reference.name: Triangle data
reference.note: RHS uses a right angle, hypotenuse and one other side.

toolkit.strategy: For a transformation, track named corresponding points and specify every parameter. For a construction, start from the exact givens, use the instrument sequence, leave arcs visible and justify the resulting relationships.

methods.title: Translate a point, segment or triangle
methods.when: Every corresponding point makes the same displacement.
methods.rule: Vector (a,b): (x,y)↦(x+a,y+b); image−original=(a,b) for every vertex.
steps: Find horizontal and vertical changes from one pair.
Apply the same vector to every other endpoint or vertex.
Join image vertices in their original order.
methods.example: Translation (4,−2) maps (−1,3) to (3,1) and (2,5) to (6,3).
methods.check: Differences between image endpoints equal those between original endpoints.
methods.trap: Finding a vector from one vertex but using a different one for another.

methods.title: Reflect in a specified line
methods.when: Points lie on opposite sides of one candidate mirror line.
methods.rule: In x=a: (x,y)↦(2a−x,y); in y=b: (x,y)↦(x,2b−y); in y=x: (y,x); in y=−x: (−y,−x).
steps: For each non-fixed pair, locate its midpoint.
Check the proposed mirror passes through every midpoint at right angles to each joining segment.
Keep points on the mirror fixed.
methods.example: Reflection in x=2 maps (5,1) to (−1,1).
methods.check: The midpoint is (2,1) and the joining segment is horizontal.
methods.trap: Accepting a mirror that works for one pair but fails for the remaining vertices.

methods.title: Central and axial symmetry
methods.when: A shape is claimed to match itself after a half-turn or a reflection.
methods.rule: Central symmetry about (h,k): (x,y)↦(2h−x,2k−y). Axial symmetry means reflection in a line maps the entire shape to itself.
steps: Test all defining vertices or boundary features.
For central symmetry, check the centre is the midpoint of every paired point.
For axial symmetry, check one common perpendicular-bisector line.
methods.example: Every parallelogram has central symmetry at its diagonal midpoint; a general slanted parallelogram need not have any mirror axis.
methods.check: In a parallelogram that is neither a rectangle nor a rhombus, no single line is the perpendicular bisector of every vertex–partner segment, so it has no axis.
methods.trap: Treating central symmetry as reflection in an arbitrary line through the centre.

methods.title: Rotate with complete information
methods.when: A shape turns around a fixed centre.
methods.rule: About origin: 90° anticlockwise (−y,x), 90° clockwise (y,−x), 180° (−x,−y). About (h,k), translate to the origin, rotate, then translate back.
steps: State the centre, turn angle and direction.
Measure the original centre-to-point distance and preserve it.
Apply the same turn to every point.
For 180°, use the centre as the midpoint of each pair.
methods.example: About (2,1), a 90° anticlockwise turn sends (5,1) to (2,4).
methods.check: Both points are 3 units from (2,1), and their directions differ by 90°.
methods.trap: Giving only “a rotation” or rotating around the wrong centre.

methods.title: Describe and distinguish full transformations
methods.when: One shape or ordered vertex list must map onto another.
methods.rule: Translation needs a vector; reflection needs a mirror line; rotation needs centre, angle and direction. An ordered mapping fixes the vertex correspondence.
steps: Write at least two named point correspondences.
Test each proposed transformation on all vertices.
Give every defining parameter.
If several transformations map one point, use the rest of the shape to distinguish them.
methods.example: A→C and B→D in a parallelogram are achieved by a half-turn about the intersection of the diagonals.
methods.check: The same centre must bisect both AC and BD.
methods.trap: Calling a point match enough evidence for a whole-shape mapping.

methods.title: Perpendicular bisector of a segment
methods.when: You need a midpoint and a perpendicular, or points equally far from A and B.
methods.rule: Use equal radius r>AB/2 from A and B; joining the two intersections gives the perpendicular bisector.
steps: Open the compass more than halfway across AB.
Draw arcs above and below the segment from A.
Without changing the opening, draw arcs from B to meet them at P and Q.
Use a straightedge to draw PQ; its crossing M with AB is the midpoint.
methods.example: For AB=8 cm, a radius 5 cm works; the bisector crosses 4 cm from either endpoint.
methods.check: PA=PB and QA=QB; SSS congruence gives equal halves and right angles at M.
methods.trap: Changing the compass opening between A and B.

methods.title: Bisect a given angle
methods.when: Split an existing angle into two equal angles.
methods.rule: From vertex V mark VA=VB; find P with PA=PB using equal arcs; ray VP bisects ∠AVB.
steps: With centre V, draw one arc crossing both rays at A and B.
From A and B draw equal-radius arcs meeting inside the angle at P.
Join V to P with a straightedge.
Leave both sets of arcs visible.
methods.example: Bisecting a given 70° angle produces 35° and 35°; bisecting one half again gives 17.5°.
methods.check: Triangles VAP and VBP have VA=VB, AP=BP and common VP, so SSS gives equal vertex angles.
methods.trap: Joining A to B instead of V to P.

methods.title: Perpendicular at a point on a line
methods.when: A right angle is required at a specified point P on a line.
methods.rule: Mark PA=PB on opposite sides; a point Q with QA=QB gives PQ perpendicular to AB.
steps: Use the compass centred at P to mark A and B on the line.
With equal openings from A and B, draw crossing arcs at Q off the line.
Join P to Q.
methods.example: If PA=PB=3 cm, equal arcs of radius 4 cm meet off the line and locate Q.
methods.check: P and Q both lie on AB’s perpendicular bisector.
methods.trap: Placing A and B at unequal distances from P.

methods.title: Perpendicular from a point off a line
methods.when: The required perpendicular must pass through an outside point P.
methods.rule: One circle centred at P cuts the line at A,B with PA=PB; a second equal-distance point Q fixes their bisector PQ.
steps: Draw a sufficiently large arc centred at P to cut the line twice at A and B.
From A and B draw equal-radius arcs meeting at Q on the opposite side of the line from P.
Draw PQ with a straightedge.
Mark its intersection with the line as the perpendicular foot.
methods.example: Equal distances PA=PB and QA=QB force PQ to be the perpendicular bisector of AB.
methods.check: Verify the foot lies on the original line and PQ passes through P.
methods.trap: Drawing from P to just one crossing A instead of the matching-arc intersection.

methods.title: Parallel through a given outside point
methods.when: A new line through P must be parallel to a given line l.
methods.rule: Two distinct lines in the same plane perpendicular to the same line are parallel.
steps: Construct a perpendicular m through P to l using the off-line construction.
At P on m, construct a perpendicular n to m using equal marks and crossing arcs.
Draw and label n through P.
methods.example: l⊥m and n⊥m give l∥n.
methods.check: Check both position (through P) and direction (two right angles).
methods.trap: Drawing a parallel-looking line that misses the specified point.

methods.title: Divide a segment into equal parts
methods.when: Split AB into n equal lengths without estimating divisions.
methods.rule: Equal steps on an auxiliary ray transfer to equal parts of AB through parallel lines; n is a positive integer.
steps: Draw an auxiliary ray from A at a convenient angle to AB.
Step off n equal compass lengths along it, ending at Cₙ.
Join Cₙ to B.
Through each earlier mark, construct a parallel to CₙB; use two perpendiculars if needed.
Their intersections with AB give the required division points.
methods.example: For six parts, make six auxiliary steps and five earlier parallel connectors.
methods.check: Similar triangles give each division point k/n of the way along AB.
methods.trap: Using n−1 auxiliary steps for n required parts.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from SSS
methods.when: All three side lengths are supplied.
methods.rule: Each side must be positive; the two shorter lengths must sum to more than the longest.
steps: Draw one given side AB with a ruler.
With centre A and radius AC, draw an arc.
With centre B and radius BC, draw an intersecting arc.
Choose the required-side intersection C and join AC and BC.
methods.example: AB=7, AC=5, BC=6 cm is possible; the arcs locate C above or below AB.
methods.check: Every constructed side matches its specified compass distance.
methods.trap: Using one radius for both arcs when AC and BC differ.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from SAS
methods.when: Two sides and their included angle are supplied.
methods.rule: The angle lies between the two known sides; lengths>0 and 0°<included angle<180°.
steps: Draw the first known side from the angle vertex.
At that vertex, construct or measure the given angle ray as instructed.
Mark the second known side length along that ray using ruler or compass.
Join the two remaining endpoints.
methods.example: AB=6, AC=4, ∠BAC=50°: draw AB, a 50° ray at A, then mark C 4 cm from A.
methods.check: Check the angle is at the common endpoint of the two given sides.
methods.trap: Placing the supplied angle opposite one given side instead of between them.

methods.title: Construct a triangle from ASA
methods.when: A side and the angles at its endpoints are given.
methods.rule: For endpoint angles α,β>0, require α+β<180°; the third angle is 180°−α−β.
steps: Draw the given side AB.
At A draw the α ray from AB.
At B draw the β ray from BA into the same chosen side of AB.
Their intersection is C; join and label.
methods.check: The three interior angles total 180°.
methods.trap: Measuring B’s angle from the outward continuation rather than BA.

methods.title: Construct a right-angled triangle from RHS
methods.when: A right angle, hypotenuse and one perpendicular side are given.
methods.rule: Hypotenuse h must exceed the given perpendicular side a>0; the other perpendicular side is √(h²−a²).
steps: Draw the given perpendicular side AB.
Construct the required perpendicular at the right-angle endpoint A.
Centre the compass at B with radius equal to the hypotenuse.
Where that arc meets the perpendicular is C; join BC.
methods.example: AB=5, BC=13 cm and right angle at A give AC=12 cm.
methods.check: 5²+12²=13² checks the finished triangle.
methods.trap: Centring the hypotenuse arc at the right-angle vertex.

methods.title: Construct a rectangle and check its diagonal
methods.when: Length and width, or one side and a diagonal, define a rectangle.
methods.rule: Opposite sides equal and parallel; all angles 90°; diagonal²=length²+width².
steps: Draw the known base AB.
Construct perpendiculars at A and B on the same side.
For a known width, transfer it equally to both perpendiculars; for diagonal AC, locate C by an arc centred at A.
Through C construct a parallel to AB, meeting the A-perpendicular at D.
Check the four right angles, equal opposite sides and equal diagonals.
methods.example: Base 9 cm and diagonal 15 cm give width 12 cm by Pythagoras.
methods.check: 9²+12²=15² and the opposite sides agree.
methods.trap: Using the diagonal as the rectangle’s width.

checks: Name a translation’s vector, a reflection’s mirror line, or a rotation’s centre, angle and direction.
A mapping of one point does not prove the same transformation maps the whole shape.
Preserve required compass openings; leave construction arcs visible.
Check triangle existence and positive lengths before constructing.
Use exact coordinate or congruence checks alongside the drawing; appearance alone is not proof.

challenges.title: Construct two bisectors and verify a distance
challenges.question: Draw an angle BAC of 110° using a protractor, then put the protractor aside. (a) Construct its bisector with ruler and compass, leaving arcs visible. (b) Bisect the angle between AB and the first bisector again. State all resulting angle sizes from AB. (c) Mark P on the first bisector with AP=6 cm. Drop perpendiculars PF and PG to the two original arms. Explain why PF=PG. (d) Find that common distance to the nearest 0.01 cm.
hints: Use equal marks from A, then equal crossing arcs from those marks.
For the distance, each right-angled triangle has hypotenuse AP=6 and angle at A equal to 55°.

solution.title: Construct the first bisector
solution.math: From A mark equal-radius intersections U,V on the arms; equal arcs from U,V meet at Q; draw AQ.
solution.reason: AU=AV, UQ=VQ and common AQ give SSS, so each angle at A is 55°.

solution.title: Bisect again
solution.math: Repeat the compass construction inside ∠BAQ: the new ray is 27.5° from AB; AQ is 55° from AB; AC is 110° from AB.
solution.reason: An angle bisector halves the angle to which it is applied.

solution.title: Justify equal distances
solution.math: Right-angled triangles APF and APG have common hypotenuse AP and equal acute angle 55° at A. Their other acute angles are both 35°, so ASA gives congruence.
solution.reason: The shared side AP lies between the two equal acute angles; hence PF=PG.

solution.title: Calculate the distance
solution.reason: The perpendicular distance is opposite the 55° angle in either right-angled triangle.

challenges.answer: (a) First bisector at 55°. (b) Second ray at 27.5° from AB; first at 55°, original second arm at 110°. (c) Congruent right-angled triangles give PF=PG. (d) Both distances≈4.91 cm.
challenges.check: The adjacent lengths AF and AG both equal 6cos55°; each right-angled triangle satisfies (6sin55°)²+(6cos55°)²=36.

challenges.title: An outside point and a verified perpendicular
challenges.question: Draw AB=8 cm. Using arcs of radius 5 cm centred at A and B, construct their intersection P above AB and join AP and BP. (a) Construct a perpendicular from P to the line AB using an arc from P and matching arcs from its two crossings; do not simply estimate a midpoint. Call the foot M. (b) Explain why M is the midpoint of AB. (c) Find PM exactly. (d) State two independent checks on the drawing.
hints: The original construction ensures PA=PB. A second point equally far from A and B locates the perpendicular bisector.
Once AM is known, use Pythagoras in the right-angled triangle APM.

solution.title: Construct the perpendicular
solution.math: Centre an arc at P to cross AB in U,V. Draw equal arcs from U,V meeting at Q on the opposite side, then draw PQ; let M=PQ∩AB.
solution.reason: P and Q are equally far from U,V, so PQ is their perpendicular bisector.

solution.title: Use the original equal distances
solution.math: PA=PB=5 cm; P lies on AB’s perpendicular bisector. The perpendicular through P is unique, so AM=MB=4 cm.
solution.reason: The constructed perpendicular must be the same perpendicular-bisector line.

solution.title: Find the height
solution.reason: Triangle APM is right-angled at M.

solution.title: Check independently
solution.reason: Distance and right-angle checks test different parts of the construction.

challenges.answer: (a) Construction route above. (b) M is the midpoint, with AM=MB=4 cm. (c) PM=3 cm. (d) For example equal 5 cm sloping sides and a right angle at M.
challenges.check: Both right-angled triangles have sides 3,4,5; their combined base is 8 cm as required.

challenges.title: Which transformation maps the whole shape?
challenges.question: Parallelogram ABCD has A=(0,0), B=(6,0), D=(2,4) and C=(8,4). (a) Describe completely a translation mapping the ordered segment AD to BC. (b) Describe completely a rotation mapping triangle ABD to triangle CDB, in that order. (c) Could one reflection map A→B and D→C simultaneously? Prove your answer using the candidate mirror lines. (d) Under the rotation in (b), find the image of E=(1,1).
hints: Check at least two corresponding pairs rather than one point alone.
The mirror for A→B must perpendicularly bisect AB; compare it with the mirror required for D→C.

solution.title: Find the translation
solution.reason: Both endpoints make the same displacement.

solution.title: Find the half-turn centre
solution.math: Midpoint of AC=(4,2); midpoint of BD=(4,2). A 180° rotation about (4,2) maps A→C, B→D, D→B.
solution.reason: A half-turn exchanges each pair whose midpoint is the centre; clockwise and anticlockwise are identical at 180°.

solution.title: Test a reflection on both pairs
solution.math: A→B requires mirror x=3; D→C requires mirror x=5
solution.reason: One reflection cannot have two different mirror lines, so none gives those named correspondences.

solution.title: Apply the complete rotation
solution.reason: The centre is the midpoint of E and its image.

challenges.answer: (a) Translation vector (6,0). (b) 180° about (4,2), either direction. (c) No: required mirrors are x=3 and x=5. (d) E′=(7,3).
challenges.check: Midpoint of (1,1) and (7,3) is (4,2), and the vectors from that centre are opposites.

challenges.title: Build a rectangle, divide and rotate
challenges.question: Construct rectangle ABCD in cyclic order with AB=6 cm and diagonal AC=10 cm, choosing C above AB. (a) Give and carry out a ruler-and-compass construction from these data, leaving arcs. (b) Calculate BC exactly as a check. (c) Divide AB into three equal parts by an auxiliary ray and parallels; call the division point nearer A, E. (d) Let O be the rectangle’s diagonal intersection. A 180° rotation about O sends E to E′. Locate E′ precisely on side DC, stating its distances from D and C.
hints: Construct the perpendicular at B, then use an arc centred at A with radius 10 cm to find C.
For part (d), you may use coordinates A=(0,0), B=(6,0), with the calculated height.

solution.title: Construct the rectangle
solution.math: Draw AB=6. Construct a perpendicular at B. An arc centred at A, radius 10, meets it above AB at C. Construct a parallel to AB through C and a perpendicular to AB through A; their intersection is D.
solution.reason: The arc enforces AC=10; the perpendicular and parallel directions create a rectangle.

solution.title: Check the missing side
solution.reason: ABC is a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse AC.

solution.title: Divide the base accurately
solution.math: From A draw an auxiliary ray; step off three equal compass lengths U₁,U₂,U₃. Join U₃B and construct parallels through U₁,U₂ to meet AB. AE=2 cm.
solution.reason: Equal auxiliary steps transfer by similar triangles to equal thirds of AB.

solution.title: Apply the half-turn
solution.reason: A half-turn sends (x,y) to (6−x,8−y).

solution.title: State the location on the requested side
solution.reason: The image lies on DC and keeps the corresponding endpoint distance.

challenges.answer: (a) Construction route above. (b) BC=8 cm. (c) AE=2 cm. (d) E′ lies on DC, 4 cm from D and 2 cm from C.
challenges.check: The rectangle has diagonal √(6²+8²)=10. O is the midpoint of E=(2,0) and E′=(4,8), verifying the rotation.
